articles.title: When someone offends me

statement.t: Whoever wrongs me does it against their will and cannot harm me, and I teach them or bear with them.

parts.words: Whoever wrongs me
does it against their will
cannot harm me
I teach them or bear with them

statement.kind: Grounds, a practice and the answer they lead to
statement.form: Claims 1 to 3 are the grounds: why people do wrong, why it cannot harm me, and that the gods are kind to them as well. Claims 4 and 5 say what I do, and claim 6 is the exercise of looking into them and into myself. Claim 7 is what failing looks like, and claim 8 what holds if there was no wrong at all.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claims 2, 5 and 6 gain a second author. The practice gains a habit of reading words and looks generously, and the side of failing gains three things: going on giving after ingratitude, that how far anger goes depends on the soul a provocation reaches, and not copying bad people because they are many. He challenges claim 1, holding that people know what evil is and do not care, and claim 2, holding that the least part of a wrong does reach the one wronged; he limits claim 4 to those willing to listen.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, except that two of its grounds are disputed: he holds that people who do wrong know what evil is and are indifferent to it, and that the least part of a wrong reaches the one it is done to. It gains a habit for doubtful cases, leaning toward the better reading, and he would teach only those willing to listen.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Allow any man who so desires to insult you and work you wrong; but if only virtue dwells with you, you will suffer nothing.
piece.follows: Whoever insults or wrongs me, I suffer nothing so long as virtue dwells in me.
piece.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: Seneca quotes Socrates, who put the highest wisdom in telling good from evil. “You” is anyone following his rules; the wrong is insult and injury from others.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let her strip off your faults, rather than assist you to decry the faults of others.
piece.follows: Philosophy should strip away my own faults, not help me condemn other people’s.
piece.context: Letter 103, on the dangers of mixing with people, closes by warning against vaunting philosophy. “Her” is philosophy, which is to be used on my own faults.
gives: turn to myself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: If you wish to be happy, if you would be in good faith a good man, let one person or another despise you.
piece.follows: To be happy and truly good, I should let this person or that despise me.
piece.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: Seneca quotes Socrates on being happy and good, letting others insult you, think you a fool and despise you. “You” is the one following his rules.
gives: If someone despises me
that is for them to see to

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: one should listen in an unruffled spirit to the railings of the ignorant; when one is marching toward the goal of honour, one should scorn scorn itself.
piece.follows: I should hear the mockery of the ignorant calmly and, on the way to what is honourable, disregard their contempt.
piece.context: Letter 76, on learning wisdom in old age: the crowd mocks the few who attend lectures on how to be a good man as idlers. “The railings of the ignorant” are that mockery.
gives: I do not need their good opinion

items.label: practice
items.t: I do not put a wrong construction on a word or a look; I read what happens generously, and in a doubtful case I lean toward the better reading. The wrongs done to me I forget, and on purpose.
items.why: Marcus asks whether it was a wrong at all (claim 8), looks into the person who did it (claim 6), and in 6.19 says to overlook many things. Seneca adds two habits: deliberate forgetting of wrongs, and reading a doubtful word or look toward the better interpretation. Article 28 adds the same habit from the same letter.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: He will not misinterpret a word or a look; he makes light of all mishaps by interpreting them in a generous way.
support.follows: The wise man does not misread a word or a look, and he makes light of mishaps by reading them generously.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca’s portrait of the wise man weighing a person’s kindnesses against their injuries. “He” is the wise man; the words and looks are other people’s.
gives: I do not put a wrong construction on a word or a look
I read what happens generously

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the spirit of kindliness always tries to bend every doubtful case toward the better interpretation
support.follows: Kindliness always tries to turn every doubtful case toward the better reading.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: weighing a person’s good deeds against their bad, as a tied vote acquits a defendant, kindliness settles a doubtful case in that person’s favour.
gives: in a doubtful case I lean toward the better reading

support.author: seneca
support.quote: He despises the wrongs done him; he forgets them, not accidentally, but voluntarily.
support.follows: The wise man disregards the wrongs done to him and forgets them deliberately.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: unlike evil men, the wise man keeps a lasting joy from benefits received. “He” is the wise man; “them” are the wrongs done to him.
gives: The wrongs done to me I forget, and on purpose

items.label: breaks
items.t: When someone proves ungrateful, I do not stop doing good. It is better to get no return than to confer no benefits; after a poor crop, one sows again.
items.why: 9.43 says that if I blame someone as ungrateful, the mistake was mine for looking for a return, and that the good done is complete in itself. Marcus does not say that I go on giving to the one who proved ungrateful; Seneca says to sow again.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is better, however, to get no return than to confer no benefits. Even after a poor crop one should sow again
support.follows: Getting nothing back is better than giving nothing, and after a bad harvest one sows again.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Lucilius complains of an ungrateful person, and Seneca answers that caution would only make him ungenerous. The “benefits” are favours done for others.
gives: It is better to get no return than to confer no benefits
after a poor crop, one sows again

items.label: breaks
items.t: What matters is not how great the provocation is but what kind of soul it reaches. Great anger ends in madness, so I avoid anger, to keep my mind healthy.
items.why: Marcus calls anger weakness and against nature (claim 7). Seneca adds that the state of the soul, not the size of the offence, decides how far anger goes, and that great anger ends in madness.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And it makes no difference how important the provocation may be, but into what kind of soul it penetrates.
support.follows: The size of the provocation makes no difference; what decides is the kind of soul it reaches.
support.context: Letter 18, on festivals and fasting, ends on anger: “it” is the provocation, which, like a flame, does little to solid timber and sets dry stuff ablaze.
gives: What matters is not how great the provocation is but what kind of soul it reaches

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the outcome of a mighty anger is madness, and hence anger should be avoided, not merely that we may escape excess, but that we may have a healthy mind.
support.follows: Great anger ends in madness, so anger should be avoided for the sake of a healthy mind.
support.context: Letter 18, on festivals and fasting: the end of Seneca’s comparison of anger with fire, where what burns depends on what the flame falls upon.
gives: Great anger ends in madness
I avoid anger, to keep my mind healthy

items.label: breaks
items.t: I do not copy bad people because there are many of them.
items.why: Marcus warns against hating them (1.15, 6.19) and against feeling toward the inhuman what they feel (7.36). Seneca names the other way to fail among bad people: copying them because they are many. The other half of his sentence, not hating the many, is already Seneca’s addition to Article 1.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: you should not copy the bad simply because they are many
support.follows: I should not imitate bad people just because there are many of them.
support.context: Letter 7, on crowds: the world’s vices rub off on us, so that we either imitate it or loathe it, and Seneca rejects both. “The bad” are that crowd.
gives: I do not copy bad people because there are many of them

items.t: Seneca disagrees that people do wrong out of ignorance. Men, he says, are not ignorant of what evil is but indifferent to it, and each enjoys his own crimes; the proof is that all of them hide their sins. He grants that an idea of good conduct remains even in depraved souls, and elsewhere he says that all men suffer from ignorance of the truth (Ep. 118.7), so he is not consistent on this.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: but on the other hand every man enjoys his own crimes.
support.follows: Unlike a craftsman who regrets his failures, everyone enjoys his own crimes.
support.context: Letter 97, on the degeneracy of the age: the pilot, the physician and the orator are not glad of failure, but each man delights in his own wrongdoing.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: there is an idea of good conduct present subconsciously in souls which have been led even into the most depraved ways, and that men are not ignorant of what evil is but indifferent
support.follows: Even depraved people keep some idea of good conduct; they know what evil is and do not care.
support.context: Letter 97, on the degeneracy of the age: the proof follows at once, that all men hide their sins. “Men” are wrongdoers, who show by hiding it that they know it is evil.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Now all men suffer from ignorance of the truth; deceived by common report, they make for these ends as if they were good
support.follows: Misled by common opinion, everyone pursues certain things as good without knowing the truth about them.
support.context: Letter 118, on the vanity of place-seeking: “these ends” are riches, honours and power, which men chase as goods and later find evil or empty.

items.t: Seneca limits the teaching to those willing to listen. One must not talk to a man who is unwilling to hear; wisdom chooses those who will make progress and withdraws from the hopeless, though not too soon. This narrows the claim and does not contradict it. He is not consistent: to readers who resent his remedies he says he will speak words that help men even against their will (Ep. 89.19).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: for one must not talk to a man unless he is willing to listen.
support.follows: Advice should be given only to someone willing to hear it.
support.context: Letter 29, on Marcellinus, who avoids Seneca for fear of hearing the truth. The “man” is anyone being advised; Seneca goes on to question the Cynics, who advised everyone.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: choosing only those who will make progress, but withdrawing from those whom it has come to regard as hopeless,—yet not abandoning them too soon
support.follows: Wisdom should advise those who will make progress and withdraw from the hopeless, but not give up on them too early.
support.context: Letter 29, on whether to advise everyone: “it” is wisdom, which Seneca calls an art that aims its advice instead of scattering it by the handful.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall utter words that will help men even against their will.
support.follows: Seneca will say what helps people even when they do not want to hear it.
support.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy, ends with Seneca turning on readers who resent his remedies for their vices and saying he will keep on talking.

items.t: Seneca agrees that the worst of a wrong stays with the one who does it, and quotes Attalus: evil drinks the largest portion of its own poison. But he does not say that none of it reaches the other person: the least and lightest portion flows back on the one wronged (Ep. 81.22). Marcus says the one wronged is not harmed at all. Article 28 reads the same letter the same way. He is not consistent on this point: in Ep. 71.7, quoted here as backing claim 2, he gives Socrates’s word that whoever has virtue suffers nothing from those who wrong him.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When we do wrong, only the least and lightest portion of it flows back upon our neighbour; the worst and, if I may use the term, the densest portion of it stays at home and troubles the owner.
support.follows: Of a wrong we do, only the least part falls on our neighbour; the worst part stays with us and troubles us.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca says to avoid ingratitude for our own sake. “It” is the wrong we do; the “neighbour” is the one it is done to.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Evil herself drinks the largest portion of her own poison.
support.follows: Wickedness harms the one who has it more than it harms anyone else.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca quotes his teacher Attalus. “Evil” is the wrongdoer’s own wickedness, whose poison stays mostly with its owner.

amend.t: ; yet people do not do wrong in ignorance: they know what evil is and are indifferent to it, and each enjoys his own crimes
; but I teach only someone willing to listen, and I withdraw from the hopeless, though not too soon
; and in a doubtful case I lean toward the better reading
; yet the least and lightest part of a wrong does reach the one it is done to

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: Socrates, who recalled the whole of philosophy to rules of conduct, and asserted that the highest wisdom consisted in distinguishing between good and evil, said: “Follow these rules, if my words carry weight with you, in order that you may be happy; and let some men think you even a fool. Allow any man who so desires to insult you and work you wrong; but if only virtue dwells with you, you will suffer nothing. If you wish to be happy, if you would be in good faith a good man, let one person or another despise you.” No man can accomplish this unless he has come to regard all goods as equal, for the reason that no good exists without that which is honourable, and that which is honourable is in every case equal.

passages.title: On the dangers of association with our fellow-men [ 1 ]
passages.text: But this very philosophy must never be vaunted by you; for philosophy when employed with insolence and arrogance has been perilous to many. Let her strip off your faults, rather than assist you to decry the faults of others. Let her not hold aloof from the customs of mankind, nor make it her business to condemn whatever she herself does not do. A man may be wise without parade and without arousing enmity. Farewell.

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: But I am ashamed of mankind, as often as I enter the lecture-hall. On my way to the house of Metronax I am compelled to go, as you know, right past the Neapolitan Theatre. The building is jammed; men are deciding, with tremendous zeal, who is entitled to be called a good flute-player; even the Greek piper and the herald draw their crowds. But in the other place, where the question discussed is: “What is a good man?” and the lesson which we learn is “How to be a good man,” very few are in attendance, and the majority think that even these few are engaged in no good business; they have the name of being empty-headed idlers. I hope I may be blessed with that kind of mockery; for one should listen in an unruffled spirit to the railings of the ignorant; when one is marching toward the goal of honour, one should scorn scorn itself.

passages.title: On benefits. [ 1 ]
passages.text: He does not put a wrong construction upon everything, or seek for someone whom he may hold responsible for each happening; he rather ascribes even the sins of men to chance. He will not misinterpret a word or a look; he makes light of all mishaps by interpreting them in a generous way. He does not remember an injury rather than a service. As far as possible, he lets his memory rest upon the earlier and the better deed, never changing his attitude towards those who have deserved well of him, except in cases where the bad deeds far outdistance the good, and the space between them is obvious even to one who closes his eyes to it; even then only to this extent, that he strives, after receiving the preponderant injury, to resume the attitude which he held before he received the benefit. For when the injury merely equals the benefit, a certain amount of kindly feeling is left over.

passages.title: On benefits. [ 1 ]
passages.text: Just as a defendant is acquitted when the votes are equal, and just as the spirit of kindliness always tries to bend every doubtful case toward the better interpretation, so the mind of the wise man, when another’s merits merely equal his bad deeds, will, to be sure, cease to feel an obligation, but does not cease to desire to feel it, and acts precisely like the man who pays his debts even after they have been legally cancelled.

passages.title: On benefits. [ 1 ]
passages.text: Evil men have but one pleasure in benefits, and a very short-lived pleasure at that; it lasts only while they are receiving them. But the wise man derives therefrom an abiding and eternal joy. For he takes delight not so much in receiving the gift as in having received it; and this joy never perishes; it abides with him always. He despises the wrongs done him; he forgets them, not accidentally, but voluntarily.

passages.title: On benefits. [ 1 ]
passages.text: You complain that you have met with an ungrateful person. If this is your first experience of that sort, you should offer thanks either to your good luck or to your caution. In this case, however, caution can effect nothing but to make you ungenerous. For if you wish to avoid such a danger, you will not confer benefits; and so, that benefits may not be lost with another man, they will be lost to yourself. It is better, however, to get no return than to confer no benefits. Even after a poor crop one should sow again; for often losses due to continued barrenness of an unproductive soil have been made good by one year's fertility.

passages.title: On festivals and fasting
passages.text: But indeed this emotion blazes out against all sorts of persons; it springs from love as much as from hate, and shows itself not less in serious matters than in jest and sport. And it makes no difference how important the provocation may be, but into what kind of soul it penetrates. Similarly with fire; it does not matter how great is the flame, but what it falls upon. For solid timbers have repelled a very great fire; conversely, dry and easily inflammable stuff nourishes the slightest spark into a conflagration. So it is with anger, my dear Lucilius; the outcome of a mighty anger is madness, and hence anger should be avoided, not merely that we may escape excess, but that we may have a healthy mind. Farewell.

passages.title: On crowds
passages.text: But both courses are to be avoided; you should not copy the bad simply because they are many, nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.

passages.title: On the degeneracy of the age
passages.text: The pilot is not glad when his ship is thrown on her beam-ends; the physician is not glad when he buries his patient; the orator is not glad when the defendant loses a case through the fault of his advocate; but on the other hand every man enjoys his own crimes. A. delights in an intrigue—for it was the very difficulty which attracted him thereto. B. delights in forgery and theft, and is only displeased with his sin when his sin has failed to hit the mark. And all this is the result of perverted habits.

passages.title: On the degeneracy of the age
passages.text: Conversely, however, in order that you may know that there is an idea of good conduct present subconsciously in souls which have been led even into the most depraved ways, and that men are not ignorant of what evil is but indifferent—I say that all men hide their sins, and, even though the issue be successful, enjoy the results while concealing the sins themselves. A good conscience, however, wishes to come forth and be seen of men; wickedness fears the very shadows.

passages.title: On the vanity of place-seeking
passages.text: Now all men suffer from ignorance of the truth; deceived by common report, they make for these ends as if they were good, and then, after having won their wish, and suffered much, they find them evil, or empty, or less important than they had expected. Most men admire that which deceives them at a distance, and by the crowd good things are supposed to be big things.

passages.title: On the critical condition of marcellinus
passages.text: You have been inquiring about our friend Marcellinus and you desire to know how he is getting along. He seldom comes to see me, for no other reason than that he is afraid to hear the truth, and at present he is removed from any danger of hearing it; for one must not talk to a man unless he is willing to listen. That is why it is often doubted whether Diogenes and the other Cynics, who employed an undiscriminating freedom of speech and offered advice to any who came in their way, ought to have pursued such a plan.

passages.title: On the critical condition of marcellinus
passages.text: This very thing, my dear Lucilius, is, I believe, exactly what a great-souled man ought not to do; his influence is weakened; it has too little effect upon those whom it might have set right if it had not grown so stale. The archer ought not to hit the mark only sometimes; he ought to miss it only sometimes. That which takes effect by chance is not an art. Now wisdom is an art; it should have a definite aim, choosing only those who will make progress, but withdrawing from those whom it has come to regard as hopeless,—yet not abandoning them too soon, and just when the case is becoming hopeless trying drastic remedies.

passages.title: On the parts of philosophy
passages.text: “I ought to be asking you ‘How long will these unending sins of yours go on?’” Do you really desire my remedies to stop before your vices? But I shall speak of my remedies all the more, and just because you offer objections I shall keep on talking. Medicine begins to do good at the time when a touch makes the diseased body tingle with pain. I shall utter words that will help men even against their will. At times you should allow words other than compliments to reach your ears, and because as individuals you are unwilling to hear the truth, hear it collectively.

passages.title: On benefits. [ 1 ]
passages.text: Let us therefore avoid being ungrateful, not for the sake of others but for our own sakes. When we do wrong, only the least and lightest portion of it flows back upon our neighbour; the worst and, if I may use the term, the densest portion of it stays at home and troubles the owner. My master Attalus used to say: “Evil herself drinks the largest portion of her own poison.” The poison which serpents carry for the destruction of others, and secrete without harm to themselves, is not like this poison; for this sort is ruinous to the possessor.

claims.t: Whoever wrongs me does it against their will, out of ignorance of what is good and bad, and with a disposition like theirs they can do nothing else. To require that bad people do no wrong is to demand the impossible.
claims.shared: 7.34 and 11.16 both say it is done against the will (“against its will”, “against their will”), and 11.16 repeats the saying 7.34 quotes. 1.15 and 11.16 both say it comes from ignorance (“through ignorance”, “in ignorance”). 9.43 and 11.16 both call the demand that there be no such people, or that they do no wrong, a demand for “the impossible”.
claims.changed: 1.15 names kinds of people (a meddler, an ungrateful person and others); the claim says “whoever wrongs me”. 12.12 asks “what are they to do?”; the claim states the answer the question implies. 12.12 speaks of not wanting the bad person to do wrong, 11.16 of requiring it; the claim uses 11.16’s word.

support.quote: “Every soul,” he says, “is deprived of truth against its will.” So too, then, of justice and self-control and kindness and everything of that kind. It is most necessary to remember this continually, for you will be gentler toward everyone.
support.follows: No soul loses truth, justice, self-control or kindness willingly, and keeping this in mind makes me gentler toward everyone.
gives: against their will

support.quote: and if not rightly, then plainly they do them against their will and in ignorance.
support.follows: If what they do is not right, they do it against their will and without knowing better.
gives: against their will
out of ignorance

support.quote: All these things have come upon them through ignorance of what is good and bad.
support.follows: The faults of the people I will meet come from not knowing what is good and what is bad.
gives: out of ignorance
of what is good and bad

support.quote: For what are they to do, having a disposition like that?
support.follows: Someone with that disposition cannot be expected to act otherwise.
gives: with a disposition like theirs they can do nothing else

support.quote: whoever does not want the bad person to do wrong is like someone who does not want the fig tree to bear sap in its figs, or babies to cry, or the horse to neigh, or any of the other things that have to be.
support.follows: Wanting a bad person not to do wrong is like wanting a fig tree to have no sap: it wants what has to be not to be.
gives: To require that bad people do no wrong

support.quote: that to require bad people not to do wrong is madness, for it aims at the impossible.
support.follows: Requiring bad people not to do wrong is madness, because it asks for the impossible.
gives: To require that bad people do no wrong
to demand the impossible

support.quote: “Is it possible, then, for there to be no shameless people in the universe?” It is not possible. Then do not demand the impossible.
support.follows: There cannot be a world without shameless people, so I should not demand one.
gives: to demand the impossible

claims.t: No one who wrongs me can harm me, for what is bad for me can exist only in my own mind. The one who does the wrong is the one harmed.
claims.shared: 1.15, 9.43 and 11.16 all say that the one who wrongs me does me no harm: “can neither be harmed by any of them”, “what harm have you in fact suffered?”, “I shall certainly not be harmed”. 11.16 and 12.12 both put the harm on the one who does the wrong: “it is you who are being harmed”; “like tearing one’s own face”.
claims.changed: 1.15 gives as its reason that no one can wrap me in what is shameful; the claim gives 9.43’s reason, that what is bad for me exists only in my mind. 12.12 says the wrongdoer has condemned themselves; the claim says “harmed”, as 11.16 does.

support.quote: can neither be harmed by any of them, for no one will wrap me in what is shameful
support.follows: None of the people I will meet can harm me, because none of them can wrap me in what is shameful.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me

support.quote: And what harm have you in fact suffered? For you will find that none of those you are provoked at has done anything of a kind that was going to make your mind worse; and it is there that what is bad for you, and what harms you, has its whole existence.
support.follows: No one who provokes me has made my mind worse, and only there can anything be bad for me or harm me.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me
what is bad for me can exist only in my own mind

support.quote: I shall certainly not be harmed; it is you who are being harmed, child.
support.follows: To someone trying to hurt me I can say: I will not be harmed; you are the one being harmed.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me
The one who does the wrong is the one harmed

support.quote: And if they did do wrong, that they have condemned themselves, and so this is like tearing one’s own face.
support.follows: If they did wrong, they have condemned themselves, and the wrong tears at the one who did it.
gives: The one who does the wrong is the one harmed

claims.t: I wish them well, for by nature they are friends. The gods too are kind to such people and help them toward the things they care about (health, wealth, reputation); I am free to be as kind.
claims.shared: Both passages say that the gods too help the very people who offend: “the gods too help them” (9.25), “The gods too are kind to such people … they even work with them” (9.9), and both send that help toward particular things. Only 9.25 marks those things as what the people themselves care about; 9.9 names them: health, wealth, reputation.
claims.changed: “Kind” is 9.9’s word; 9.25 says the gods help them in every kind of way. 9.25 lists the means (dreams, oracles) and 9.9 the ends (health, wealth, reputation); the claim keeps the ends. 9.9 presents the help as the gods’ goodness; the claim does not say whether it is limited. 9.9 asks “who is stopping you?”; the claim says I am free.

support.quote: You must wish them well, however; for by nature they are friends, and the gods too help them in every kind of way, through dreams, through oracles, yet toward the things those people care about.
support.follows: I should wish them well, since they are friends by nature and the gods too help them toward what they care about.
gives: I wish them well, for by nature they are friends
The gods too
help them toward
the things they care about

support.quote: The gods too are kind to such people, and toward some things they even work with them, toward health, toward wealth, toward reputation: so good are they. You may be so too; or tell me, who is stopping you?
support.follows: The gods are kind even to such people and help them toward health, wealth and reputation, and nothing stops me being kind too.
gives: The gods too
are kind to such people
help them toward
health, wealth, reputation
I am free to be as kind

claims.role: Teaching them, or bearing with them
claims.t: I teach them kindly and show them what they fail to see, without reproach. If I cannot, I bear with them: kindness and gentleness were given to me for this.
claims.shared: 10.4, 9.9, 8.56 and 9.43 all say to teach them (“teach them kindly”, “teach them otherwise”, “teach them”, “teach … to think otherwise”). 10.4 and 11.12 both say “show” them “what they are failing to see”. 10.4 and 9.9 both go on to the case where I cannot (“if you cannot”, “if not”). 9.9 and 9.43 both say that what I need for it was given to me: “kindness has been given to you”, nature “has given … gentleness”.
claims.changed: 8.56 offers teaching and bearing as two choices; 10.4 and 9.9 put teaching first and the other way only if it fails, and the claim follows them. 10.4 then says to blame myself, or not even myself; the claim leaves that out. 9.43 says gentleness is given to every human being; the claim says “to me”.

support.quote: If someone is mistaken, teach them kindly and show them what they are failing to see.
support.follows: When someone is mistaken, I should teach them kindly and show them what they are missing.
gives: I teach them
kindly
show them what they fail to see

support.quote: But I am kind and well-disposed to everyone, and ready to show this very person what they are failing to see, not with reproach, nor as if making a show of putting up with them, but genuinely and good-heartedly
support.follows: I am ready to show this person what they are missing, sincerely, without reproach and without making a show of my patience.
gives: kindly
show them what they fail to see
without reproach

support.quote: If you can, teach them otherwise; and if not, remember that kindness has been given to you for this.
support.follows: I should teach them if I can, and if I cannot, remember that I was given kindness for just this case.
gives: I teach them
If I cannot
kindness and gentleness were given to me for this

support.quote: But if you cannot, blame yourself, or not even yourself.
support.follows: If I cannot teach them, the blame is mine, or perhaps not even mine.
gives: If I cannot

support.quote: Human beings have come into being for one another’s sake. So either teach them or bear with them.
support.follows: Since people exist for one another’s sake, I either teach them or put up with them.
gives: I teach them
I bear with them

support.quote: It is useful too to think at once of this: what virtue nature has given to a human being to meet this wrong. For it has given, as an antidote, gentleness against the unfeeling person, and against another some other power. And in general you are free to teach the one who has gone astray to think otherwise
support.follows: Nature gave people gentleness and other powers as antidotes to wrongs, and I am free to teach whoever has gone astray.
gives: I teach them
kindness and gentleness were given to me for this

claims.t: If someone despises me or hates me, that is for them to see to, and I do not need their good opinion. My part is to do and say nothing that deserves contempt.
claims.shared: 9.25 and 7.34 both say I do not need what these people think of me (“you need not be torn apart so that these people may think this or that of you”; “nor need their testimony”), and both reach it by looking inside them. 11.12 and 9.25 both begin from someone who hates me.
claims.changed: 9.25 speaks of being blamed and hated, 11.12 of being despised and hated; the claim keeps “despises” from 11.12 and “hates” from both. 7.34 speaks of the testimony I want in my favour; the claim calls it their good opinion.

support.quote: Will someone despise me? That is for them to see to. But I will see to it that I am not found doing or saying anything that deserves to be despised. Will they hate me? That is for them to see to.
support.follows: Whether others despise or hate me is their concern; mine is not to deserve contempt by what I do or say.
gives: If someone despises me
hates me
that is for them to see to
My part is to do and say nothing that deserves contempt

support.quote: When someone else blames you or hates you, or people voice things of that kind
support.follows: Others will at times blame me, hate me or speak against me.
gives: hates me

support.quote: You will see that you need not be torn apart so that these people may think this or that of you.
support.follows: Once I see what such people are like, I need not torment myself over what they think of me.
gives: I do not need their good opinion

support.quote: Keep turning your attention to who these people are whose testimony in your favour you want, and what ruling parts they have. For you will neither blame those who stumble against their will nor need their testimony, if you look into the springs of their judgment and impulse.
support.follows: If I look at the minds of those whose praise I want, I stop needing their praise and stop blaming them.
gives: I do not need their good opinion

claims.role: Looking into them, then into myself
claims.t: When someone wrongs me, I at once look into them, at what they took to be good or bad and at what sort of people they are, and turn to myself to count the wrongs of the same kind that I do; then my anger goes.
claims.shared: 7.19, 10.30 and 11.16 all turn from the other’s wrong to my own of “the same kind” (7.19, 11.16) or “a similar kind” (10.30). 9.25 and 11.16 both ask “what sort of people they are”. Both 7.19 and 10.30 make the response immediate (“at once”): 7.19 for looking at what they judged good, 10.30 for turning to myself. Both end with the anger gone: “neither surprised nor angry”, “you will quickly forget your anger”.
claims.changed: 10.30 begins from a wrong that offends me, not necessarily one done to me; the claim, and the statement’s “Whoever wrongs me”, take it as a wrong done to me. 9.25 begins from someone who blames or hates me; the claim takes only its looking inside. 7.19 counts judgments of the same kind (“judge the same thing to be good”); 10.30 counts such judgments as wrongs (“judging money to be a good”), and the claim follows 10.30. 7.19 also says “you will pity them”; the claim leaves pity out.

support.quote: Whenever someone does you some wrong, consider at once what they judged to be good or bad when they did the wrong. For once you have seen this you will pity them, and will be neither surprised nor angry.
support.follows: When someone wrongs me, seeing what they took to be good or bad turns my anger and surprise into pity.
gives: When someone wrongs me
at once
look into them
what they took to be good or bad
my anger goes

support.quote: go to their little souls, pass inside and see what sort of people they are.
support.follows: I should go inside the minds of those who blame or hate me and see what they are like.
gives: look into them
what sort of people they are

support.quote: Second: what sort of people they are at table, in bed, and so on; and above all, what compulsions their principles have laid on them
support.follows: I should keep in mind what these people are like in daily life and what their principles force on them.
gives: what sort of people they are

support.quote: Whenever you take offence at someone’s wrongdoing, turn at once to yourself and reckon up what wrong of a similar kind you do: for example, judging money to be a good, or pleasure, or a scrap of reputation, and so on, kind by kind. For when you put your mind to this you will quickly forget your anger
support.follows: When someone’s wrong offends me, counting my own wrongs of the same kind soon makes me forget my anger.
gives: When someone wrongs me
at once
turn to myself to count
the wrongs of the same kind that I do
my anger goes

support.quote: For either you yourself still judge the same thing to be good as they do, or another thing of the same kind; so you must forgive.
support.follows: If I still judge the same thing, or a thing of the same kind, to be good, I must forgive them.
gives: the wrongs of the same kind that I do

support.quote: Fourth: that you yourself also do many wrongs and are another of the same kind
support.follows: I too do many wrongs and am one of the same kind as those who wrong me.
gives: the wrongs of the same kind that I do

claims.t: Being indignant and turning away from them is against nature, and so is a scowl on my face. Anger and harshness toward them are weakness: in anger I have given in, and in harshness I desert my post as surely as if I had fled my work in fright.
claims.shared: 1.15 and 7.18 both say it “is against nature”: being indignant and turning away (1.15), the scowl (7.18). 11.16 and 11.8 both call it weakness (“a weak person”, “weakness”). 11.16 says the angry person has “given in”; 11.8 sets harshness beside giving in from fright as an equal weakness and calls both “deserters from their post”.
claims.changed: 11.16 speaks of anger, 11.8 of being harsh with those who stand in my way and of becoming estranged from them; the claim joins them as anger and harshness toward people who wrong me. 7.18 does not say whose scowl it is or why; its Greek word means a grudging, wrathful look, and the claim takes it as my own angry face.

support.quote: So to work against one another is against nature; and to be indignant and to turn away is working against.
support.follows: Working against one another is against nature, and being indignant and turning away is a way of working against.
gives: Being indignant and turning away from them
is against nature

support.quote: A scowl on the face is very much against nature.
support.follows: An angry look on the face goes against nature.
gives: is against nature
a scowl on my face

support.quote: And just as distress belongs to a weak person, so does anger; for both have been wounded and have given in.
support.follows: Anger, like distress, belongs to the weak: the angry person has been wounded and has given in.
gives: Anger
are weakness
in anger I have given in

support.quote: For this too is weakness, to be harsh with them, just as it is to abandon the action and give in from fright. For both are equally deserters from their post: the one who has flinched, and the one who has become estranged from a person who is by nature kin and friend.
support.follows: Being harsh with those who block me is as weak as abandoning my action in fright: both desert their post.
gives: harshness toward them
are weakness
in harshness I desert my post as surely as if I had fled my work in fright

claims.t: I may not even know whether it was a wrong, for much is done for a purpose I cannot see. And if it was done rightly, there is nothing to be annoyed at.
claims.shared: Both passages question the wrong itself: “how do I know whether this is a wrong?” (12.12); “you have not even grasped for certain whether they are doing wrong” (11.16).
claims.changed: Only 11.16 gives the reason (a purpose not seen) and the case in which it was done rightly.

support.quote: In the case of someone who has given the impression of having done wrong: “But how do I know whether this is a wrong?”
support.follows: When someone seems to have done wrong, I should first ask how I know that it was a wrong.
gives: I may not even know whether it was a wrong

support.quote: Fifth: that you have not even grasped for certain whether they are doing wrong; for many things are done with some further purpose in view
support.follows: I often do not know for certain that they did wrong, since many acts serve a purpose I cannot see.
gives: I may not even know whether it was a wrong
much is done for a purpose I cannot see

support.quote: Third: that if they do these things rightly, one should not be annoyed
support.follows: If what they did was right, there is no cause for annoyance.
gives: if it was done rightly, there is nothing to be annoyed at

single.quote: To people with jaundice honey appears bitter, and to those bitten by a mad dog water appears frightening, and to small children their little ball appears beautiful. Why, then, am I angry? Or do you think that a false belief has less power than the bile has over the person with jaundice and the poison over the one bitten by a mad dog?
single.label: A false belief is strong
single.t: To someone with jaundice honey tastes bitter. A false belief has no less power over a person than that illness has over the body, so I have no cause to be angry.
single.why: Claim 1 says that wrongs come from ignorance. Only this passage says how strong a false belief is, by setting it beside an illness of the body.
single.follows: A false belief rules a person as bile rules the jaundiced, so it makes no sense for me to be angry at them.

single.quote: Well then, you have reason too: stir a rational disposition with a rational disposition; show them, remind them. For if they listen, you will cure them, and there is no need of anger.
single.label: Reason answering reason
single.t: If they have reason, so do I: I use my reason on theirs, show them and remind them. If they listen, I cure them, and there is no need of anger.
single.why: Its “show them” is the teaching of claim 4, which already rests on five passages, the most one claim can carry on the page. It stands apart for what it alone says: that my reason is what I use on theirs, and that a cure leaves no need of anger.
single.follows: I have reason as they do, so I can show and remind them; if they listen, they are cured and anger is not needed.

single.quote: At dawn, say to yourself beforehand: I shall meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one, an unsocial one.
single.label: Each morning
single.t: At dawn I tell myself beforehand that I will meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one and an unsocial one.
single.why: Only this passage prepares for the day before anyone has done anything. The others answer a wrong once it is done.
single.follows: Each morning I should expect to meet difficult people, naming beforehand the kinds I will meet.

single.quote: Seventh: that it is not their actions that trouble us, for those are in their ruling parts, but our own judgments. At any rate, take away the verdict that this is something terrible, and be willing to let it go, and the anger is gone.
single.label: Taking away the verdict
single.t: What troubles me is not what they do but my own judgment of it. If I take away the verdict that it is something terrible, and am willing to let it go, the anger is gone.
single.why: Claim 2 says that what is bad for me exists only in my mind. Only this heading turns that into an exercise: remove the verdict and the anger goes.
single.follows: My anger comes from my judgment, not from their act; when I drop the verdict that it is terrible, the anger goes.

single.quote: In the gymnasium someone has scratched us with their nails, and butted us with their head and landed a blow; but we do not mark them down, nor take offence, nor suspect them afterwards of plotting against us. We are on our guard, certainly, yet not as against an enemy, nor with suspicion, but with a kindly stepping aside. Let something like this happen in the other parts of life too: let us overlook many things in those who are, as it were, our training partners.
single.label: Training partners
single.t: I treat the people around me as training partners. When one of them hurts me, I do not mark them down or suspect them; I am on my guard, but I step aside kindly and let many things pass.
single.why: Only this passage gives the image of training, and only it says to step aside and overlook. That is neither teaching nor bearing, the two ways of claim 4.
single.follows: As in the gymnasium, I should be careful without being suspicious, step aside kindly, and let many things pass.

single.quote: How cruel it is not to let people go after the things that appear to them to suit them and to be good for them. And yet in a way you do not allow them to do this, whenever you are indignant that they do wrong.
single.label: Indignation is cruel
single.t: When I am indignant that people do wrong, I am in a way refusing to let them go after what seems good to them, and that is cruel.
single.why: Only this passage calls indignation cruel. It goes on to say “teach them and show them”, as claim 4 does; those words are not quoted, since claim 4 already rests on five passages.
single.follows: Being indignant at people’s wrongs is cruel, because it refuses them the pursuit of what looks good to them.

single.quote: Above all, whenever you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For plainly the wrong is yours, whether you trusted that a person with such a disposition would keep faith, or whether, in doing a favour, you did not do it as something finished in itself, nor so as to have received the whole fruit at once from the act itself.
single.label: Blaming the ungrateful
single.t: When I blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, the mistake is mine: I trusted such a person to keep faith, or I did them a favour and looked for something back, as if the act were not complete in itself.
single.why: 10.30 also says to turn to myself, but there to count my own wrongs of the same kind. Here it is to find that my expectation was the mistake, and no other passage says that a favour is complete when it is done.
single.follows: If I blame someone for ingratitude, the fault is mine, for trusting them or for wanting a return for a favour.

single.quote: See that you never come to feel toward the inhuman anything like what the inhuman feel toward human beings.
single.label: Not becoming like them
single.t: I never let myself feel toward inhuman people anything like what the inhuman feel toward human beings.
single.why: Only this passage warns that meeting inhumanity can make me answer it in kind.
single.follows: However inhuman someone is, I must not come to feel toward them what they feel toward others.

single.quote: Sixth: that, whenever you are extremely indignant or even take it hard, human life is a moment long, and in a little while we are all laid out.
single.label: Life is short
single.t: Whenever I am deeply indignant or take something hard, I remember that a human life lasts a moment, and in a little while we are all laid out.
single.why: Only this heading brings in death. It holds even if they did wrong willingly and did harm me.
single.follows: However indignant I am, a human life lasts a moment, and soon we will all be dead.

members.text:
When at any time thou art offended with any one's impudency, put
presently this question to thyself: 'What? Is it then possible, that
there should not be any impudent men in the world! Certainly it is not
possible.' Desire not then that which is impossible. For this one, (thou
must think) whosoever he be, is one of those impudent ones, that
the world cannot be without. So of the subtile and crafty, so of the
perfidious, so of every one that offendeth, must thou ever be ready to
reason with thyself. For whilst in general thou dost thus reason with
thyself, that the kind of them must needs be in the world, thou wilt be
the better able to use meekness towards every particular. This also
thou shalt find of very good use, upon every such occasion, presently
to consider with thyself, what proper virtue nature hath furnished man
with, against such a vice, or to encounter with a disposition vicious
in this kind. As for example, against the unthankful, it hath given
goodness and meekness, as an antidote, and so against another vicious
in another kind some other peculiar faculty. And generally, is it not
in thy power to instruct him better, that is in an error? For whosoever
sinneth, doth in that decline from his purposed end, and is certainly
deceived, And again, what art thou the worse for his sin? For thou shalt
not find that any one of these, against whom thou art incensed, hath in
very deed done anything whereby thy mind (the only true subject of
thy hurt and evil) can be made worse than it was. And what a matter of
either grief or wonder is this, if he that is unlearned, do the deeds of
one that is unlearned? Should not thou rather blame thyself, who, when
upon very good grounds of reason, thou mightst have thought it very
probable, that such a thing would by such a one be committed, didst not
only not foresee it, but moreover dost wonder at it, that such a thing
should be. But then especially, when thou dost find fault with either an
unthankful, or a false man, must thou reflect upon thyself. For without
all question, thou thyself art much in fault, if either of one that were
of such a disposition, thou didst expect that he should be true unto
thee: or when unto any thou didst a good turn, thou didst not there
bound thy thoughts, as one that had obtained his end; nor didst not
think that from the action itself thou hadst received a full reward of
the good that thou hadst done. For what wouldst thou have more? Unto him
that is a man, thou hast done a good turn: doth not that suffice thee?
What thy nature required, that hast thou done. Must thou be rewarded for
it? As if either the eye for that it seeth, or the feet that they go,
should require satisfaction. For as these being by nature appointed for
such an use, can challenge no more, than that they may work according
to their natural constitution: so man being born to do good unto others
whensoever he doth a real good unto any by helping them out of error; or
though but in middle things, as in matter of wealth, life, preferment,
and the like, doth help to further their desires he doth that for which
he was made, and therefore can require no more.
members.english: Whenever you take offence at someone’s shamelessness, ask yourself at once: “Is it possible, then, for there to be no shameless people in the universe?” It is not possible. Then do not demand the impossible. For this person too is one of those shameless people who must exist in the universe. Have the same thought ready to hand for the scoundrel, and for the faithless person, and for everyone who does wrong in any way whatever. For as soon as you are reminded that it is impossible for this kind of people not to exist, you will be kinder toward each one of them. It is useful too to think at once of this: what virtue nature has given to a human being to meet this wrong. For it has given, as an antidote, gentleness against the unfeeling person, and against another some other power. And in general you are free to teach the one who has gone astray to think otherwise; for everyone who does wrong misses what they were aiming at and has gone astray. And what harm have you in fact suffered? For you will find that none of those you are provoked at has done anything of a kind that was going to make your mind worse; and it is there that what is bad for you, and what harms you, has its whole existence. And what new or strange thing has happened, if the untaught person does what an untaught person does? See whether you ought not rather to blame yourself, because you did not expect that this person would do this wrong. For you did have from reason the means to reflect that this person was likely to do this wrong, and yet you forgot it and are surprised that they have done wrong. Above all, whenever you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For plainly the wrong is yours, whether you trusted that a person with such a disposition would keep faith, or whether, in doing a favour, you did not do it as something finished in itself, nor so as to have received the whole fruit at once from the act itself. For what more do you want when you have done good to a person? Is it not enough that you have done something in accord with your own nature, but you look for a wage for it? As if the eye demanded a return because it sees, or the feet because they walk. For just as these have come into being for one particular thing, and in doing it according to their own build they receive in full what is their own, so too a human being, who is by nature a doer of good, whenever they do some good, or in some other way work together toward things of the middle kind, has done what they were built for, and has what is their own.
members.greek: Ὅταν τινὸς ἀναισχυντίᾳ προσκόπτῃς, εὐθὺς πυνθάνου σεαυτοῦ· δύνανται οὖν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἀναίσχυντοι μὴ εἶναι; οὐ δύνανται· μὴ οὖν ἀπαίτει τὸ ἀδύνατον· εἷς γὰρ καὶ οὗτός ἐστιν ἐκείνων τῶν ἀναισχύντων, οὓς ἀνάγκη ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ εἶναι. τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ πανούργου καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀπίστου καὶ παντὸς τοῦ ὁτιοῦν ἁμαρτάνοντος ἔστω σοι πρόχειρον· ἅμα γὰρ τῷ ὑπομνησθῆναι ὅτι τὸ γένος τῶν τοιούτων ἀδύνατόν ἐστι μὴ ὑπάρχειν, εὐμενέστερος ἔσῃ πρὸς τοὺς καθ’ ἕνα. εὔχρηστον δὲ κἀκεῖνο εὐθὺς ἐννοεῖν, τίνα ἔδωκεν ἡ φύσις τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἀρετὴν πρὸς τοῦτο τὸ ἁμάρτημα· ἔδωκε γὰρ ὡς ἀντιφάρμακον πρὸς μὲν τὸν ἀγνώμονα τὴν πρᾳότητα, πρὸς δὲ ἄλλον ἄλλην τινὰ δύναμιν, ὅλως δὲ ἔξεστί σοι μεταδιδάσκειν τὸν πεπλανημένον· πᾶς γὰρ ὁ ἁμαρτάνων ἀφαμαρτάνει τοῦ προκειμένου καὶ πεπλάνηται. τί δὲ καὶ βέβλαψαι; εὑρήσεις γὰρ μηδένα τούτων, πρὸς οὓς παροξύνῃ, πεποιηκότα τι τοιοῦτον, ἐξ οὗ ἡ διάνοιά σου χείρων ἔμελλε γενήσεσθαι· τὸ δὲ κακόν σου καὶ τὸ βλαβερὸν ἐνταῦθα πᾶσαν τὴν ὑπόστασιν ἔχει. τί δὲ καινὸν ἢ ξένον γέγονεν, εἰ ὁ ἀπαίδευτος τὰ τοῦ ἀπαιδεύτου πράσσει; ὅρα μὴ σεαυτῷ μᾶλλον ἐγκαλεῖν ὀφείλῃς, ὅτι οὐ προσεδόκησας τοῦτον τοῦτο ἁμαρτήσεσθαι· σὺ γὰρ καὶ ἀφορμὰς ἐκ τοῦ λόγου εἶχες πρὸς τὸ ἐνθυμηθῆναι ὅτι εἰκός ἐστι τοῦτον τοῦτο ἁμαρτήσεσθαι, καὶ ὅμως ἐπιλαθόμενος θαυμάζεις εἰ ἡμάρτηκε. μάλιστα δέ, ὅταν ὡς ἀπίστῳ ἢ ἀχαρίστῳ μέμφῃ, εἰς σεαυτὸν ἐπιστρέφου· προδήλως γὰρ σὸν τὸ ἁμάρτημα, εἴτε περὶ τοῦ τοιαύτην τὴν διάθεσιν ἔχοντος ἐπίστευσας ὅτι τὴν πίστιν φυλάξει, εἴτε τὴν χάριν διδοὺς μὴ καταληκτικῶς ἔδωκας μηδὲ ὥστε ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς πράξεως εὐθὺς ἀπειληφέναι πάντα τὸν καρπόν. τί γὰρ πλέον θέλεις εὖ ποιήσας ἄνθρωπον; οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τοῦτο, ὅτι κατὰ φύσιν τὴν σήν τι ἔπραξας, ἀλλὰ τούτου μισθὸν ζητεῖς; ὡσεὶ ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς ἀμοιβὴν ἀπῄτει, ὅτι βλέπει, ἢ οἱ πόδες, ὅτι βαδίζουσιν. ὥσπερ γὰρ ταῦτα πρὸς τόδε τι γέγονεν, ὅπερ κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν ἐνεργοῦντα ἀπέχει τὸ ἴδιον, οὕτως καὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος εὐεργετικὸς πεφυκώς, ὁπόταν τι εὐεργετικὸν ἢ ἄλλως εἰς τὰ μέσα συνεργητικὸν πράξῃ, πεποίηκε, πρὸς ὃ κατεσκεύασται, καὶ ἔχει τὸ ἑαυτοῦ.

members.text:
Thou must continually ponder and consider with thyself, what
manner of men they be, and for their minds and understandings what is
their present estate, whose good word and testimony thou dost desire.
For then neither wilt thou see cause to complain of them that offend
against their wills; or find any want of their applause, if once
thou dost but penetrate into the true force and ground both of their
opinions, and of their desires. 'No soul (saith he) is willingly bereft
of the truth,' and by consequent, neither of justice, or temperance, or
kindness, and mildness; nor of anything that is of the same kind. It is
most needful that thou shouldst always remember this. For so shalt thou
be far more gentle and moderate towards all men.
members.english:
Keep turning your attention to who these people are whose testimony in your favour you want, and what ruling parts they have. For you will neither blame those who stumble against their will nor need their testimony, if you look into the springs of their judgment and impulse.

“Every soul,” he says, “is deprived of truth against its will.” So too, then, of justice and self-control and kindness and everything of that kind. It is most necessary to remember this continually, for you will be gentler toward everyone.
members.greek:
Συνεχῶς ἐφιστάναι, τίνες εἰσὶν οὗτοι, ὑφ’ ὧν μαρτυρεῖσθαι θέλεις, καὶ τίνα ἡγεμονικὰ ἔχουσιν· οὔτε γὰρ μέμψῃ τοῖς ἀκουσίως πταίουσιν οὔτε ἐπιμαρτυρήσεως δεήσῃ, ἐμβλέπων εἰς τὰς πηγὰς τῆς ὑπολήψεως καὶ ὁρμῆς αὐτῶν.

ʽΠᾶσα ψυχή, φησίν, ἄκουσα στέρεται ἀληθείας·ʼ οὕτως οὖν καὶ δικαιοσύνης καὶ σωφροσύνης καὶ εὐμενείας καὶ παντὸς τοῦ τοιούτου. ἀναγκαιότατον δὲ τὸ διηνεκῶς τούτου μεμνῆσθαι· ἔσῃ γὰρ πρὸς πάντας πρᾳότερος.

members.text:
Of everything thou must consider from whence it came, of what
things it doth consist, and into what it will be changed: what will be
the nature of it, or what it will be like unto when it is changed; and
that it can suffer no hurt by this change. And as for other men's either
foolishness or wickedness, that it may not trouble and grieve thee;
first generally thus; What reference have I unto these? and that we are
all born for one another's good: then more particularly after another
consideration; as a ram is first in a flock of sheep, and a bull in a
herd of cattle, so am I born to rule over them. Begin yet higher, even
from this: if atoms be not the beginning of all things, than which to
believe nothing can be more absurd, then must we needs grant that there
is a nature, that doth govern the universe. If such a nature, then are
all worse things made for the better's sake; and all better for one
another's sake. Secondly, what manner of men they be, at board, and upon
their beds, and so forth. But above all things, how they are forced by
their opinions that they hold, to do what they do; and even those things
that they do, with what pride and self-conceit they do them. Thirdly,
that if they do these things rightly, thou hast no reason to be grieved.
But if not rightly, it must needs be that they do them against their
wills, and through mere ignorance. For as, according to Plato's opinion,
no soul doth willingly err, so by consequent neither doth it anything
otherwise than it ought, but against her will. Therefore are they
grieved, whensoever they hear themselves charged, either of injustice,
or unconscionableness, or covetousness, or in general, of any injurious
kind of dealing towards their neighbours. Fourthly, that thou thyself
doest transgress in many things, and art even such another as they are.
And though perchance thou doest forbear the very act of some sins, yet
hast thou in thyself an habitual disposition to them, but that either
through fear, or vainglory, or some such other ambitious foolish
respect, thou art restrained. Fifthly, that whether they have sinned or
no, thou doest not understand perfectly. For many things are done by
way of discreet policy; and generally a man must know many things
first, before he be able truly and judiciously to judge of another
man's action. Sixthly, that whensoever thou doest take on grievously, or
makest great woe, little doest thou remember then that a man's life is
but for a moment of time, and that within a while we shall all be in our
graves. Seventhly, that it is not the sins and transgressions themselves
that trouble us properly; for they have their existence in their
minds and understandings only, that commit them; but our own opinions
concerning those sins. Remove then, and be content to part with that
conceit of thine, that it is a grievous thing, and thou hast removed
thine anger. But how should I remove it? How? reasoning with thyself
that it is not shameful. For if that which is shameful, be not the only
true evil that is, thou also wilt be driven whilest thou doest follow
the common instinct of nature, to avoid that which is evil, to commit
many unjust things, and to become a thief, and anything, that will
make to the attainment of thy intended worldly ends. Eighthly, how many
things may and do oftentimes follow upon such fits of anger and grief;
far more grievous in themselves, than those very things which we are so
grieved or angry for. Ninthly, that meekness is a thing unconquerable,
if it be true and natural, and not affected or hypocritical. For how
shall even the most fierce and malicious that thou shalt conceive, be
able to hold on against thee, if thou shalt still continue meek and
loving unto him; and that even at that time, when he is about to do
thee wrong, thou shalt be well disposed, and in good temper, with all
meekness to teach him, and to instruct him better? As for example; My
son, we were not born for this, to hurt and annoy one another; it will
be thy hurt not mine, my son: and so to show him forcibly and fully,
that it is so in very deed: and that neither bees do it one to another,
nor any other creatures that are naturally sociable. But this thou must
do, not scoffingly, not by way of exprobation, but tenderly without
any harshness of words. Neither must thou do it by way of exercise, or
ostentation, that they that are by and hear thee, may admire thee: but
so always that nobody be privy to it, but himself alone: yea, though
there be more present at the same time. These nine particular heads, as
so many gifts from the Muses, see that thou remember well: and begin one
day, whilest thou art yet alive, to be a man indeed. But on the other
side thou must take heed, as much to flatter them, as to be angry with
them: for both are equally uncharitable, and equally hurtful. And in thy
passions, take it presently to thy consideration, that to be angry is
not the part of a man, but that to be meek and gentle, as it savours of
more humanity, so of more manhood. That in this, there is strength
and nerves, or vigour and fortitude: whereof anger and indignation is
altogether void. For the nearer everything is unto unpassionateness,
the nearer it is unto power. And as grief doth proceed from weakness,
so doth anger. For both, both he that is angry and that grieveth, have
received a wound, and cowardly have as it were yielded themselves unto
their affections. If thou wilt have a tenth also, receive this tenth
gift from Hercules the guide and leader of the Muses: that is a mad
man's part, to look that there should be no wicked men in the world,
because it is impossible. Now for a man to brook well enough, that there
should be wicked men in the world, but not to endure that any
should transgress against himself, is against all equity, and indeed
tyrannical.
members.english:
Where each thing has come from, and what underlying materials each is made of, and what it is changing into, and what it will be like when it has changed, and that it will suffer nothing bad.

And first: what my relation to them is, and that we have come into being for one another’s sake; and that, on another account, I have come into being to stand at their head, as a ram stands at the head of a flock or a bull of a herd. But go back further and start from this: if not atoms, then nature is what governs the whole; if that is so, the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another. Second: what sort of people they are at table, in bed, and so on; and above all, what compulsions their principles have laid on them; and these very things, with what conceit they do them. Third: that if they do these things rightly, one should not be annoyed; and if not rightly, then plainly they do them against their will and in ignorance. For every soul is deprived against its will, as of the truth, so too of dealing with each person as they deserve. At any rate they are aggrieved to hear themselves called unjust and unfeeling and greedy and, in a word, prone to do wrong to their neighbours. Fourth: that you yourself also do many wrongs and are another of the same kind; and if you do hold back from certain wrongs, you still have the disposition that brings them on, even if it is through cowardice or hunger for reputation or some such bad thing that you hold back from wrongs like theirs. Fifth: that you have not even grasped for certain whether they are doing wrong; for many things are done with some further purpose in view, and in general one must first learn many things in order to pronounce on another’s action with a sure grasp. Sixth: that, whenever you are extremely indignant or even take it hard, human life is a moment long, and in a little while we are all laid out. Seventh: that it is not their actions that trouble us, for those are in their ruling parts, but our own judgments. At any rate, take away the verdict that this is something terrible, and be willing to let it go, and the anger is gone. How, then, will you take it away? By reasoning that it is not shameful. For if what is shameful is not the only bad thing, you too must do many wrongs and become a robber and anything at all. Eighth: how much harder are the things that our fits of anger and distress over such things bring on than the things themselves are at which we are angry and distressed. Ninth: that kindness is unbeatable, if it is genuine and not a grin or play-acting. For what will the most insolent person do to you, if you go on being kind to them and, if the chance comes, gently advise them and teach them otherwise, at your ease, at the very moment when they are trying to do you harm: “No, child. We are made by nature for something else. I shall certainly not be harmed; it is you who are being harmed, child.” And show, with a light touch and in general terms, that this is so: that not even bees do it, nor any of the creatures that are by nature herd animals. And it must be done neither with irony nor with reproach, but with affection and with no bite in your soul; and not as in a lecture room, nor so that someone else standing by may admire, but to that person alone, even if some others are standing around. Remember these nine headings as gifts you have received from the Muses, and begin at last to be a human being, while you live. One must guard against flattering them just as much as against being angry with them, for both are unsocial and lead to harm. And in your fits of anger have this ready to hand: that it is not flying into a rage that is manly, but that what is gentle and mild, as it is more human, is also more masculine; and that it is this that has a share of strength and sinew and manly courage, not the one who is indignant and discontented. For the closer this is to freedom from passion, the closer it is to power. And just as distress belongs to a weak person, so does anger; for both have been wounded and have given in. And if you like, take a tenth gift too, from the Leader of the Muses: that to require bad people not to do wrong is madness, for it aims at the impossible. And to allow them to be such to others, but to require that they not do wrong to you, is unfeeling and tyrannical.
members.greek:
Πόθεν ἐλήλυθεν ἕκαστον καὶ ἐκ τίνων ἕκαστον ὑποκειμένων καὶ εἰς τί μεταβάλλει καὶ οἷον ἔσται μεταβαλὸν καὶ ὡς οὐδὲν κακὸν πείσεται.

Καὶ Πρῶτον, τίς ἡ πρὸς αὐτούς μοι σχέσις καὶ ὅτι ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν γεγόναμεν καὶ καθ’ ἕτερον λόγον προστησόμενος αὐτῶν γέγονα ὡς κριὸς ποίμνης ἢ ταῦρος ἀγέλης. ἄνωθεν δὲ ἔπιθι ἀπὸ τοῦ· εἰ μὴ ἄτομοι, φύσις ἡ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦσα· εἰ τοῦτο, τὰ χείρονα τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν, ταῦτα δὲ ἀλλήλων. Δεύτερον δέ, ὁποῖοί τινές εἰσιν ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης, ὲν τῷ κλιναρίῳ, τἄλλα· μάλιστα δέ, οἵας ἀνάγκας δογμάτων κειμένας ἔχουσι· καὶ αὐτὰ δὲ ταῦτα, μεθ’ οἵου τύφου ποιοῦσιν. Τρίτον, ὅτι, εἰ μὲν ὀρθῶς ταῦτα ποιοῦσιν, οὐ δεῖ δυσχεραίνειν· εἰ ὀ οὐκ ὀρθῶς, δηλονότι ἄκοντες καὶ ἀγνοοῦντες. πᾶσα γὰρ ψυχὴ ἄκουσα στέρεται, ὥσπερ τοῦ ἀληθοῦς, οὕτως καὶ τοῦ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἑκάστῳ προσφέρεσθαι. ἄχθονται γοῦν ἀκούοντες ἄδικοι καὶ ἀγνώμονες καὶ πλεονέκται καὶ καθάπαξ ἁμαρτητικοὶ περὶ τοὺς πλησίον. Τέταρτον, ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸς πολλὰ ἁμαρτάνεις καὶ ἄλλος τοιοῦτος εἷ· καὶ εἴ τινων δὲ ἁμαρτημάτων ἀπέχῃ, ἀλλὰ τήν γε ἕξιν ἐποιστικὴν ἔχεις, εἰ καὶ διὰ δειλίαν ἢ δοξοκοπίαν ἢ τοιοῦτό τι κακὸν ἀπέχῃ τῶν ὁμοίων ἁμαρτημάτων. Πέμπτον, ὅτι οὐδὲ εἰ ἁμαρτάνουσι κατείληφας· πολλὰ γὰρ κατ’ οἰκονομίαν γίνεται καὶ ὅλως πολλὰ δεῖ πρότερον μαθεῖν, ἵνα τις περὶ ἀλλοτρίας πράξεως καταληπτικῶς τι ἀποφήνηται. Ἕκτον, ὅτι, ὅταν λίαν ἀγανακτῇς ἢ καὶ δυσπαθῇς, ἀκαριαῖος ὁ ἀνθρώπειος βίος καὶ μετ’ ὀλίγον πάντες ἐξετάθημεν. Ἕβδομον, ὅτι οὐχ αἱ πράξεις αὐτῶν ἐνοχλοῦσιν ἡμῖν· ἐκεῖναι γάρ εἰσιν ἐν τοῖς ἐκείνων ἡγεμονικοῖς· ἀλλὰ αἱ ἡμέτεραι ὑπολήψεις. ἆρον γοῦν καὶ θέλησον ἀφεῖναι τὴν ὡς περὶ δεινοῦ κρίσιν καὶ ἀπῆλθεν ἡ ὀργή. πῶς οὖν ἀρεῖς; λογισάμενος ὅτι οὐκ αἰσχρόν· ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ μόνον ᾖ τὸ αἰσχρὸν κακόν, ἀνάγκη καὶ σὲ πολλὰ ἁμαρτάνειν καὶ λῃστὴν καὶ παντοῖον γενέσθαι. Ὄγδοον, ὅσῳ χαλεπώτερα ἐπιφέρουσιν αἱ ὀργαὶ καὶ λῦπαι αἱ ἐπὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις, ἤπερ αὐτά ἐστιν ἐφ’ οἷς ὀργιζόμεθα καὶ λυπούμεθα. Ἔνατον, ὅτι τὸ εὐμενὲς ἀνίκητον, ἐὰν γνήσιον ᾖ καὶ μὴ σεσηρὸς μηδὲ ὑπόκρισις. τί γάρ σοι ποιήσει ὁ ὑβριστικώτατος, ἐὰν διατελῇς εὐμενὴς αὐτῷ καί, εἰ οὕτως ἔτυχε, πρᾴως παραινῇς καὶ μεταδιδάσκῃς εὐσχολῶν παρ’ αὐτὸν ἐκεῖνον τὸν καιρὸν ὅτε κακοποιεῖν σε ἐπιχειρεῖ· ʽμή, τέκνον· πρὸς ἄλλο πεφύκαμεν. ἐγὼ μὲν οὐ μὴ βλαβῶ, σὺ δὲ βλάπτῃ, τέκνον.ʼ καὶ δεικνύναι εὐαφῶς καὶ ὁλικῶς ὅτι τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχει, ὅτι οὐδὲ μέλισσαι αὐτὸ ποιοῦσιν οὐδ’ ὅσα συναγελαστικὰ πέφυκε. δεῖ δὲ μήτε εἰρωνικῶς αὐτὸ ποιεῖν μήτε ὀνειδιστικῶς, ἀλλὰ φιλοστόργως καὶ ἀδήκτως τῇ ψυχῇ καὶ μὴ ὡς ἐν σχολῇ μηδὲ ἵνα ἄλλος παραστὰς θαυμάσῃ, ἀλλ’ ἤτοι πρὸς μόνον καὶ ἐὰν ἄλλοι τινὲς περιεστήκωσι. Τούτων τῶν ἐννέα κεφαλαίων μέμνησο ὡς παρὰ τῶν Μουσῶν δῶρα εἰληφὼς καὶ ἄρξαι ποτὲ ἄνθρωπος εἶναι, ἕως ζῇς. φυλακτέον δὲ ἐπίσης τῷ ὀργίζεσθαι αὐτοῖς τὸ κολακεύειν αὐτούς· ἀμφότερα γὰρ ἀκοινώνητα καὶ πρὸς βλάβην φέρει. πρόχειρον δὲ ἐν ταῖς ὀργαῖς ὅτι οὐχὶ τὸ θυμοῦσθαι ἀνδρικόν, ἀλλὰ τὸ πρᾷον καὶ ἥμερον ὥσπερ ἀνθρωπικώτερον, οὕτως καὶ ἀρρενικώτερον καὶ ἰσχύος καὶ νεύρων καὶ ἀνδρείας τούτῳ μέτεστιν, οὐχὶ τῷ ἀγανακτοῦντι καὶ δυσαρεστοῦντι· ὅσῳ γὰρ ἀπαθείᾳ τοῦτο οἰκειότερον, τοσούτῳ καὶ δυνάμει. ὥσπερ τε ἡ λύπη ἀσθενοῦς, οὕτως καὶ ἡ ὀργή· ἀμφότεροι γὰρ τέτρωνται καὶ ἐνδεδώκασιν. Εἰ δὲ βούλει, καὶ δέκατον παρὰ τοῦ Μουσηγέτου δῶρον λάβε, ὅτι τὸ μὴ ἀξιοῦν ἁμαρτάνειν τοὺς φαύλους μανικόν· ἀδυνάτου γὰρ ἐφίεται. τὸ δὲ συγχωρεῖν ἄλλοις μὲν εἶναι τοιούτους, ἀξιοῦν δὲ μὴ εἰς σὲ ἁμαρτάνειν, ἄγνωμον καὶ τυραννικόν.

members.text:
Whensoever any man doth trespass against other, presently consider
with thyself what it was that he did suppose to be good, what to be
evil, when he did trespass. For this when thou knowest, thou wilt pity
him thou wilt have no occasion either to wonder, or to be angry. For
either thou thyself dust yet live in that error and ignorance, as that
thou dust suppose either that very thing that he doth, or some other
like worldly thing, to be good; and so thou art bound to pardon him if
he have done that which thou in the like case wouldst have done thyself.
Or if so be that thou dost not any more suppose the same things to be
good or evil, that he doth; how canst thou but be gentle unto him that
is in an error?
members.english: Whenever someone does you some wrong, consider at once what they judged to be good or bad when they did the wrong. For once you have seen this you will pity them, and will be neither surprised nor angry. For either you yourself still judge the same thing to be good as they do, or another thing of the same kind; so you must forgive. But if you no longer judge such things to be good and bad, you will more easily be kind to one who fails to see.
members.greek: Ὅταν τις ἁμάρτῃ τι εἰς σέ, εὐθὺς ἐνθυμοῦ τί ἀγαθὸν ἢ κακὸν ὑπολαβὼν ἥμαρτε. τοῦτο γὰρ ἰδὼν ἐλεήσεις αὐτὸν καὶ οὔτε θαυμάσεις οὔτε ὀργισθήσῃ. ἤτοι γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸς τὸ αὐτὸ ἐκείνῳ ἀγαθὸν ἔτι ὑπολαμβάνεις ἢ ἄλλο ὁμοειδές· δεῖ οὖν συγγινώσκειν. εἰ δὲ μηκέτι ὑπολαμβάνεις τὰ τοιαῦτα ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακά, ῥᾷον εὐμενὴς ἔσῃ τῷ παρορῶντι.

members.text:
When thou art offended with any man's transgression, presently
reflect upon thyself; and consider what thou thyself art guilty of in
the same kind. As that thou also perchance dost think it a happiness
either to be rich, or to live in pleasure, or to be praised and
commended, and so of the rest in particular. For this if thou shalt call
to mind, thou shalt soon forget thine anger; especially when at the same
time this also shall concur in thy thoughts, that he was constrained by
his error and ignorance so to do: for how can he choose as long as he
is of that opinion? Do thou therefore if thou canst, take away that from
him, that forceth him to do as he doth.
members.english: Whenever you take offence at someone’s wrongdoing, turn at once to yourself and reckon up what wrong of a similar kind you do: for example, judging money to be a good, or pleasure, or a scrap of reputation, and so on, kind by kind. For when you put your mind to this you will quickly forget your anger, as it strikes you at the same time that they are being forced: for what are they to do? Or, if you can, take away from them what is forcing them.
members.greek: Ὅταν προσκόπτῃς ἐπί τινος ἁμαρτίᾳ, εὐθὺς μεταβὰς ἐπιλογίζου τί παρόμοιον ἁμαρτάνεις· οἷον, ἀργύριον ἀγαθὸν εἶναι κρίνων ἢ τὴν ἡδονὴν ἢ τὸ δοξάριον καὶ κατ’ εἶδος. τούτῳ γὰρ ἐπιβάλλων ταχέως ἐπιλήσῃ τῆς ὀργῆς, συμπροσπίπτοντος τοῦ ὅτι βιάζεται· τί γὰρ ποιήσει; ἤ, εἰ δύνασαι, ἄφελε αὐτοῦ τὸ βιαζόμενον.

members.text:
In the country of the Quadi at Granua, these. Betimes in the morning
say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man,
with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an
unsociable uncharitable man. All these ill qualities have happened unto
them, through ignorance of that which is truly good and truly bad. But I
that understand the nature of that which is good, that it only is to
be desired, and of that which is bad, that it only is truly odious and
shameful: who know moreover, that this transgressor, whosoever he be, is
my kinsman, not by the same blood and seed, but by participation of the
same reason, and of the same divine particle; How can I either be
hurt by any of those, since it is not in their power to make me incur
anything that is truly reproachful? or angry, and ill affected towards
him, who by nature is so near unto me? for we are all born to be
fellow-workers, as the feet, the hands, and the eyelids; as the rows of
the upper and under teeth: for such therefore to be in opposition, is
against nature; and what is it to chafe at, and to be averse from, but
to be in opposition?
members.english: At dawn, say to yourself beforehand: I shall meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one, an unsocial one. All these things have come upon them through ignorance of what is good and bad. But I, who have seen the nature of the good, that it is honourable, and of the bad, that it is shameful, and the nature of the very person who does wrong, that they are akin to me, sharing not the same blood or seed but mind and a portion of the divine, can neither be harmed by any of them, for no one will wrap me in what is shameful, nor be angry with one who is akin to me, nor hate them. For we have come into being to work together, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. So to work against one another is against nature; and to be indignant and to turn away is working against.
members.greek: Ἕωθεν προλέγειν ἑαυτῷ· συντεύξομαι περιέργῳ, ἀχαρίστῳ, ὑβριστῇ, δολερῷ, βασκάνῳ, ἀκοινωνήτῳ· πάντα ταῦτα συμβέβηκεν ἐκείνοις παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τῶν ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν. ἐγὼ δὲ τεθεωρηκὼς τὴν φύσιν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ὅτι καλόν, καὶ τοῦ κακοῦ ὅτι αἰσχρόν, καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἁμαρτάνοντος φύσιν ὅτι μοι συγγενής, οὐχὶ αἵματος ἢ σπέρματος τοῦ αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ νοῦ καὶ θείας ἀπομοίρας μέτοχος, οὔτε βλαβῆναι ὑπό τινος αὐτῶν δύναμαι· αἰσχρῷ γάρ με οὐδεὶς περιβαλεῖ· οὔτε ὀργίζεσθαι τῷ συγγενεῖ δύναμαι οὔτε ἀπέχθεσθαι αὐτῷ. γεγόναμεν γὰρ πρὸς συνεργίαν ὡς πόδες, ὡς χεῖρες, ὡς βλέφαρα, ὡς οἱ στοῖχοι τῶν ἄνω καὶ κάτω ὀδόντων. τὸ οὖν ἀντιπράσσειν ἀλλήλοις παρὰ φύσιν· ἀντιπρακτικὸν δὲ τὸ ἀγανακτεῖν καὶ ἀποστρέφεσθαι.

members.text:
At the conceit and apprehension that such and such a one hath
sinned, thus reason with thyself; What do I know whether this be a sin
indeed, as it seems to be? But if it be, what do I know but that he
himself hath already condemned himself for it? And that is all one as
if a man should scratch and tear his own face, an object of compassion
rather than of anger. Again, that he that would not have a vicious man
to sin, is like unto him that would not have moisture in the fig, nor
children to welp nor a horse to neigh, nor anything else that in the
course of nature is necessary. For what shall he do that hath such an
habit? If thou therefore beest powerful and eloquent, remedy it if thou
canst.
members.english: In the case of someone who has given the impression of having done wrong: “But how do I know whether this is a wrong?” And if they did do wrong, that they have condemned themselves, and so this is like tearing one’s own face. That whoever does not want the bad person to do wrong is like someone who does not want the fig tree to bear sap in its figs, or babies to cry, or the horse to neigh, or any of the other things that have to be. For what are they to do, having a disposition like that? So if you are vigorous, cure that disposition.
members.greek: Ἐπὶ τοῦ φαντασίαν παρασχόντος ὅτι ἥμαρτε· τί δαὶ οἶδα εἰ τοῦτο ἁμάρτημα; εἰ δὲ καὶ ἥμαρτεν, ὅτι κατέκρινεν αὐτὸς ἑαυτόν, καὶ οὕτως ὅμοιον τοῦτο τῷ καταδρύπτειν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ὄψιν. Ὅτι ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸν φαῦλον ἁμαρτάνειν ὅμοιος τῷ μὴ θέλοντι τὴν συκῆν ὀπὸν ἐν τοῖς σύκοις φέρειν καὶ τὰ βρέφη κλαυθμυρίζεσθαι καὶ τὸν ἵππον χρεμετίζειν καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα ἀναγκαῖα. τί γὰρ πάθῃ τὴν ἕξιν ἔχων τοιαύτην; εἰ οὖν γοργὸς εἶ, ταύτην θεράπευσον.

members.text:
When any shall either impeach thee with false accusations, or
