hatefully reproach thee, or shall use any such carriage towards thee,
get thee presently to their minds and understandings, and look in them,
and behold what manner of men they be. Thou shalt see, that there is no
such occasion why it should trouble thee, what such as they are think of
thee. Yet must thou love them still, for by nature they are thy friends.
And the Gods themselves, in those things that they seek from them as
matters of great moment, are well content, all manner of ways, as by
dreams and oracles, to help them as well as others.
members.english: When someone else blames you or hates you, or people voice things of that kind, go to their little souls, pass inside and see what sort of people they are. You will see that you need not be torn apart so that these people may think this or that of you. You must wish them well, however; for by nature they are friends, and the gods too help them in every kind of way, through dreams, through oracles, yet toward the things those people care about.
members.greek: Ὅταν ἄλλος ψέγῃ σε ἢ μισῇ ἢ τοιαῦτά τινα ἐκφωνῶσιν, ἔρχου ἐπὶ τὰ ψυχάρια αὐτῶν, δίελθε ἔσω καὶ ἴδε ποῖοί τινές εἰσιν. ὄψει ὅτι οὐ δεῖ σε σπᾶσθαι, ἵνα τούτοις τί ποτε περὶ σοῦ δοκῇ. εὐνοεῖν μέντοι αὐτοῖς δεῖ· φύσει γὰρ φίλοι, καὶ οἱ θεοὶ δὲ παντοίως αὐτοῖς βοηθοῦσι, δι’ ὀνείρων, διὰ μαντειῶν, πρὸς ταῦτα μέντοι, πρὸς ἃ ἐκεῖνοι διαφέρονται.

members.text:
Will any contemn me? let him look to that, upon what grounds he
does it: my care shall be that I may never be found either doing or
speaking anything that doth truly deserve contempt. Will any hate me?
let him look to that. I for my part will be kind and loving unto all,
and even unto him that hates me, whom-soever he be, will I be ready to
show his error, not by way of exprobation or ostentation of my patience,
but ingenuously and meekly: such as was that famous Phocion, if so be
that he did not dissemble. For it is inwardly that these things must be:
that the Gods who look inwardly, and not upon the outward appearance,
may behold a man truly free from all indignation and grief. For what
hurt can it be unto thee whatsoever any man else doth, as long as thou
mayest do that which is proper and suitable to thine own nature? Wilt
not thou (a man wholly appointed to be both what, and as the common good
shall require) accept of that which is now seasonable to the nature
of the universe?
members.english: Will someone despise me? That is for them to see to. But I will see to it that I am not found doing or saying anything that deserves to be despised. Will they hate me? That is for them to see to. But I am kind and well-disposed to everyone, and ready to show this very person what they are failing to see, not with reproach, nor as if making a show of putting up with them, but genuinely and good-heartedly, like the famous Phocion, if indeed he was not pretending. For what is within must be like this, and a human being must be seen by the gods to be one who is not disposed to be indignant at anything and makes a grievance of nothing. For what is bad for you, if you yourself are now doing what is proper to your nature, and are accepting what is now in season for the nature of the whole, a human being straining toward this: that what is good for all in common should come about, by whatever means?
members.greek: Καταφρονήσει μού τις; ὄψεται. ἐγὼ δὲ ὄψομαι ἵνα μή τι καταφρονήσεως ἄξιον πράσσων ἣ λέγων εὑρίσκωμαι. μισήσει; ὄψεται. ἀλλὰ ἐγὼ εὐμενὴς καὶ εὔνους παντὶ καὶ τούτῳ αὐτῷ ἕτοιμος τὸ παρορώμενον δεῖξαι, οὐκ ὀνειδιστικῶς οὐδὲ ὡς κατεπιδεικνύμενος ὅτι ἀνέχομαι, ἀλλὰ γνησίως καὶ χρηστῶς, οἷος ὁ Φωκίων ἐκεῖνος, εἴ γε μὴ προσεποιεῖτο. τὰ ἔσω γὰρ δεῖ τοιαῦτα εἶναι καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν βλέπεσθαι ἄνθρωπον πρὸς μηδὲν ἀγανακτικῶς διατιθέμενον μηδὲ δεινοπαθοῦντα. τί γάρ σοι κακόν, εἰ αὐτὸς νῦν ποιεῖς τὸ τῇ φύσει σου οἰκεῖον καὶ δέχῃ τὸ νῦν τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει εὔκαιρον, ἄνθρωπος τεταμένος πρὸς τὸ γίνεσθαι δι’ ὅτου δὴ τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον;

members.text:
Suppose that at the palestra somebody hath all to-torn thee with
his nails, and hath broken thy head. Well, thou art wounded. Yet thou
dost not exclaim; thou art not offended with him. Thou dost not suspect
him for it afterwards, as one that watcheth to do thee a mischief. Yea
even then, though thou dost thy best to save thyself from him, yet not
from him as an enemy. It is not by way of any suspicious indignation,
but by way of gentle and friendly declination. Keep the same mind and
disposition in other parts of thy life also. For many things there be,
which we must conceit and apprehend, as though we had had to do with an
antagonist at the palestra. For as I said, it is very possible for us to
avoid and decline, though we neither suspect, nor hate.
members.english: In the gymnasium someone has scratched us with their nails, and butted us with their head and landed a blow; but we do not mark them down, nor take offence, nor suspect them afterwards of plotting against us. We are on our guard, certainly, yet not as against an enemy, nor with suspicion, but with a kindly stepping aside. Let something like this happen in the other parts of life too: let us overlook many things in those who are, as it were, our training partners. For it is possible, as I said, to step aside, and neither to suspect nor to hate.
members.greek: Ἐν τοῖς γυμνασίοις καὶ ὄνυξι κατέδρυψέ τις καὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ ἐρραγεὶς πληγὴν ἐποίησεν, ἀλλ’ οὔτε ἐπισημαινόμεθα οὔτε προσκόπτομεν οὔτε ὑφορώμεθα ὕστερον ὡς ἐπίβουλον· καίτοι φυλαττόμεθα, οὐ μέντοι ὡς ἐχθρὸν οὐδὲ μεθ’ ὑποψίας, ἀλλ’ ἐκκλίσεως εὐμενοῦς. τοιοῦτόν τι γινέσθω καὶ ἐν τοῖς λοιποῖς μέρεσι τοῦ βίου· πολλὰ παρενθυμώμεθα τῶν οἷον προσγυμναζομένων. ἔξεστι γάρ, ὡς ἔφην, ἐκκλίνειν καὶ μήτε ὑποπτεύειν μήτε ἀπέχθεσθαι.

members.text:
Is it not a cruel thing to forbid men to affect those things, which
they conceive to agree best with their own natures, and to tend most
to their own proper good and behoof? But thou after a sort deniest them
this liberty, as often as thou art angry with them for their sins. For
surely they are led unto those sins whatsoever they be, as to
their proper good and commodity. But it is not so (thou wilt object
perchance). Thou therefore teach them better, and make it appear unto
them: but be not thou angry with them.
members.english: How cruel it is not to let people go after the things that appear to them to suit them and to be good for them. And yet in a way you do not allow them to do this, whenever you are indignant that they do wrong. For they are certainly being carried toward things as suiting them and good for them. “But it is not so.” Then teach them and show them, without being indignant.
members.greek: Πῶς ὠμόν ἐστι μὴ ἐπιτρέπειν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ὁρμᾶν ἐπὶ τὰ φαινόμενα αὐτοῖς οἰκεῖα καὶ συμφέροντα. καίτοι τρόπον τινὰ οὐ συγχωρεῖς αὐτοῖς τοῦτο ποιεῖν, ὅταν ἀγανακτῇς, ὅτι ἁμαρτάνουσι· φέρονται γὰρ πάντως ὡς ἐπὶ οἰκεῖα καὶ συμφέροντα αὐτοῖς. —ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔχει οὕτως.— οὐκοῦν δίδασκε καὶ δείκνυε μὴ ἀγανακτῶν.

members.text:
An angry countenance is much against nature, and it is oftentimes
the proper countenance of them that are at the point of death. But were
it so, that all anger and passion were so thoroughly quenched in thee,
that it were altogether impossible to kindle it any more, yet herein
must not thou rest satisfied, but further endeavour by good consequence
of true ratiocination, perfectly to conceive and understand, that all
anger and passion is against reason. For if thou shalt not be sensible
of thine innocence; if that also shall be gone from thee, the comfort of
a good conscience, that thou doest all things according to reason: what
shouldest thou live any longer for? All things that now thou seest,
are but for a moment. That nature, by which all things in the world are
administered, will soon bring change and alteration upon them, and then
of their substances make other things like unto them: and then soon
after others again of the matter and substance of these: that so by
these means, the world may still appear fresh and new.
members.english:
A scowl on the face is very much against nature. When it is often there, the look of the face dies in it, or in the end has been put out, so that it cannot be kindled at all. Try to grasp at least this very point, that it is against reason. For if even the awareness of doing wrong is going to go, what cause is there still for living?

Everything you see, the nature that governs the whole will change in almost no time, and will make other things out of their substance, and again others out of the substance of those, so that the universe may always be young.
members.greek:
Τὸ ἐπίκοτον τοῦ προσώπου λίαν παρὰ φύσιν, ὅταν πολλάκις ἐναποθνῄσκειν ᾖ πρόσχημα ἢ τὸ τελευταῖον ἀπεσβέσθη, ὥστε ὅλως ἐξαφθῆναι μὴ δύνασθαι. αὐτῷ γε τούτῳ παρακολουθεῖν πειρῶ, ὅτι παρὰ τὸν λόγον. εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἡ συναίσθησις τοῦ ἁμαρτάνειν οἰχήσεται, τίς ἔτι τοῦ ζῆν αἰτία;

Πάντα ὅσα ὁρᾷς ὅσον οὔπω μεταβαλεῖ ἡ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦσα φύσις καὶ ἄλλα ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν ποιήσει καὶ πάλιν ἄλλα ἐκ τῆς ἐκείνων οὐσίας, ἵνα ἀεὶ νεαρὸς ᾖ ὁ κόσμος.

members.text:
Either teach them better if it be in thy power; or if it be not,
remember that for this use, to bear with them patiently, was mildness
and goodness granted unto thee. The Gods themselves are good unto such;
yea and in some things, (as in matter of health, of wealth, of honour,)
are content often to further their endeavours: so good and gracious are
they. And mightest thou not be so too? or, tell me, what doth hinder
thee?
members.english: If you can, teach them otherwise; and if not, remember that kindness has been given to you for this. The gods too are kind to such people, and toward some things they even work with them, toward health, toward wealth, toward reputation: so good are they. You may be so too; or tell me, who is stopping you?
members.greek: Εἰ μὲν δύνασαι, μεταδίδασκε· εἰ δὲ μή, μέμνησο ὅτι πρὸς τοῦτο ἡ εὐμένειά σοι δέδοται. καὶ οἱ θεοὶ δὲ εὐμενεῖς τοῖς τοιούτοις εἰσίν, εἰς ἔνια δὲ καὶ συνεργοῦσιν, εἰς ὑγίειαν, εἰς πλοῦτον, εἰς δόξαν· οὕτως εἰσὶ χρηστοί. ἔξεστι δὲ καὶ σοί· ἢ εἰπέ, τίς ὁ κωλύων;

members.text:
To grow together like fellow branches in matter of good
correspondence and affection; but not in matter of opinions. They that
shall oppose thee in thy right courses, as it is not in their power to
divert thee from thy good action, so neither let it be to divert thee
from thy good affection towards them. But be it thy care to keep thyself
constant in both; both in a right judgment and action, and in true
meekness towards them, that either shall do their endeavour to hinder
thee, or at least will be displeased with thee for what thou hast done.
For to fail in either (either in the one to give over for fear, or in
the other to forsake thy natural affection towards him, who by nature is
both thy friend and thy kinsman) is equally base, and much savouring of
the disposition of a cowardly fugitive soldier.
members.english:
To grow on the same stem, but not to hold the same principles.

Just as those who stand in your way as you go forward in accord with right reason will not be able to turn you aside from sound action, so let them not knock you out of your kindness toward them either; but keep watch over yourself on both counts alike: not only in steady judgment and action, but also in gentleness toward those who try to hinder you or are otherwise annoyed. For this too is weakness, to be harsh with them, just as it is to abandon the action and give in from fright. For both are equally deserters from their post: the one who has flinched, and the one who has become estranged from a person who is by nature kin and friend.
members.greek:
Ὁμοθαμνεῖν μέν, μὴ ὁμοδογματεῖν δέ.

Οἱ ἐνιστάμενοι προιόντι σοι κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον ὥσπερ ἀπὸ τῆς ὑγιοῦς πράξεως ἀποτρέψαι σε οὐ δυνήσονται, οὕτως μηδὲ τῆς πρὸς αὐτοὺς εὐμενείας ἐκκρουέτωσαν, ἀλλὰ φύλασσε σεαυτὸν ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέρων ὁμοίως, μὴ μόνον ἐπὶ τῆς εὐσταθοῦς κρίσεως καὶ πράξεως, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς πρὸς τοὺς κωλύειν ἐπιχειροῦντας ἢ ἄλλως δυσχεραίνοντας πρᾳότητος. καὶ γὰρ τοῦτο ἀσθενές, τὸ χαλεπαίνειν αὐτοῖς, ὥσπερ τὸ ἀποστῆναι τῆς πράξεως καὶ ἐνδοῦναι καταπλαγέντα· ἀμφότεροι γὰρ ἐπίσης λειποτάκται, ὁ μὲν ὑποτρέσας, ὁ δὲ ἀλλοτριωθεὶς πρὸς τὸν φύσει συγγενῆ καὶ φίλον.

members.text:
Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose
arm holes, are offensive. What can he do? such is his breath naturally,
and such are his arm holes; and from such, such an effect, and such
a smell must of necessity proceed. 'O, but the man (sayest thou) hath
understanding in him, and might of himself know, that he by standing
near, cannot choose but offend.' And thou also (God bless thee!) hast
understanding. Let thy reasonable faculty, work upon his reasonable
faculty; show him his fault, admonish him. If he hearken unto thee, thou
hast cured him, and there will be no more occasion of anger.
members.english: Surely you are not angry with the person who stinks like a goat? Surely you are not angry with the one whose breath smells? What do you want them to do? The person has that kind of mouth, has that kind of armpits; from such things such a smell must come. “But a human being has reason,” someone says, “and can work out, by stopping to think, where they are at fault.” Good for you! Well then, you have reason too: stir a rational disposition with a rational disposition; show them, remind them. For if they listen, you will cure them, and there is no need of anger.
members.greek: Τῷ γράσωνι μήτι ὀργίζῃ, μήτι τῷ ὀζοστόμῳ ὀργίζῃ; τί σοι ποιήσει; τοιοῦτον στόμα ἔχει, τοιαύτας μάλας ἔχει, ἀνάγκη τοιαύτην ἀποφορὰν ἀπὸ τοιούτων γίνεσθαι. —ἀλλ’ ὁ ἄνθρωπος λόγον ἔχει, φησί, καὶ δύναται συννοεῖν ἐφιστάνων τί πλημμελεῖ.—εὖ σοι γένοιτο· τοιγαροῦν καὶ σὺ λόγον ἔχεις, κίνησον λογικῇ διαθέσει λογικὴν διάθεσιν, δεῖξον, ὑπόμνησον· εἰ γὰρ ἐπαίει, θεραπεύσεις καὶ οὐ χρεία ὀργῆς.

members.text:
Him that offends, to teach with love and meek ness, and to show him
his error. But if thou canst not, then to blame thyself; or rather not
thyself neither, if thy will and endeavours have not been wanting.
members.english: If someone is mistaken, teach them kindly and show them what they are failing to see. But if you cannot, blame yourself, or not even yourself.
members.greek: Εἰ μὲν σφάλλεται, διδάσκειν εὐμενῶς καὶ τὸ παρορώμενον δεικνύναι. εἰ δὲ ἀδυνατεῖς, σεαυτὸν αἰτιᾶσθαι ἢ μηδὲ σεαυτόν.

members.text:
Take heed lest at any time thou stand so affected, though towards
unnatural evil men, as ordinary men are commonly one towards another.
members.english: See that you never come to feel toward the inhuman anything like what the inhuman feel toward human beings.
members.greek: Ὅρα μήποτέ τι τοιοῦτον πάθῃς πρὸς τοὺς ἀπανθρώπους, οἷον οἱ ἀπάνθρωποι πρὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους.

members.text:
To them that are sick of the jaundice, honey seems bitter; and to
them that are bitten by a mad dog, the water terrible; and to children,
a little ball seems a fine thing. And why then should I be angry? or
do I think that error and false opinion is less powerful to make men
transgress, than either choler, being immoderate and excessive, to cause
the jaundice; or poison, to cause rage?
members.english: To people with jaundice honey appears bitter, and to those bitten by a mad dog water appears frightening, and to small children their little ball appears beautiful. Why, then, am I angry? Or do you think that a false belief has less power than the bile has over the person with jaundice and the poison over the one bitten by a mad dog?
members.greek: Ἰκτεριῶσι τὸ μέλι πικρὸν φαίνεται καὶ λυσσοδήκτοις τὸ ὕδωρ φοβερὸν καὶ παιδίοις τὸ σφαιρίον καλόν. τί οὖν ὀργίζομαι; ἢ δοκεῖ σοι ἔλασσον ἰσχύειν τὸ διεψευσμένον ἢ τὸ χόλιον τῷ ἰκτεριῶντι καὶ ὁ ἰὸς τῷ λυσσοδήκτῳ;

members.why: About counterfeit frankness, a “wolf’s friendship”, and how real goodness shows in the eyes. It does not speak of meeting someone who wrongs me.
members.text:
How rotten and insincere is he, that saith, I am resolved to carry
myself hereafter towards you with all ingenuity and simplicity. O man,
what doest thou mean! what needs this profession of thine? the thing
itself will show it. It ought to be written upon thy forehead. No sooner
thy voice is heard, than thy countenance must be able to show what is in
thy mind: even as he that is loved knows presently by the looks of his
sweetheart what is in her mind. Such must he be for all the world, that
is truly simple and good, as he whose arm-holes are offensive, that
whosoever stands by, as soon as ever he comes near him, may as it were
smell him whether he will or no. But the affectation of simplicity
is nowise laudable. There is nothing more shameful than perfidious
friendship. Above all things, that must be avoided. However true
goodness, simplicity, and kindness cannot so be hidden, but that as
we have already said in the very eyes and countenance they will show
themselves.
members.english: How rotten and counterfeit is the person who says: “I have chosen to be straightforward with you.” What are you doing, man? This is not a thing to announce beforehand. It will show of itself. It ought to be written on the forehead. At once the voice has that ring, at once it stands out in the eyes, just as the one who is loved at once knows everything in the look of the lovers. In short, the straightforward and good person must be like someone who stinks like a goat, so that whoever stands near notices as soon as they come up, whether they want to or not. But a studied straightforwardness is a dagger. Nothing is more shameful than a wolf’s friendship: shun this above all things. The good and straightforward and kind person has these things in the eyes, and it does not escape notice.
members.greek: Ὡς σαπρὸς καὶ κίβδηλος ὁ λέγων· ἐγὼ προῄρημαι ἁπλῶς σοι προσφέρεσθαι. τί ποιεῖς, ἄνθρωπε; τοῦτο οὐ δεῖ προλέγειν. αὐτὸ φανήσεται· ἐπὶ τοῦ μετώπου γεγράφθαι ὀφείλει· εὐθὺς ἡ φωνὴ τοιοῦτον ἠχεῖ, εὐθὺς ἐν τοῖς ὄμμασιν ἐξέχει, ὡς τῶν ἐραστῶν ἐν τῷ βλέμματι πάντα εὐθὺς γνωρίζει ὁ ἐρώμενος. τοιοῦτον ὅλως δεῖ τὸν ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι, οἶον γράσωνα, ἵνα ὁ παραστὰς ἅμα τῷ προσελθεῖν, θέλει οὐ θέλει, αἴσθηται. ἐπιτήδευσις δὲ ἁπλότητος σκάλμη ἐστίν. οὐδέν ἐστιν αἴσχιον λυκοφιλίας· πάντων μάλιστα τοῦτο φεῦγε. ὁ ἀγαθὸς καὶ ἁπλοῦς καὶ εὐμενὴς ἐν τοῖς ὄμμασιν ἔχουσι ταῦτα καὶ οὐ λανθάνει.

members.text:
All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or
bear with them.
members.english: Human beings have come into being for one another’s sake. So either teach them or bear with them.
members.greek: Οἱ ἄνθρωποι γεγόνασιν ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν· ἢ δίδασκε οὖν ἢ φέρε.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 9.43 is 9.42, 7.34 is 7.62–63, 11.16 is 11.17–18, 7.19 is 7.26, 1.15 is 2.1, 12.12 is 12.16, 9.25 is 9.27, 11.12 is 11.13, 6.19 is 6.20, 6.25 is 6.27, 7.18 is 7.24–25, 9.9 is 9.11, 11.8 is 11.8b–9, 5.22 is 5.28a, 7.36 is 7.65, 6.52 is 6.57 and 8.56 is 8.59; 10.30 and 10.4 are the same.

Keeps eight fused claims, more than the three to five of a smaller section. The section has twenty passages, and each claim rests on words that two of them say; merging any two would join things the passages keep apart, such as being wronged and being despised.

Keeps claim 4 at five passages, the most one claim can carry on the page. 5.22 and 6.25 also say to show or teach them; they are quoted as said-once items for what each says alone, and their words on teaching are not counted.

Reads the scowl of 7.18 as an angry face, from its Greek word for a grudging look. Its next sentence is reconstructed from Greek that does not construe and is not quoted. Claim 3’s “the things they care about” rests on a reading of 9.25 (9.27 in modern editions) that the translators mark as unchecked; their other reading, “the things those people quarrel over”, would not support it.
articles.limit: 11.16, Marcus’s nine headings against anger, feeds five of the eight claims and two said-once items, so the article leans on one passage, and in the statement “bear with them” is 8.56’s word alone. Much of it is said elsewhere: Article 28 (claim 1, and 9.37) that a wrong harms only the one who does it and that perhaps no wrong was done, Article 8 (claim 2) that harm lies in my judgment, Article 7 that taking the judgment away removes the trouble (this article’s 11.16 heading), Article 15 (claim 4, and 7.41) that I set them right if I can and that the gods bear with bad people, Article 26 (claim 5) that I ask what they hold good and bad and begin with myself, Article 29 that I must not become like them (this article’s 7.36), Article 10’s 7.16 that they go wrong through ignorance and we will both soon be dead, Article 22 (claim 1) that blame does not pull me away, Articles 1 and 5 that we are kin and made for one another, and Article 2 (claim 1) that I mean well by my own kind, to which claim 3 here adds that the gods too are kind to those who offend; what this article adds is the moment of being wronged, gathered in one place: why they act as they do, the exercise of looking into them and into myself, what failing looks like, and the doubt whether it was a wrong at all. It disagrees with Article 28, which holds that the wrongdoer can be rid of the wrong as soon as they wish and that a wrong done from desire comes from one’s own impulse (2.7), while claim 1 here says they act against their will and can do nothing else; this section never considers the willing wrongdoer, so the two articles are not reconciled.

articles.title: Taking a thing apart: material, cause, purpose and time

statement.t: I look at what each thing itself is, I take it apart into its material, its cause and its purpose, and I ask how long it lasts.

parts.words: I look at what each thing itself is
I take it apart into its material, its cause and its purpose
I ask how long it lasts

statement.kind: What I look at, then how I take it apart
statement.form: Claim 2 says what I look at: the thing itself behind the impression, and what is its own. Claim 1 gives the method: 12.14, 12.7 and 8.10 divide a thing under the same heads. The statement puts the two in that order.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the division into material and cause gains a second author, and so does asking what each thing is and what it is worth. The article gains what Marcus leaves out here: why to look, since what I fear, seen as it is at bottom, holds nothing but my fear; what failing looks like; a rule that the parts must not be countless and tiny; and what holds if I cannot be certain which account of what causes things is true.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a reason: what I fear, stripped of what disturbs and confuses and seen as it is at bottom, holds nothing fearful except my fear.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: there must be, in the case of each thing, that from which it is made, and, next, an agent by which it is made. The former is its material, the latter its cause.
piece.follows: Every thing has something it is made from, its material, and an agent that makes it, its cause.
piece.context: Letter 65, on the first cause, sets out the Stoic view that everything comes from cause and matter. “Each thing” is any thing that is made.
gives: its material
its cause

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Cause, however, by which we mean reason, moulds matter and turns it in whatever direction it will, producing thereby various concrete results.
piece.follows: The cause, which is reason, shapes matter as it wills and so produces particular things.
piece.context: Letter 65 gives the Stoic account of cause and matter: matter lies idle until something moves it, and the cause, reason, is what moves and shapes it.
gives: the active element that shapes the material into this thing

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called
piece.follows: I should give each thing its value by asking what it is, not what it is called.
piece.context: Letter 95, on why precepts need principles: before using things, decide what to think of each, such as poverty, riches, renown, disgrace and exile.
gives: what the thing itself is
its worth

items.label: why
items.t: When I strip what I fear of all that disturbs and confuses and see what it is at bottom, I find nothing fearful in it except my fear.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section says why I should look at the thing itself. Seneca gives a reason for the things I fear: seen as they are, they hold nothing fearful but the fear.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom
support.follows: I should strip things of whatever disturbs and confuses, and see what each one is at bottom.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: Lucilius fears a lawsuit an angry opponent threatens. The “things” are what he fears: losing the case and, as the letter goes on, pain and death.
gives: I strip what I fear of all that disturbs and confuses
see what it is at bottom

support.author: seneca
support.quote: you will then comprehend that they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear.
support.follows: Once seen as they are, the things I fear turn out to hold nothing fearful except the fear.
support.context: Letter 24, advice to Lucilius under threat of a lawsuit. “They” are the feared things once stripped of what disturbs and seen as they are at bottom.
gives: I find nothing fearful in it except my fear

items.label: breaks
items.t: I fail when I agree too quickly with what people say and do not examine what I fear; then I retreat like soldiers who leave their camp because cattle raised a cloud of dust. The way back is to strip the mask from things and give each its own face again.
items.why: Marcus says in this section what to look at and how to take it apart, but not what it looks like when I fail to. Seneca names the failure in Letter 13, believing report instead of testing what I fear, and the unmasking in Letter 24. Joining the second to the first as the way back is the editor’s step; Seneca does not offer it as the cure for rumour.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: we agree too quickly with what people say. We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear; we do not examine into them; we blench and retreat just like soldiers who are forced to abandon their camp because of a dust-cloud raised by stampeding cattle
support.follows: We agree too quickly with what people say, we do not test what we fear, and we retreat like soldiers from a dust cloud raised by cattle.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: Lucilius fears trouble to come, and Seneca tells him to test whether the signs of it are sure, since rumour misleads us.
gives: I agree too quickly with what people say
do not examine what I fear
I retreat like soldiers who leave their camp because cattle raised a cloud of dust

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We should strip the mask, not only from men, but from things, and restore to each object its own aspect.
support.follows: We should take the mask off things as well as people, and let each be seen as it is.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: children are terrified by people they love wearing masks, and adults are the same with the things they fear, such as pain and death.
gives: strip the mask from things
give each its own face again

items.label: doubt
items.t: I cannot be certain which account of what causes things is absolutely true; I can still judge which seems truest.
items.why: No passage of Marcus here asks what holds if taking a thing apart does not reach the truth. Seneca, judging between the schools’ accounts of cause, says flatly that absolute truth is beyond us, and asks only for the account that seems truest. Placing his judgment on the schools’ accounts of the first cause beside Marcus’s method for taking a single thing apart is the editor’s step.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: state who seems to you to say what is truest, and not who says what is absolutely true. For to do that is as far beyond our ken as truth itself.
support.follows: I can judge which account seems truest; which is absolutely true is beyond what we can know.
support.context: Letter 65, on the first cause: after setting out the Stoic, Aristotle’s and Plato’s accounts of what causes things, Seneca asks Lucilius to judge between them.
gives: I cannot be certain which account of what causes things is absolutely true
I can still judge which seems truest

items.label: practice
items.t: When I break a large thing into parts to know it better, the parts must not be countless and tiny: a thing cut as fine as dust is as hard to grasp as one not divided at all.
items.why: Marcus divides a thing under four heads and says nothing of how far division should go. Seneca, before dividing philosophy, gives a rule for breaking any large thing into parts, such as a people or an army.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Whatever has grown to greater size is more easily identified if it is broken up into parts; but the parts, as I have remarked, must not be countless in number and diminutive in size.
support.follows: A large thing is easier to know when divided into parts, but the parts must not be countless or tiny.
support.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy: before dividing philosophy for Lucilius, Seneca says how any large thing, like a people or an army, should be divided.
gives: When I break a large thing into parts to know it better
the parts must not be countless and tiny

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For over-analysis is faulty in precisely the same way as no analysis at all; whatever you cut so fine that it becomes dust is as good as blended into a mass again.
support.follows: Dividing too finely is as bad as not dividing: what is cut to dust becomes one mass again.
support.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy: Seneca will divide philosophy into parts but not into scraps, and says why too fine a division fails.
gives: a thing cut as fine as dust is as hard to grasp as one not divided at all

amend.t: ; what I fear, stripped of what disturbs and confuses and seen as it is at bottom, holds nothing fearful except my fear

passages.title: On the first cause
passages.text: So conversation was substituted for writing; and from this conversation I shall communicate to you the topic which is still the subject of debate; for we have appointed you referee. You have more of a task on your hands than you suppose, for the argument is threefold. Our Stoic philosophers, as you know, declare that there are two things in the universe which are the source of everything,—namely, cause and matter. Matter lies sluggish, a substance ready for any use, but sure to remain unemployed if no one sets it in motion. Cause, however, by which we mean reason, moulds matter and turns it in whatever direction it will, producing thereby various concrete results. Accordingly, there must be, in the case of each thing, that from which it is made, and, next, an agent by which it is made. The former is its material, the latter its cause.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: Next, after considering gods and men, let us see how we should make use of things. It is useless for us to have mouthed out precepts, unless we begin by reflecting what opinion we ought to hold concerning everything—concerning poverty, riches, renown, disgrace, citizenship, exile. Let us banish rumour and set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called.

passages.title: On despising death [ 1 ]
passages.text: Therefore, when your enemy threatens, listen unconcernedly. Although your conscience makes you confident, yet, since many things have weight which are outside your case, both hope for that which is utterly just, and prepare yourself against that which is utterly unjust. Remember, however, before all else, to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom; you will then comprehend that they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear.

passages.title: On groundless fears
passages.text: “But,” you say, “something will happen to it.” First of all, consider whether your proofs of future trouble are sure. For it is more often the case that we are troubled by our apprehensions, and that we are mocked by that mocker, rumour, which is wont to settle wars, but much more often settles individuals. Yes, my dear Lucilius; we agree too quickly with what people say. We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear; we do not examine into them; we blench and retreat just like soldiers who are forced to abandon their camp because of a dust-cloud raised by stampeding cattle, or are thrown into a panic by the spreading of some unauthenticated rumour.

passages.title: On despising death [ 1 ]
passages.text: What you see happening to boys happens also to ourselves, who are only slightly bigger boys: when those whom they love, with whom they daily associate, with whom they play, appear with masks on, the boys are frightened out of their wits. We should strip the mask, not only from men, but from things, and restore to each object its own aspect.

passages.title: On the first cause
passages.text: The purpose is his object in so doing. Do you ask what God’s purpose is? It is goodness. Plato, at any rate, says: “What was God’s reason for creating the world? God is good, and no good person is grudging of anything that is good. Therefore, God made it the best world possible.” Hand down your opinion, then, O judge; state who seems to you to say what is truest, and not who says what is absolutely true. For to do that is as far beyond our ken as truth itself.

passages.title: On the parts of philosophy
passages.text: The people are divided into tribes, the army into centuries. Whatever has grown to greater size is more easily identified if it is broken up into parts; but the parts, as I have remarked, must not be countless in number and diminutive in size. For over-analysis is faulty in precisely the same way as no analysis at all; whatever you cut so fine that it becomes dust is as good as blended into a mass again.

claims.t: I take each thing apart into its material and its cause, the active element that shapes the material into this thing. I ask what it is for and what it does in the universe, and how long it lasts before it is over.
claims.shared: 12.14 and 12.7 both say “dividing” and name the same heads: the material (12.7: “matter”), the cause and the purpose. 8.10 asks for the same heads as questions, “what in it is substance and material, and what is cause?”, and, like 12.14, it asks about the time: how long the thing lasts.
claims.changed: “The active element that shapes the material into this thing” is the editor’s gloss on “cause”, taken from the translators’ note: in Stoic use the cause is not an earlier event. 12.14’s “open it out” is folded into “take apart”. 12.7 has no time. 8.10 asks what the thing does in the universe where the other two say “purpose”; the claim keeps both.

support.quote: open it out, dividing it into the cause, into the material, into the purpose, into the time within which it will have to be over
support.follows: I should open a thing out by dividing it into its cause, its material, its purpose and the time by which it will be over.
gives: I take each thing apart
its material
its cause
what it is for
how long it lasts
before it is over

support.quote: dividing them into matter, cause, purpose
support.follows: I should divide things into their matter, their cause and their purpose.
gives: I take each thing apart
its material
its cause
what it is for

support.quote: What in it is substance and material, and what is cause?
support.follows: Of a thing I can ask what in it is its material and what is its cause.
gives: its material
its cause

support.quote: What does it do in the universe?
support.follows: Of a thing I can ask what it does in the universe.
gives: what it does in the universe

support.quote: And how long does it last?
support.follows: Of a thing I can ask how long it lasts.
gives: how long it lasts

claims.t: When something makes an impression on me, I always look to see in full what the thing itself is: its own make-up, its own quality and its worth. I look inside it and do not let its quality or its worth run past me.
claims.shared: 12.14 and 8.10 both ask what the thing itself is (12.14: “what that thing itself is”; 8.10: “what is it in itself”). 8.10 and 6.3 both point to what is the thing’s own (“its own make-up”, “its own quality”; the Greek has the same word for “own” in both).
claims.changed: 12.14 speaks of the thing that produces the impression; 8.10 and 6.3 do not mention impressions. 6.3’s “Look inside” could also mean inside myself; the claim reads it, with the translation, as inside the thing. “See in full” follows the translation of εἰς τὸ πᾶν; the Greek could also mean “look to the whole”.

support.quote: Always see in full what that thing itself is which produces the impression in you
support.follows: Each time something makes an impression on me, I should see in full what the thing itself is.
gives: When something makes an impression on me
I always look to see in full
what the thing itself is

support.quote: This thing, what is it in itself, in its own make-up?
support.follows: Of a thing before me I can ask what it is in itself, in the way it is made up.
gives: what the thing itself is
its own make-up

support.quote: Look inside. With any thing, do not let either its own quality or its worth run past you.
support.follows: I should look inside, and not let the quality or the worth of any thing go by me unnoticed.
gives: its own quality and its worth
I look inside it
do not let its quality or its worth run past me

single.quote: Continually, and with every impression if possible, reason about nature, reason about the passions, practise dialectic.
single.label: Three studies
single.t: Continually, and with every impression if I can, I reason about nature, I reason about the passions, and I practise dialectic, the art of reasoning correctly.
single.why: Only this passage names these three studies. 12.14 also says “always” and speaks of an impression, but it asks for a different act, seeing what the thing is, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: With every impression I can, I should keep reasoning about nature and about the passions, and keep practising dialectic.

single.quote: Pay attention to the thing before you, or to the principle, or to the activity, or to what is meant.
single.label: Four things to attend to
single.t: I pay attention to the thing before me, or to the principle involved, or to the activity going on, or to what the words mean.
single.why: Only this passage names these four. Its first, the thing before me, is near 12.14’s “that thing itself”, but no other passage names the other three, and its “or” offers a choice among four rather than a division of one thing.
single.follows: I should attend to the thing before me, or to the principle, or to the activity, or to what is meant.

members.text:
Of everything that presents itself unto thee, to consider what the
true nature of it is, and to unfold it, as it were, by dividing it into
that which is formal: that which is material: the true use or end of it,
and the just time that it is appointed to last.
members.english: Always see in full what that thing itself is which produces the impression in you, and open it out, dividing it into the cause, into the material, into the purpose, into the time within which it will have to be over.
members.greek: εἰς τὸ πᾶν ἀεὶ ὁρᾶν, τί ἐστιν αὐτὸ ἐκεῖνο τὸ τὴν φαντασίαν σοι ποιοῦν, καὶ ἀναπτύσσειν διαιροῦντα εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικόν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον, ἐντὸς οὗ πεπαῦσθαι αὐτὸ δεήσει.

members.text:
All worldly things thou must behold and consider, dividing them
into matter, form, and reference, or their proper end.
members.english: See things as being of this kind, dividing them into matter, cause, purpose.
members.greek: Τοιαῦτα τὰ πράγματα ὁρᾶν, διαιροῦντα εἰς ὕλην, αἴτιον, ἀναφοράν.

members.text:
This, what is it in itself, and by itself, according to its proper
constitution? What is the substance of it? What is the matter, or proper
use? What is the form or efficient cause? What is it for in this world,
and how long will it abide? Thus must thou examine all things, that
present themselves unto thee.
members.english: This thing, what is it in itself, in its own make-up? What in it is substance and material, and what is cause? What does it do in the universe? And how long does it last?
members.greek: Τοῦτο τί ἐστιν αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ, τί μὲν τὸ οὐσιῶδες αὐτοῦ καὶ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες, τί δὲ ποιεῖ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, πόσον δὲ χρόνον ὑφίσταται;

members.text:
As every fancy and imagination presents itself unto thee, consider
(if it be possible) the true nature, and the proper qualities of it, and
reason with thyself about it.
members.english: Continually, and with every impression if possible, reason about nature, reason about the passions, practise dialectic.
members.greek: Διηνεκῶς καὶ ἐπὶ πάσης, εἰ οἶόν τε, φαντασίας φυσιολογεῖν, παθολογεῖν, διαλεκτικεύεσθαι.

members.text:
Look in, let not either the proper quality, or the true worth of
anything pass thee, before thou hast fully apprehended it.
members.english: Look inside. With any thing, do not let either its own quality or its worth run past you.
members.greek: Ἔσω βλέπε· μηδενὸς πράγματος μήτε ἡ ἰδία ποιότης μήτε ἡ ἀξία παρατρεχέτω σε.

members.text:
That which must be the subject of thy consideration, is either the
matter itself, or the dogma, or the operation, or the true sense and
signification.
members.english: Pay attention to the thing before you, or to the principle, or to the activity, or to what is meant.
members.greek: Πρόσεχε τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ ἢ τῷ δόγματι ἢ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ ἢ τῷ σημαινομένῳ.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s: 12.14 is 12.17b in modern editions, 12.7 is 12.10, 8.10 is 8.11, 8.12 is 8.13 and 8.20 is 8.22a; 6.3 is 6.3 in both.

Explains “cause” in claim 1 as the active element that shapes the material, following the translators’ note. No quote of Marcus is mapped to these words; Seneca’s Ep. 65.2 backs them when his voice is on.
Keeps 8.10’s question “What does it do in the universe?” beside “purpose” as its own item. The translators read the two as the same head of the list; the claim does not merge them.
Reads 6.3’s “Look inside” as looking inside the thing, as the translation leans. The Greek could also mean looking inside oneself.
Follows the translation’s “see in full” in 12.14 (claim 2). The Greek εἰς τὸ πᾶν could also mean “look to the whole”, the whole of the thing or the universe.

Adds the editor’s glosses to two said-once items, from the translators’ notes: in 8.12 “the art of reasoning correctly” for dialectic; in 8.20 “involved”, “going on” and “what the words mean” for Marcus’s bare “the principle”, “the activity” and “what is meant”.
Leaves out 12.7’s first words, “See things as being of this kind”: “of this kind” points to nothing in the passage, and the translators’ note leaves it open.
articles.limit: Article 4, claim 4 already says that I ask what causes each thing, the power at work in it apart from its matter. Article 11, claim 4 is the same exercise: I look at whatever comes up stripped bare, what it is in its substance, what it is put together from, how long it lasts and what it is worth; and Article 7, claim 5 says I see things as they are. This article adds Marcus’s full division into material, cause, purpose and time, and the rule to look past the impression to the thing itself. No passage of the section says why I should do this, or what failing at it looks like. The two fused claims both lean on 12.14 and 8.10.

articles.title: Wiping out impressions, checking impulses

statement.t: It is up to me to keep wiping out impressions and to make every impulse with a reservation, on condition that nothing prevents it.

parts.words: It is up to me
to keep wiping out impressions
to make every impulse with a reservation

statement.kind: A power and its daily exercise
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the ground: what is in my soul is up to me, and the mind kept to itself cannot be harmed. Claims 3 to 6 exercise that power on impressions, impulses, desire and acts, including what to do when an act is blocked.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claim 2 (my mind cannot be harmed) and claim 4 (impulse by worth, desire kept out) gain a second author, and the article gains how an impression leads to an act, worth, impulse and action as three steps in order, what being carried along by impulse looks like, and what to do if I leave open what is in my power. He limits claim 1: once a passion is let in, it is no longer in my power; and claim 4: keeping desire out still leaves me free to wish.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains one clause: my actions must then agree with my impulses.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: The soul stands on unassailable ground, if it has abandoned external things; it is independent in its own fortress; and every weapon that is hurled falls short of the mark.
piece.follows: A soul that has let go of external things stands where it cannot be attacked, and nothing thrown at it reaches it.
piece.context: Letter 82, on the fear of death: no retreat keeps fear and pain out, so Seneca tells Lucilius to wall himself in with philosophy. “It” is the soul.
gives: my mind cannot be harmed

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: For it is easier to keep a thing out than to keep it under after you have let it in.
piece.follows: Keeping a thing out is easier than holding it down once it has been let in.
piece.context: Letter 85 argues against keeping the passions moderate. The “thing” is a passion, such as the sadness, fear and desire named two sections before.
gives: I keep desire out

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: impulse toward an object arises in each case from the worth of the object
piece.follows: Each impulse toward an object arises from that object’s worth.
piece.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy, after its three duties of worth, impulse and action: life agrees with itself when each impulse matches its object’s worth.
gives: I go by the worth of each thing

items.label: why
items.t: Nothing moves me to act until an impression stirs me; then an impulse comes, and my assent confirms it. I walk only after giving myself the order and approving it.
items.why: In this section Marcus tells me to wipe out impressions and to check impulses, but he does not say how the two lead to an act. Seneca gives the order: an impression, then an impulse, then my assent.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Every living thing possessed of reason is inactive if it is not first stirred by some external impression; then the impulse comes, and finally assent confirms the impulse.
support.follows: A reasoning being does nothing until an impression stirs it; the impulse follows, and assent confirms the impulse.
support.context: Letter 113, arguing that the virtues are not living things. Seneca first sets out how any reasoning being comes to act.
gives: Nothing moves me to act until an impression stirs me
then an impulse comes, and my assent confirms it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do walk, but only after uttering the command to myself and approving this opinion of mine.
support.follows: Seneca walks only after he has told himself to and has approved that judgment.
support.context: Letter 113, Seneca’s example of assent. “This opinion of mine” is his judgment that he ought to take a walk.
gives: I walk only after giving myself the order and approving it

items.label: action
items.t: I first weigh what each thing is worth, then form an ordered impulse toward it, and then make my actions agree with my impulse.
items.why: Marcus says here that an impulse should be according to worth (11.31), but not that this is one of three steps in order. Seneca sets them out: settle what a thing is worth, then form the impulse, then make action agree with it. The last step is new.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the first duty is to determine severally what things are worth; the second, to conceive with regard to them a regulated and ordered impulse; the third, to make your impulse and your actions harmonize
support.follows: First settle what each thing is worth, then form an ordered impulse toward it, then make impulse and action agree.
support.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy: Seneca splits its moral part into three, the worth of things, impulse and action. “Them” are the things whose worth is set.
gives: I first weigh what each thing is worth
then form an ordered impulse toward it
then make my actions agree with my impulse

items.label: breaks
items.t: It is a disgrace to be carried along by impulse instead of going forward, and then to ask, dazed, in the middle of events: “How did I get into this condition?”
items.why: Marcus shows failure here as the divine part beaten by the body (11.17). Seneca shows another failure: being driven by impulse without forethought, and waking up in the middle of events. Joining “driven by impulse” and “carried along” into one sentence is the editor’s; in the letter they are two sentences apart.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: He has not been led to that pass by forethought; he has been driven to it by impulse.
support.follows: Whoever craves something got there by impulse, not by thinking ahead.
support.context: Letter 37, on the oath a person takes to virtue. “He” is any man who craves something without knowing how he came to crave it.
gives: by impulse

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is disgraceful, instead of proceeding ahead, to be carried along, and then suddenly, amid the whirlpool of events, to ask in a dazed way: “How did I get into this condition?”
support.follows: It is disgraceful to be swept along and then to ask, in a daze, how one came to be where one is.
support.context: The close of Letter 37: it is shameful to be swept along by events instead of advancing. The “condition” is the state a man finds himself in.
gives: It is a disgrace to be carried along
instead of going forward
to ask, dazed, in the middle of events: “How did I get into this condition?”

items.label: doubt
items.t: Even if I leave open what is in my own control, I do not let my eagerness for wisdom weaken: I hold fast to it until it becomes a habit of mind.
items.why: No passage of Marcus here asks what holds if the matter is not up to me. Seneca sets that question aside without answering it, and says what to do all the same.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: it is not my purpose now to be led into a discussion as to what is within our own control
support.follows: Seneca declines, for now, to argue about what lies within our own control.
support.context: Letter 16, on philosophy as the guide of life. Seneca has asked whether fate, God or chance rules us; what lies in our control is the question he leaves aside.
gives: Even if I leave open what is in my own control

support.author: seneca
support.quote: that you should not allow the impulse of your spirit to weaken and grow cold
support.follows: Lucilius should not let the eager impulse of his spirit weaken and cool.
support.context: Letter 16 opens by urging Lucilius to keep up the study of wisdom; “the impulse of your spirit” is his eagerness for it.
gives: I do not let my eagerness for wisdom weaken

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Hold fast to it and establish it firmly, in order that what is now impulse may become a habit of the mind.
support.follows: An impulse held fast and made firm can become a settled habit of the mind.
support.context: Letter 16, the same advice. “It” is Lucilius’s impulse toward philosophy, which Seneca wants turned into a settled habit.
gives: I hold fast to it until it becomes a habit of mind

items.t: Seneca limits the claim’s broad wording, that what is in my soul is up to me. What is in my power is to keep a passion out; once I let sadness, fear or desire in, it no longer lies within my power, because what stirs it is outside me. On keeping passions out, 8.27 and Seneca agree.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: if you grant any privileges to sadness, fear, desire, and all the other wrong impulses, they will cease to lie within our jurisdiction
support.follows: Passions given any room stop being under our control.
support.context: Letter 85, against the view that passions should be kept moderate. The “wrong impulses” are passions; “our jurisdiction” is what lies in our own power.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Simply because the means of arousing them lie outside our own power.
support.follows: Passions once admitted are not ours to govern, because what stirs them is outside our power.
support.context: Letter 85, Seneca’s reason for that claim. “Them” are the passions; what arouses them is the outside things that cause fear or the hope of gain.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: How have I the power to bring something to a close, when I have not had the power to check it at the beginning?
support.follows: If I had no power to stop a thing at its start, I have none to bring it to an end.
support.context: Letter 85, closing the argument against moderate passions. “Something” is a passion that was let in.

items.t: Seneca limits keeping away from desire. He bans the desires, but still allows the wish to do the same things without fear and with better judgment. For him, keeping desire out does not mean wanting nothing.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: after I have issued my prohibition against the desires, I shall still allow you to wish that you may do the same things fearlessly and with greater accuracy of judgment
support.follows: Banning the desires still leaves room to wish to act without fear and with better judgment.
support.context: Letter 116, on self-control: should emotions be moderate or absent? Seneca says absent. “The same things” are what Lucilius strives for as necessary, useful or pleasant.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall simply strip away the vice.
support.follows: Seneca takes away only the vice, not the things Lucilius strives for.
support.context: Letter 116: Seneca promises to be indulgent to what Lucilius strives for. “The vice” is the passion attached to those things.
