seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: a ground, that what a pilot answers for is the work and not its success; how far to go along with other people, which 6.32 says only of craftsmen; and, under “When it breaks”, philosophy that courts applause. He backs nothing in the one claim, and he limits the picture it uses: a pilot’s or a physician’s skill is for the good of other people, and the wise person’s good is their own as well.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause on praise, which he says of philosophy only: my philosophy does not court applause. His limit falls on the claim that pictures steering and doctoring, not on the statement: the statement’s likeness to a doctor is about holding to a rule, and his limit is about whose good the skill serves.

items.label: why
items.t: What a pilot has promised me is a serviceable performance of the task, not a prosperous voyage. A storm interferes with the pilot’s success, not with the pilot’s work.
items.why: 6.50 fixes attention on what keeps those on board safe and says nothing of a voyage that ends badly. Seneca, with the same picture, says what the pilot answers for: the work, not its success. He says it of the pilot only; applying it to my own work is left to the reader. Article 2 says of every act that the work is the act itself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The pilot has promised you, not a prosperous voyage, but a serviceable performance of his task
support.follows: A pilot owes those who sail with him a competent performance of his task, not a good voyage.
support.context: Seneca answers the objection that a storm makes a pilot worse at his work, as pain might make a wise man worse. “You” is anyone who sails with the pilot.
gives: What a pilot has promised me is a serviceable performance of the task, not a prosperous voyage

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the storm does not interfere with the pilot’s work, but only with his success
support.follows: A storm gets in the way of the pilot’s success; it does not get in the way of his work.
support.context: Letter 85, on whether hardship harms the wise man as a storm harms a pilot. Seneca’s own answer: a pilot who keeps the ship on an even keel as it sinks has met his art’s demands.
gives: A storm interferes with the pilot’s success, not with the pilot’s work

items.label: action
items.t: Outwardly I conform to the customs of the people around me; inwardly I am different in every respect. I try to keep a higher standard of life than most people, but not a contrary one, or I would drive away the very people I am trying to improve.
items.why: 6.32 says that craftsmen adapt to laymen “up to a point”. It does not apply this to me, and it does not say where the point is or why they adapt at all. Seneca says it of those who practise philosophy: he draws the line between the outward life and the inward one, and gives a reason, that a contrary way of life repels the people one hopes to improve.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Inwardly, we ought to be different in all respects, but our exterior should conform to society.
support.follows: A person who practises philosophy should differ from others inwardly and conform to them outwardly.
support.context: Seneca warns Lucilius not to show off his philosophy by odd dress or habits. “We” are those who practise philosophy; “society” is the customs of the people they live among.
gives: Outwardly I conform to the customs of the people around me
inwardly I am different in every respect

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let us try to maintain a higher standard of life than that of the multitude, but not a contrary standard; otherwise, we shall frighten away and repel the very persons whom we are trying to improve.
support.follows: The standard should be higher than the multitude’s but not contrary to it, or it repels the people one is trying to improve.
support.context: Letter 5, on living as a philosopher without making a display of it. “The multitude” are ordinary people, whom the philosopher hopes to improve and must not frighten off.
gives: I try to keep a higher standard of life than most people, but not a contrary one
I would drive away the very people I am trying to improve

items.label: breaks
items.t: Nothing is baser than philosophy that courts applause: a sick man does not praise the surgeon during the operation. I take no pleasure in being praised by people whom I could not praise myself.
items.why: 6.50 speaks only of being spoken ill of. Seneca, with the same picture of a healer and the sick, takes the other case, being praised. He says it of philosophy, not of every kind of work, and it shows what failing looks like there: doing philosophy for the sake of the praise.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For what is baser than philosophy courting applause? Does the sick man praise the surgeon while he is operating?
support.follows: Philosophy that courts applause is as base as anything can be; a patient does not praise the surgeon in the middle of an operation.
support.context: On choosing teachers: Seneca allows public lecturers only if they aim to improve people. The surgeon is the philosopher who teaches; the sick man is his hearer.
gives: Nothing is baser than philosophy that courts applause
a sick man does not praise the surgeon during the operation

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Why do you take pleasure in being praised by men whom you yourself cannot praise?
support.follows: There is no reason to enjoy praise from people one cannot praise oneself.
support.context: Letter 52, on philosophers who lecture in public. “You” is a lecturer who goes home happy because an audience of ignorant people applauded him.
gives: I take no pleasure in being praised by people whom I could not praise myself

items.t: Seneca takes the same two crafts as 6.50, the pilot’s and the physician’s, and marks where the likeness ends. Their art is for the good of other people, the passengers and the patients. The wise man’s good is common: it belongs to the people he lives among and to himself as well. The limit falls on the picture the claim uses, steering and doctoring, and not on its rule of attention, about which Ep. 85.36 says nothing. It does not contradict Marcus, whose 6.32 implies that a person’s own reason deserves no less respect than the reason of a craft. Seneca is not quite steady on the pilot: in Ep. 85.33 the storm does not interfere with the pilot’s work, and three sections later it hinders the services he has promised to others.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the pilot’s art is another’s good—it concerns his passengers just as a physician’s art concerns his patients
support.follows: A pilot’s art, like a physician’s, is for the good of other people: the passengers and the patients.
support.context: Seneca argues that hardship harms the wise man less than a storm harms a pilot. “Another’s good”: the art serves the passengers or patients, not the one who practises it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But the wise man’s good is a common good—it belongs both to those in whose company he lives, and to himself also.
support.follows: The wise man’s good belongs to the people he lives with and to himself as well.
support.context: Letter 85, comparing the wise man with a pilot in a storm. The wise man’s good, set against the pilot’s art, is said in this sentence to belong to others and to himself.

amend.t: , and my philosophy does not court applause
; but unlike a pilot’s or a physician’s skill, which is for others’ good, my good, if I am wise, belongs to those I live among and to me

passages.title: On some vain syllogisms
passages.text: For myself, I maintain that a different answer should be given: that the pilot’s art is never made worse by the storm, nor the application of his art either. The pilot has promised you, not a prosperous voyage, but a serviceable performance of his task—that is, an expert knowledge of steering a ship. And the more he is hampered by the stress of fortune, so much the more does his knowledge become apparent. He who has been able to say, “Neptune, you shall never sink this ship except on an even keel,” has fulfilled the requirements of his art; the storm does not interfere with the pilot’s work, but only with his success.

passages.title: The philosopher’s mean
passages.text: Repellent attire, unkempt hair, slovenly beard, open scorn of silver dishes, a couch on the bare earth, and any other perverted forms of self-display, are to be avoided. The mere name of philosophy, however quietly pursued, is an object of sufficient scorn; and what would happen if we should begin to separate ourselves from the customs of our fellow-men? Inwardly, we ought to be different in all respects, but our exterior should conform to society.

passages.title: The philosopher’s mean
passages.text: Do not wear too fine, nor yet too frowzy, a toga. One needs no silver plate, encrusted and embossed in solid gold; but we should not believe the lack of silver and gold to be proof of the simple life. Let us try to maintain a higher standard of life than that of the multitude, but not a contrary standard; otherwise, we shall frighten away and repel the very persons whom we are trying to improve. We also bring it about that they are unwilling to imitate us in anything, because they are afraid lest they might be compelled to imitate us in everything.

passages.title: On choosing our teachers
passages.text: Of course I would not prevent you from listening also to those philosophers who are wont to hold public meetings and discussions, provided they appear before the people for the express purpose of improving themselves and others, and do not practise their profession for the sake of self-seeking. For what is baser than philosophy courting applause? Does the sick man praise the surgeon while he is operating?

passages.title: On choosing our teachers
passages.text: How mad is he who leaves the lecture-room in a happy frame of mind simply because of applause from the ignorant! Why do you take pleasure in being praised by men whom you yourself cannot praise? Fabianus used to give popular talks, but his audience listened with self-control. Occasionally a loud shout of praise would burst forth, but it was prompted by the greatness of his subject, and not by the sound of oratory that slipped forth pleasantly and softly.

passages.title: On some vain syllogisms
passages.text: Again, the pilot’s art is another’s good—it concerns his passengers just as a physician’s art concerns his patients. But the wise man’s good is a common good—it belongs both to those in whose company he lives, and to himself also. Hence our pilot may perhaps be harmed, since his services, which have been promised to others, are hindered by the storm;

claims.t: I attend only to what I am doing now. If I were steering a ship or treating the sick, and the sailors or my patients spoke ill of me, I would still attend to nothing but how to keep those on board safe or make those I was treating well.
claims.shared: 9.42 and 6.50 both shut everything else out of attention, and each has its word of exclusion: 9.42 “only” with what is being done now, 6.50 “anything other than” how I myself bring the work about. This is the one component of the claim that two passages say; the steering, the doctoring and the abuse are 6.50’s alone.
claims.changed: 9.42 is an instruction with no subject and 6.50 a question about an imagined case; the claim states both in the first person. 6.50’s “how I myself might bring about” is read as the act being done now. In 9.42 the word “only” covers the act and the instrument together; the claim takes the act, and the instrument stands as a said-once item. 6.32 is not in the claim: it shares the doctor with 6.50 but says nothing of attention, and in 6.50 nobody asks the helmsman or the doctor to give anything up.

support.quote: To be occupied only with what is being done now
support.follows: My attention is to stay on what is being done now.
gives: I attend only to what I am doing now

support.quote: If the sailors were speaking ill of me while I was steering, or the sick while I was their doctor, would I be attending to anything other than how I myself might bring about what keeps those on board safe, or what makes those under treatment healthy?
support.follows: If the sailors or the sick spoke ill of me while I steered or treated them, I would still attend only to keeping those on board safe or making the sick well.
gives: I attend only to what I am doing now
If I were steering a ship or treating the sick, and the sailors or my patients spoke ill of me
I would still attend to nothing but how to keep those on board safe or make those I was treating well

single.quote: Do you not see how craftsmen in the manual trades adapt themselves to laymen up to a point, but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it?
single.label: Up to a point
single.t: I look at how craftsmen work: they adapt to people outside the craft up to a point, but they keep to the rule the craft works by and will not give it up.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of adapting to others and of where the adapting stops. It is the first half of 6.32’s argument and says what craftsmen do; the passage does not go on to say that I adapt to others up to a point. 6.50 has people who speak ill, but nobody there asks for anything to be given up, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: Craftsmen fit in with people outside the craft up to a point, but they keep to the craft’s own rule and refuse to give it up.

single.quote: Is it not shocking if the master builder and the doctor are to have more respect for the reason of their own craft than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods?
single.label: My own reason
single.t: It would be shocking if a master builder or a doctor respected the reason of their craft, the rule their work is done by, more than I respect my own reason, which I share with the gods.
single.why: Only this passage gives a ground. It sets the reason of a craft beside a person’s own reason and uses one word, “reason”, for both; the line adds “the rule their work is done by” only to say what the reason of a craft is. It argues from the smaller thing to the greater and does not call reason a craft.
single.follows: A human being’s own reason, shared with the gods, deserves at least the respect a builder or a doctor has for the reason of a craft.

single.quote: and with the instrument through which you act
single.label: The instrument
single.t: In what I am doing now, I keep my mind also on the instrument through which I act.
single.why: Only this passage names an instrument, and it does not say which one: the body, the mind, or the tool in hand. It is kept as a point of attention I can return to at any moment.
single.follows: I am to be occupied also with the instrument through which I act.

members.text:
Dost thou not see, how even those that profess mechanic arts,
though in some respect they be no better than mere idiots, yet they
stick close to the course of their trade, neither can they find in
their heart to decline from it: and is it not a grievous thing that
an architect, or a physician shall respect the course and mysteries of
their profession, more than a man the proper course and condition of his
own nature, reason, which is common to him and to the Gods?
members.english: Do you not see how craftsmen in the manual trades adapt themselves to laymen up to a point, but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it? Is it not shocking if the master builder and the doctor are to have more respect for the reason of their own craft than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods?
members.greek: Οὐχ ὁρᾷς πῶς οἱ βάναυσοι τεχνῖται ἁρμόζονται μὲν μέχρι τινὸς πρὸς τοὺς ἰδιώτας, οὐδὲν ἧσσον μέντοι ἀντέχονται τοῦ λόγου τῆς τέχνης καὶ τούτου ἀποστῆναι οὐχ ὑπομένουσιν; οὐ δεινὸν εἰ ὁ ἀρχιτέκτων καὶ ὁ ἰατρὸς μᾶλλον αἰδέσονται τὸν τῆς ἰδίας τέχνης λόγον ἢ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ, ὃς αὐτῷ κοινός ἐστι πρὸς τοὺς θεούς;

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition: 6.32 is 6.35 in modern editions and 6.50 is 6.55; 9.42 is the end of 9.41, the last words of one sentence and the sentence after it.

States in the first person what 6.32 only asks. No passage says “I keep to my own reason”: 6.32 sets the reason of a craft beside a person’s own reason and asks whether the second deserves less respect. It does not call reason a craft, and it does not say that I adapt to others as craftsmen do; the title’s “craft” is the picture, not an identification.

Reads 6.50 with “I” as the one who attends. The Greek quoted is Leopold’s edition of 1908 in its Perseus copy, which prints the first-person ἐνεργοίην, “I myself might bring about”; but even so ἂν προσεῖχον can be third person plural, “would they be attending”, with the sailors and the sick still the subject, and the translators’ notes give both that reading and a third-person form of the second verb. Taking ἂν προσεῖχον as first person is allowed by the printed Greek but not required; on the other reading 6.50 still backs “speak ill of me” but not “I attend only”, and the article would have no fused claim.

Lets two of the three parts of the statement rest on one passage each: the likeness on 6.32, the abuse on 6.50. This is an exception to rule 8, for the owner to approve: with three passages, of which only two say the same thing, no more is available. Does not quote the opening words of 9.42, “… is common to every school”, because their subject stands before the cut; places the instrument of 9.42 under Practice, although the Greek leaves open which instrument is meant.
articles.limit: The section’s three passages yield one fused claim, carried by two of them, and it rests on reading ἂν προσεῖχον in 6.50 as first person (“would I be attending”), which the printed Greek allows but does not require; on the third-person reading nothing here is fused. That claim, attending to my work alone when those I work for speak ill of me, is already Article 22’s claim 1 (when I act well and am spoken ill of, I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away), and Article 2 already says that my work is the act itself. What this article adds is only the likeness to a craft from 6.32, that I owe my own reason at least the respect a builder or a doctor gives the reason of the craft, which Article 24’s claim 1 (I treat living as a skill, learned by training) comes near from another side.

articles.title: Training, and the use of reason

statement.t: I treat living as a skill: I learn it by training, I bring reason to it and wait for nothing else, and I use it to face what happens.

parts.words: I treat living as a skill
I learn it by training
I bring reason to it and wait for nothing else
to face what happens

statement.kind: A likeness, with its means and its use
statement.form: Two passages set living beside a trained skill: writing and reading in 11.27, wrestling in 7.33. Claim 1 gives the rule of any skill, that ability comes from training; in the statement, “I learn it by training” rests on 11.27 for living, and on 12.5 only for the general rule. Claim 2 says that using reason does not wait for anything else. Claim 3 says, through the wrestler, what the skill is used for. The statement lists the three side by side, with one link of the editor’s: “I bring reason to it” makes reason something brought to the skill of living, which neither 4.11 nor 4.25 says.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first two claims gain a second author, the article gains two reasons under Why, an exercise of thinking ahead and three things for when it breaks, and claims 2 and 3 are limited: I need a helping hand, and I may fall so long as I rise again.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, with one restriction: “wait for nothing else” holds for things and not for people, since I need a helping hand. It also gains its reason: becoming good is an art, and nature does not give me virtue.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Everyone approaches courageously a danger which he has prepared himself to meet long before, and withstands even hardships if he has previously practised how to meet them. But, contrariwise, the unprepared are panic-stricken even at the most trifling things.
piece.follows: People stand up to dangers and hardships they have practised meeting, and the unprepared panic even at small things.
piece.context: Letter 107, on what life is bound to bring: illness, loss, runaway slaves. To have “practised” is to have thought about such things often and in advance.
gives: I am able only where I have been trained

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: There is no reason why poverty should call us away from philosophy,—no, nor even actual want.
piece.follows: Neither poverty nor outright want is a reason to leave philosophy.
piece.context: Letter 17, on philosophy and riches: Lucilius wants an income first. Seneca answers that neither poverty nor “actual want”, meaning hunger, is a reason to wait.
gives: without bread

items.label: why
items.role: Born for it, not with it
items.t: Nature does not give me virtue: becoming good is an art. I was born to attain it, not in possession of it, and no soul has it unless it has been trained and taught and brought to perfection by unremitting practice.
items.why: Marcus says that ability comes from training and that this holds in life. He does not say in this section why goodness has to be learned at all. Seneca does: nature does not give it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For nature does not bestow virtue; it is an art to become good.
support.follows: Virtue is not given by nature; becoming good is an art.
support.context: Letter 90, on the first human beings. Seneca says they were guileless and sturdy but not wise, and this sentence gives his reason.
gives: Nature does not give me virtue: becoming good is an art

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For the attainment of this boon, but not in the possession of it, were we born
support.follows: We are born to attain virtue, and we are not born having it.
support.context: The close of Letter 90, on the first humans, who were innocent out of ignorance. “This boon” is virtue, named in the sentence before.
gives: I was born to attain it, not in possession of it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Virtue is not vouchsafed to a soul unless that soul has been trained and taught, and by unremitting practice brought to perfection.
support.follows: A soul has virtue only after it has been trained, taught and perfected by constant practice.
support.context: The conclusion of Letter 90: the first humans did no wrong because they knew no wrong, and that is not virtue. Seneca then says what virtue requires.
gives: no soul has it unless it has been trained and taught and brought to perfection by unremitting practice

items.label: why
items.t: The art of living is unlike the other arts. They deal with the tools of life and not with life as a whole; and in this one a mistake made on purpose is more shameful than one made by accident.
items.why: Marcus says that the rule of writing and reading holds “much more” in life, and stops there. Seneca also speaks of an art of living, and he says where its likeness to the other arts ends. He leaves untouched the rule that ability comes from training, so this adds to the first claim and does not limit it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Would you like to know how unlike its status is to the other arts?
support.follows: The art of life does not stand as the other arts stand.
support.context: Letter 95, on whether precepts are enough to teach wisdom. “Its status” is that of the art of life, which Seneca sets apart from the pilot’s and other crafts.
gives: The art of living is unlike the other arts

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Now all these arts are concerned with the tools of life, but not with life as a whole.
support.follows: The other arts concern things used in living, and not life as a whole.
support.context: Letter 95: an objector says the pilot’s craft is learned from precepts, so the art of living can be too. “These arts” are the pilot’s and the other crafts.
gives: They deal with the tools of life and not with life as a whole

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But in this art of living a voluntary mistake is the more shameful.
support.follows: In the art of living, a deliberate mistake is worse than an accidental one.
support.context: Seneca’s example in Letter 95: a scholar is less ashamed of a grammar slip made on purpose than of one made by accident. In the art of living it is reversed.
gives: in this one a mistake made on purpose is more shameful than one made by accident

items.label: practice
items.t: I keep reflecting on what may come, so that nothing comes upon me unforeseen and, whatever the evil is, I do not play the unschooled boy.
items.why: Marcus’s one exercise here is to practise what I have given up on (12.5), and his art of living stands ready for things that are “not foreseen” (7.33). Seneca’s exercise starts earlier: by thinking ahead he tries to leave nothing unforeseen. Article 3 already has this exercise from Letters 91, 76 and 78; here it stands beside Marcus’s “not foreseen”.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We must see to it that nothing shall come upon us unforeseen.
support.follows: We should arrange that nothing takes us by surprise.
support.context: Letter 107: Lucilius is upset that his slaves have run away. Seneca tells him to expect such things; what must not come “unforeseen” is any of life’s troubles.
gives: nothing comes upon me unforeseen

support.author: seneca
support.quote: continual reflection will give you the power, no matter what the evil may be, not to play the unschooled boy
support.follows: Constant reflection gives a person the power not to behave like an untaught boy, whatever evil comes.
support.context: Letter 107, on preparing the mind for what life brings. The “reflection” is thinking about troubles before they come; the “unschooled boy” is the unprepared.
gives: I keep reflecting on what may come
whatever the evil is, I do not play the unschooled boy

items.label: breaks
items.t: I lay hold of today’s task, and then I depend less on tomorrow’s; while I am postponing, life speeds by. Philosophy, which I have been putting off until I have enough money, should come first: I begin with it.
items.why: 8.21 names the fault, preferring tomorrow to today, and gives no way back. Seneca gives one: take hold of today’s task, and begin with the thing I was putting off. The excuse “until I have enough” is from the sentence before the quoted words of Letter 17, where Lucilius says he has not yet enough.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Lay hold of to-day’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
support.follows: Whoever takes hold of today’s task depends less on tomorrow’s, and life runs on while we postpone.
support.context: The first letter, on saving one’s time: most of life slips away unused. “To-day’s task” is what this day’s hours are for; “postponing” is leaving it for later.
gives: I lay hold of today’s task, and then I depend less on tomorrow’s
while I am postponing, life speeds by

support.author: seneca
support.quote: this ideal, which you are putting off and placing second to other interests, should be secured first of all; you should begin with it
support.follows: What is being put off behind other interests should be secured first: one should begin with it.
support.context: Letter 17: Lucilius will turn to philosophy once he has gained enough money. “This ideal” is that devotion to philosophy, which Seneca tells him to put first.
gives: which I have been putting off
should come first
I begin with it

items.label: breaks
items.t: It does me no good to control a horse with the curb if my own passions bolt with me, or to beat many opponents at wrestling or boxing and then be beaten by anger.
items.why: 7.28 says what being better at throwing an opponent leaves unimproved. Seneca says the same of the wrestler and the rider, and names what defeats them: their own anger and passions.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For what good does it do us to guide a horse and control his speed with the curb, and then find that our own passions, utterly uncurbed, bolt with us? Or to beat many opponents in wrestling or boxing, and then to find that we ourselves are beaten by anger?
support.follows: Mastering a horse or beating opponents is no use to someone whose passions run away with him and whom anger beats.
support.context: Letter 88, on which studies make a person good. Seneca has just said that neither athletic training nor the old Roman drill with horse and weapons teaches virtue.
gives: It does me no good to control a horse with the curb if my own passions bolt with me
to beat many opponents at wrestling or boxing and then be beaten by anger

items.label: breaks
items.role: While I am not yet able
items.t: While my training has not yet made me able, I do not demand of myself, a learner, what is demanded of a wise man. I press on and persevere: the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
items.why: Marcus shows one failure here, putting it off (8.21), and does not say how to go on while the training has not yet taken. Seneca admits that his own has not, and says how: a learner is judged as a learner, and presses on. He takes for granted that training is the way, so this is no answer to doubt. The opening clause comes from the end of Ep. 71.30, outside the quoted words, where Seneca says his principles are not yet so well trained that they come to his help in every crisis.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: it is a mistake on our part to make the same demands upon the wise man and upon the learner
support.follows: A learner should not be held to what is asked of a wise man.
support.context: Letter 71: Seneca grants that many who profess wisdom, himself among them, are still frightened by slight threats; his own exhortations are “not yet followed”.
gives: I do not demand of myself, a learner, what is demanded of a wise man

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Therefore let us press on and persevere. There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us; but the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
support.follows: One should press on and persevere: most of the road is still ahead, but wanting to progress is the greater part of progressing.
support.context: Near the end of Letter 71: whoever is short of perfection slips back unless he keeps struggling ahead. The “road” is the way to wisdom, most of it still ahead.
gives: I press on and persevere
the greater part of progress is the desire to progress

items.t: Seneca agrees that nothing outside me is needed: all that goes to make me a good man lies within myself (Ep. 80.3). But he also says that no one has the strength to rise above folly by himself; he needs a helping hand, and Seneca counts himself among those who need one (Ep. 52.2–3). Read in their letters the two do not conflict: 80.3 is about the equipment and expense an athlete needs, 52.2 about needing a teacher. This limits “does not wait for anything else” to things and does not extend it to people, and Marcus’s own 11.27 says that I am given the rules before I give them.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: No man by himself has sufficient strength to rise above it; he needs a helping hand, and some one to extricate him.
support.follows: Nobody is strong enough to get clear of folly alone; each needs someone to help him out.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing a teacher. “It” is folly: the wavering between plans and wishes that Seneca has just described in himself and in Lucilius.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We ourselves are not of that first class, either; we shall be well treated if we are admitted into the second.
support.follows: Seneca puts himself among those who need another’s help, not among those who find the way alone.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing a teacher. In Epicurus’s classes the first reach the truth with no one’s help and the second need a guide. “We” are Seneca and Lucilius.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: All that goes to make you a good man lies within yourself.
support.follows: Everything needed to become a good man is within oneself.
support.context: Letter 80: Seneca contrasts athletes, who need food, drink, oil and long training, with the mind, which feeds and exercises itself. “You” is Lucilius, or anyone.

items.t: Marcus’s art of living “does not fall”. Seneca’s fighter does: the only contestant who can enter with confidence has been downed in body but not in spirit, and rises as often as he falls (Ep. 13.2). In Ep. 80.3 even the mind may be laid low and trampled; what Seneca asks is that it not be conquered and that it struggle to its feet again. This limits “not to fall”: for Seneca falling is allowed, and what is not allowed is to stay down.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: who has been downed in body but not in spirit, one who, as often as he falls, rises again with greater defiance than ever
support.follows: The only contestant who can enter confidently is one who has been knocked down without losing heart and gets up every time he falls.
support.context: Letter 13: Seneca tells Lucilius that one’s powers are proved only by hard tests. The prizefighter is his figure for a person contending with Fortune.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: so that it might struggle to its feet again after it has been laid low, after it has been trampled under foot
support.follows: The mind can be toughened so that it gets up again after being knocked down and trampled.
support.context: Letter 80: Seneca hears cheering from the stadium and asks, if a fighter’s body can be trained to take blows, how much more the mind? “It” is the mind.

amend.t: ; becoming good is an art, and nature does not give me virtue: I was born to attain it
; but I do not rise above my folly by my own strength alone: I need a helping hand
; yet as often as I fall I rise again

passages.title: On obedience to the universal will
passages.text: Everyone approaches courageously a danger which he has prepared himself to meet long before, and withstands even hardships if he has previously practised how to meet them. But, contrariwise, the unprepared are panic-stricken even at the most trifling things. We must see to it that nothing shall come upon us unforeseen. And since things are all the more serious when they are unfamiliar, continual reflection will give you the power, no matter what the evil may be, not to play the unschooled boy.

passages.title: On philosophy and riches
passages.text: There is no reason why poverty should call us away from philosophy,—no, nor even actual want. For when hastening after wisdom, we must endure even hunger. Men have endured hunger when their towns were besieged, and what other reward for their endurance did they obtain than that they did not fall under the conqueror’s power? How much greater is the promise of the prize of everlasting liberty, and the assurance that we need fear neither God nor man! Even though we starve, we must reach that goal.

passages.title: On the part played by philosophy in the progress of man
passages.text: But no matter how excellent and guileless was the life of the men of that age, they were not wise men; for that title is reserved for the highest achievement. Still, I would not deny that they were men of lofty spirit and—I may use the phrase—fresh from the gods. For there is no doubt that the world produced a better progeny before it was yet worn out. However, not all were endowed with mental faculties of highest perfection, though in all cases their native powers were more sturdy than ours and more fitted for toil. For nature does not bestow virtue; it is an art to become good.

passages.title: On the part played by philosophy in the progress of man
passages.text: What, then, is the conclusion of the matter? It was by reason of their ignorance of things that the men of those days were innocent; and it makes a great deal of difference whether one wills not to sin or has not the knowledge to sin. Justice was unknown to them, unknown prudence, unknown also self-control and bravery; but their rude life possessed certain qualities akin to all these virtues. Virtue is not vouchsafed to a soul unless that soul has been trained and taught, and by unremitting practice brought to perfection. For the attainment of this boon, but not in the possession of it, were we born; and even in the best of men, before you refine them by instruction, there is but the stuff of virtue, not virtue itself. Farewell.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: Now all these arts are concerned with the tools of life, but not with life as a whole. Hence there is much to clog these arts from without and to complicate them—such as hope, greed, fear. But that art which professes to teach the art of life cannot be forbidden by any circumstance from exercising its functions; for it shakes off complications and pierces through obstacles. Would you like to know how unlike its status is to the other arts? In the case of the latter, it is more pardonable to err voluntarily rather than by accident; but in the case of wisdom the worst fault is to commit sin wilfully.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: I mean something like this: A scholar will blush for shame, not if he makes a grammatical blunder intentionally, but if he makes it unintentionally; if a physician does not recognize that his patient is failing, he is a much poorer practitioner than if he recognizes the fact and conceals his knowledge. But in this art of living a voluntary mistake is the more shameful. Furthermore, many arts, aye and the most liberal of them all, have their special doctrines, and not mere precepts of advice—the medical profession, for example. There are the different schools of Hippocrates, of Asclepiades, of Themison.

passages.title: The epistles of seneca
passages.text: What man can you show me who places any value on his time, who reckons the worth of each day, who understands that he is dying daily? For we are mistaken when we look forward to death; the major portion of death has already passed. Whatever years lie behind us are in death’s hands. Therefore, Lucilius, do as you write me that you are doing: hold every hour in your grasp. Lay hold of to-day’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by.

passages.title: On philosophy and riches
passages.text: Even the rich man copies her ways when he is in his senses. If you wish to have leisure for your mind, either be a poor man, or resemble a poor man. Study cannot be helpful unless you take pains to live simply; and living simply is voluntary poverty. Away, then, with all excuses like: “I have not yet enough; when I have gained the desired amount, then I shall devote myself wholly to philosophy.” And yet this ideal, which you are putting off and placing second to other interests, should be secured first of all; you should begin with it. You retort: “I wish to acquire something to live on.” Yes, but learn while you are acquiring it; for if anything forbids you to live nobly, nothing forbids you to die nobly.

passages.title: On liberal and vocational studies
passages.text: For what “liberal” element is there in these ravenous takers of emetics, whose bodies are fed to fatness while their minds are thin and dull? Or do we really believe that the training which they give is “liberal” for the young men of Rome, who used to be taught by our ancestors to stand straight and hurl a spear, to wield a pike, to guide a horse, and to handle weapons? Our ancestors used to teach their children nothing that could be learned while lying down. But neither the new system nor the old teaches or nourishes virtue. For what good does it do us to guide a horse and control his speed with the curb, and then find that our own passions, utterly uncurbed, bolt with us? Or to beat many opponents in wrestling or boxing, and then to find that we ourselves are beaten by anger?

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: The wise man, indeed, overcomes Fortune by his virtue, but many who profess wisdom are sometimes frightened by the most unsubstantial threats. And at this stage it is a mistake on our part to make the same demands upon the wise man and upon the learner. I still exhort myself to do that which I recommend; but my exhortations are not yet followed. And even if this were the case, I should not have these principles so ready for practice, or so well trained, that they would rush to my assistance in every crisis.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: Therefore let us press on and persevere. There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us; but the greater part of progress is the desire to progress. I fully understand what this task is. It is a thing which I desire, and I desire it with all my heart. I see that you also have been aroused and are hastening with great zeal towards infinite beauty. Let us, then, hasten; only on these terms will life be a boon to us; otherwise, there is delay, and indeed disgraceful delay, while we busy ourselves with revolting things. Let us see to it that all time belongs to us. This, however, cannot be unless first of all our own selves begin to belong to us.

passages.title: On choosing our teachers
passages.text: “But it is the fool,” you say, “who is inconsistent; nothing suits him for long.” But how or when can we tear ourselves away from this folly? No man by himself has sufficient strength to rise above it; he needs a helping hand, and some one to extricate him.

passages.title: On choosing our teachers
passages.text: Epicurus remarks that certain men have worked their way to the truth without any one’s assistance, carving out their own passage. And he gives special praise to these, for their impulse has come from within, and they have forged to the front by themselves. Again, he says, there are others who need outside help, who will not proceed unless someone leads the way, but who will follow faithfully. Of these, he says, Metrodorus was one; this type of man is also excellent, but belongs to the second grade. We ourselves are not of that first class, either; we shall be well treated if we are admitted into the second. Nor need you despise a man who can gain salvation only with the assistance of another; the will to be saved means a great deal, too.

passages.title: On worldly deceptions
passages.text: The question which I ponder most of all is this: if the body can be trained to such a degree of endurance that it will stand the blows and kicks of several opponents at once and to such a degree that a man can last out the day and resist the scorching sun in the midst of the burning dust, drenched all the while with his own blood,—if this can be done, how much more easily might the mind be toughened so that it could receive the blows of Fortune and not be conquered, so that it might struggle to its feet again after it has been laid low, after it has been trampled under foot? For although the body needs many things in order to be strong, yet the mind grows from within, giving to itself nourishment and exercise. Yonder athletes must have copious food, copious drink, copious quantities of oil, and long training besides; but you can acquire virtue without equipment and without expense. All that goes to make you a good man lies within yourself.

passages.title: On groundless fears
passages.text: This is the touchstone of such a spirit; no prizefighter can go with high spirits into the strife if he has never been beaten black and blue; the only contestant who can confidently enter the lists is the man who has seen his own blood, who has felt his teeth rattle beneath his opponent’s fist, who has been tripped and felt the full force of his adversary’s charge, who has been downed in body but not in spirit, one who, as often as he falls, rises again with greater defiance than ever.

claims.t: I treat living as a skill, and in a skill I am able only where I have been trained: in writing and reading I do not give the rules before I have been given them, and this holds still more in life.
claims.shared: 12.5 and 11.27 both make ability depend on training that came before it: the left hand holds the bridle firmly “because this is what it has had practice in”, and no one rules in writing and reading before having “been ruled”. The words they back together, “I am able only where I have been trained”, are the editor’s summary of “practice” and “been ruled”. 11.27 and 7.33 both set living beside a skill: 11.27 carries the rule of writing and reading over to life, and 7.33 speaks of “the art of living”.
claims.changed: 12.5 speaks of a hand and 11.27 of writing and reading; the claim puts both under “a skill”. 11.27’s “rule” and “been ruled” are written out as giving the rules and being given them: the master and the pupil of the translators’ note. 12.5 does not speak of living; only 11.27 says “in life”.

support.quote: the left hand, though for lack of practice it is no good at anything else, holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because this is what it has had practice in
support.follows: A hand that is no good at anything else is the stronger one at the single thing it has practised.
gives: in a skill I am able only where I have been trained

support.quote: In writing and reading you will not rule before you have been ruled. This is much more so in life.
support.follows: In writing and reading nobody gives the rules before having been given them, and this is even more true of life.
gives: I treat living as a skill
in a skill I am able only where I have been trained
in writing and reading I do not give the rules before I have been given them, and this holds still more in life

support.quote: The art of living
support.follows: Living is spoken of as an art, in the same words as the arts of wrestling and dancing.
gives: I treat living as a skill

claims.t: Using reason does not wait for anything else. I have it, so I use it, and when it is doing its own work I want nothing more; I hold to it without a tunic, without a book, without bread, and without the nourishment that learning gives.
claims.shared: Both passages turn on what a person has. In 4.11 the one thing he has is reason (“Do you have reason?” “I do.”), and once it is at work there is nothing else to want. In 4.25 the speakers “have no bread” and “do not have” learning’s nourishment, and they hold to reason all the same. Both say “reason”, and in both nothing else has to be there first.
claims.changed: 4.11 is a dialogue and 4.25 a row of philosophers; the claim speaks as “I” throughout. 4.11 says “use” and 4.25 says “hold to”; the claim keeps both verbs. “Does not wait for anything else” is the editor’s summary: 4.11 says there is nothing else to want when reason is doing its work, and 4.25 concedes each lack with “and yet”. Neither says that nothing else is needed. The “so” is 4.11’s “Then”. In 4.25 the first two people “practise philosophy”, one without a tunic and one without a book; only the man without bread and the last speaker “hold to reason”. The claim puts all four under “hold to reason”.

support.quote: “Do you have reason?” “I do.” “Then why do you not use it?
support.follows: Someone who agrees that he has reason is asked why, then, he does not use it.
gives: Using reason does not wait for anything else
I have it, so I use it

support.quote: For when it is doing its own work, what else do you want?
support.follows: Once reason is doing its own work, there is nothing else to want.
gives: Using reason does not wait for anything else
when it is doing its own work I want nothing more

support.quote: One person practises philosophy without a tunic, another without a book. Here is another, half naked: “I have no bread,” he says, “and yet I hold to reason.” And I, for my part, do not have the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason.
support.follows: People practise philosophy and hold to reason while lacking a tunic, a book, bread, or what learning would feed them.
gives: Using reason does not wait for anything else
I hold to it without a tunic, without a book, without bread, and without the nourishment that learning gives

claims.t: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing, and what it takes from wrestling is not throwing an opponent. It is to be disciplined in the face of what happens: to stand ready for what falls on me unforeseen, and not to fall.
claims.shared: Both passages take the wrestler as their figure, and both name the same thing to be good at: 7.28 being “disciplined in the face of what happens”, 7.33 standing ready for “the things that fall on it”. The words they back together are “in the face of what happens”.
claims.changed: 7.28 names throwing and 7.33 names standing; neither sets the one against the other. 7.28 does not say that discipline belongs to wrestling: its better thrower is precisely not better disciplined. The claim takes that discipline and 7.33’s standing ready as one thing, which is the editor’s reading. 7.33 speaks of the art of living as “it”; the claim says “me”.

inferences.words: what it takes from wrestling is not
inferences.why: 7.28 only denies that better throwing is better discipline; 7.33 only puts the likeness in standing ready. Setting one against the other is the editor’s step.
7.28 does not call discipline what living takes from wrestling; its better thrower lacks it. Equating it with 7.33’s standing ready is the editor’s step.

support.quote: The art of living is more like the art of wrestling than the art of dancing
support.follows: Living is an art, and it resembles wrestling more than it resembles dancing.
gives: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing

support.quote: Better at throwing an opponent
support.follows: Someone can be better at throwing an opponent and no better in the ways the sentence goes on to list.
gives: throwing an opponent

support.quote: nor better disciplined in the face of what happens
support.follows: Being better at throwing an opponent does not make a person better disciplined in the face of what happens.
gives: to be disciplined
in the face of what happens

support.quote: in that it stands ready for the things that fall on it and are not foreseen, and does not fall
support.follows: The likeness to wrestling is this: the art of living stands ready for what falls on it unforeseen, and does not fall.
gives: in the face of what happens
to stand ready for what falls on me unforeseen, and not to fall

single.quote: Practise even the things you have given up on.
single.label: A practice
single.t: I practise even the things I have given up on.
single.why: Only this passage gives the instruction. 11.27 says that training comes first; it does not say to go back to what I have written off.
single.follows: I should practise even what I have given up as hopeless.

single.quote: You deserve these things that are happening to you; you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
single.label: Putting it off
single.t: If I would rather become good tomorrow than be good today, I deserve what is happening to me.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of delay. It shows what failing looks like here. The Greek sets the two halves side by side; the “if” that joins them is the editor’s reading.
single.follows: A person who prefers becoming good tomorrow to being good today is told that he deserves what is happening to him.

single.quote: but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined in the face of what happens, nor kinder toward the oversights of those nearby
single.label: Winning without improving
single.t: I can become better at throwing an opponent and be no more social, no more modest, and no kinder toward the oversights of the people near me.
single.why: Only this passage lists what skill at winning leaves unimproved in my dealings with other people. Its one item about what happens is fused in the claim on what the skill is. The item’s opening words, “better at throwing an opponent”, come from the start of the same sentence (7.28a).
single.follows: Being better at throwing an opponent is not being more social, more modest, better disciplined, or kinder toward the oversights of those nearby.

members.text:
Use thyself even unto those things that thou doest at first despair
of. For the left hand we see, which for the most part lieth idle because
not used; yet doth it hold the bridle with more strength than the right,
because it hath been used unto it.
members.english: Practise even the things you have given up on. For in fact the left hand, though for lack of practice it is no good at anything else, holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because this is what it has had practice in.
members.greek: Ἔθιζε καὶ ὅσα ἀπογινώσκεις. καὶ γὰρ ἡ χεὶρ ἡ ἀριστερὰ πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα διὰ τὸ ἀνέθιστον ἀργὸς οὖσα τοῦ χαλινοῦ ἐρρωμενέστερον ἢ ἡ δεξιὰ κρατεῖ· τοῦτο γὰρ εἴθισται.

members.text:
In matter of writing or reading thou must needs be taught before
thou can do either: much more in matter of life. 'For thou art born a
mere slave, to thy senses and brutish affections;' destitute without
teaching of all true knowledge and sound reason.
members.english:
In writing and reading you will not rule before you have been ruled. This is much more so in life.

You are by nature a slave; you have no share in reason.
members.greek:
Ἐν τῷ γράφειν καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν οὐ πρότερον ἄρξεις πρὶν ἀρχθῇς. τοῦτο πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν τῷ βίῳ.

Δοῦλος πέφυκας, οὐ μέτεστί σοι λόγου.

members.text:
Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if
thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?
members.english: “Do you have reason?” “I do.” “Then why do you not use it? For when it is doing its own work, what else do you want?”
members.greek: “Λόγον ἔχεις;” “ἔχω.” “τί οὖν οὐ χρᾷ; τούτου γὰρ τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ποιοῦντος τί ἄλλο θέλεις;”

members.text:
There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without
so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked,
neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith
one. But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and
yet I depart not from reason.
members.english: One person practises philosophy without a tunic, another without a book. Here is another, half naked: “I have no bread,” he says, “and yet I hold to reason.” And I, for my part, do not have the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason.
members.greek: Ὁ μὲν χωρὶς χιτῶνος φιλοσοφεῖ, ὁ δὲ χωρὶς βιβλίου. ἄλλος οὗτος ἡμίγυμνος· ἄρτους οὐκ ἔχω, φησί, καὶ ἐμμένω τῷ λόγῳ.—ἐγὼ δὲ τροφὰς τὰς ἐκ τῶν μαθημάτων οὐκ ἔχω καὶ ἐμμένω.

members.text:
Most justly have these things happened unto thee: why dost not
thou amend? O but thou hadst rather become good to-morrow, than to be
so to-day.
members.english: You deserve these things that are happening to you; you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
members.greek: Δικαίως ταῦτα πάσχεις· μᾶλλον δὲ θέλεις ἀγαθὸς αὔριον γενέσθαι ἢ σήμερον εἶναι.

members.text:
He hath a stronger body, and is a better wrestler than I. What
then? Is he more bountiful? is he more modest? Doth he bear all adverse
chances with more equanimity: or with his neighbour's offences with more
meekness and gentleness than I?
members.english: Better at throwing an opponent, but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined in the face of what happens, nor kinder toward the oversights of those nearby.
members.greek: Καββαλικώτερος, ἀλλ’ οὐχὶ κοινωνικώτερος οὐδὲ αἰδημονέστερος οὐδ’ εὐτακτότερος ἐπὶ τοῖς συμβαίνουσιν οὐδὲ εὐμενέστερος πρὸς τὰ τῶν πλησίον παροράματα.

members.text:
The art of true living in this world is more like a wrestler's,
than a dancer's practice. For in this they both agree, to teach a man
whatsoever falls upon him, that he may be ready for it, and that nothing
may cast him down.
members.english: The art of living is more like the art of wrestling than the art of dancing, in that it stands ready for the things that fall on it and are not foreseen, and does not fall.
members.greek: Ἡ βιωτικὴ τῇ παλαιστικῇ ὁμοιοτέρα ἤπερ τῇ ὀρχηστικῇ κατὰ τὸ πρὸς τὰ ἐμπίπτοντα καὶ οὐ προεγνωσμενα ἕτοιμος καὶ ἀπτὼς ἑστάναι.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 12.5 is 12.6, 11.27 is 11.29 and 11.30, 4.11 is 4.13, 4.25 is 4.30, 8.21 is the second half of 8.22, 7.28 is 7.52 and 7.33 is 7.61.

Reads “rule” and “been ruled” in 11.27 as the master and the pupil, and writes it out in the claim as giving the rules and being given them; the same Greek verb can also mean “lead” and “been led”. Leaves out the second half of 11.27, “You are by nature a slave; you have no share in reason.” It is a separate chapter in modern editions (11.30), it reads like a line quoted from a play, Marcus adds no comment, and its last word may mean “speech”.

“I treat living as a skill” is the editor’s wording for what two passages do. 11.27 applies the rule of writing and reading to life; 7.33 says “the art of living”. Neither says in so many words that living is learned as a skill is.

Reads 7.28, which has no subject and no verb, as a general remark: being better at throwing an opponent is not being better in the four ways listed. Setting that throwing against the standing of 7.33, and taking 7.28’s discipline and 7.33’s standing ready as one thing, are marked in the third claim as the editor’s steps.
Keeps “practise even the things I have given up on” (12.5) and the rebuke about tomorrow (8.21) as said once. No second passage says either, though both fit the statement.
articles.limit: Articles 2 and 5 already say that my work is to use reason; this article adds that living is trained like a skill, that using reason does not wait for anything else, and what the skill is used for. Article 6 already has one passage (8.54) about standing and not falling before an obstacle. The first claim is thin: 12.5 speaks of any ability and not of living, only 11.27 says “in life”, and 7.33 gives it three words. The last sentence of 4.25 has other readings. Seneca’s exercise of thinking troubles through in advance is already in Article 3, from other letters (Ep. 91.4, 76.34, 78.29); the item from Ep. 107.4 here repeats it. Claims 1 and 2 pull in different directions: 11.27 puts being given the rules before giving them, and 4.25 holds to reason even without the nourishment that learning gives. The article keeps both. Living as a craft is also in Article 11, claim 3 (being good is my craft, with principles kept ready as a doctor keeps his instruments), and in Article 23 (I keep to my own reason as a doctor keeps to the craft); this article adds that the skill is learned by training and that it is used to face what happens. Article 35 already says, with the same Ep. 1.2, that I hurry to become good while it is possible and that I fail by putting things off (claims 3 and 4); here 8.21 is one said-once failure, and Seneca’s way back from delay repeats that ground.

articles.title: What I turn to

statement.t: I keep going back to myself and to philosophy, rest in philosophy and in acting as a member of a community, and toil without complaint.

parts.words: I keep going back
to myself and to philosophy
rest in philosophy and in acting as a member of a community

statement.kind: A habit, what it gives, and the work it serves
statement.form: The claim on going back is the habit, and the claim under Why says what the habit gives. The claim on the one thing wanted names the work and the rest found in it, and the last claim says how that work is done when it is hard, and what Marcus had to stop doing: complaining. The claim on virtue stands beside these and is not in the statement.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, going back into myself and going to philosophy each gain a witness, and the article gains a reason not to complain, justice without reward or renown, the company of the best people of any age and what to do while I am not yet fit to be alone with myself; he limits the going back into myself, and where Marcus waits on the court he would put the affairs that take up his time out of the way.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands with a limit on its first part, since for him going back into myself is for one who is already good, calm and self-restrained, and it gains a reason and an addition at its end: complaining would make what I bear heavier, and I must be just without reward or renown. His challenge, that I should put the affairs that take up my time out of the way, stands under the claim on what going back gives.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can.
piece.follows: Lucilius is told to withdraw into himself as far as he can.
piece.context: Letter 7, on crowds: Seneca admits that a crowd disturbs the calm he has forced within himself, and tells Lucilius neither to copy the many nor to hate them.
gives: into myself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: take refuge with philosophy: she will cherish you in her bosom
piece.follows: I should take refuge with philosophy, and she will hold me close and cherish me.
piece.context: Letter 103, on the harm people do to one another. After advice on dealing with them, Seneca sends Lucilius to philosophy, where he will be safer. “She” is philosophy.
gives: to philosophy

items.label: why
items.t: Complaining adds to what I bear. If I complain I make my troubles heavier of my own accord; in all the evils I complain of the one real evil is the complaining, and I am as wretched as I have convinced myself that I am.
items.why: 8.8 and 9.10 forbid the complaint and give no reason. Seneca gives one: the complaining is itself what weighs. He says it of illness and of losses, not of toil or of life at a court.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: do not of your own accord make your troubles heavier to bear and burden yourself with complaining
support.follows: Whoever complains makes his own troubles heavier, and does it of his own accord.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness, written out of Seneca’s own sickness. “Your troubles” are the pains of illness; he goes on to say that all suffering depends on opinion.
gives: Complaining adds to what I bear
If I complain I make my troubles heavier of my own accord

support.author: seneca
support.quote: in all the evils to which you refer, there is really only one—the fact that you do chafe and complain
support.follows: Of all the evils Lucilius lists, the only real one is that he chafes and complains.
support.context: Opening of Letter 96. Lucilius has complained of his troubles; Seneca answers with his own illness, losses, toil and fear, and calls them common and inevitable. “You” is Lucilius.
gives: in all the evils I complain of the one real evil is the complaining

support.author: seneca
support.quote: A man is as wretched as he has convinced himself that he is.
support.follows: How wretched a person is depends on how wretched he has persuaded himself he is.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca wants an end to complaints about past sufferings, because everyone adds to his own ills. “A man” is anyone who suffers.
gives: I am as wretched as I have convinced myself that I am

items.label: action
items.t: I must be just without reward and without renown, and I want to take pleasure in giving myself to justice of my own free will. It makes no difference how many people know that I am upright, and often I must be just and disgraced at the same time.
items.why: 9.10 tells me not to toil as someone who wants to be admired, and stops there. Seneca says the same of justice, the virtue that looks to another person’s good, and goes on to the hard case that Marcus does not name here: doing right and being disgraced for it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I must be just without reward.
support.follows: Each person should be convinced that he must be just without any reward for it.
support.context: End of Letter 113. After a dispute on whether the virtues are living things, Seneca turns to justice, which looks to another’s good. Each man is to tell himself these words.
gives: I must be just without reward

support.author: seneca
support.quote: May I take pleasure in devoting myself of my own free will to uphold this noblest of virtues.
support.follows: A person should wish to take pleasure in giving himself freely to justice.
support.context: The second thing each man is to tell himself at the end of Letter 113, worded as a wish. “This noblest of virtues” is justice, which Seneca has just said regards another’s good.
gives: I want to take pleasure in giving myself to justice of my own free will

support.author: seneca
support.quote: it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness
support.follows: How many people know of my uprightness makes no difference.
support.context: Closing advice of Letter 113 to Lucilius, on justice done without ambition or reputation. “Your uprightness” is his just conduct, whether many people know of it or few.
gives: It makes no difference how many people know that I am upright

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Are you not willing to be just without being renowned? Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced.
support.follows: I should be willing to be just without renown, and often I shall have to be just and disgraced at once.
support.context: Last lines of Letter 113: those who want their virtue advertised are striving for renown, not for virtue. “You” is Lucilius, asked to be just even when it brings disgrace.
gives: without renown
often I must be just and disgraced at the same time

items.label: practice
items.t: When I give myself to my friends I do not leave my own company, and I do not linger with those whom my official position brings to me. I spend my time with the best people of any land or age: I let my thoughts go to them.
items.why: In 6.43 Marcus looks for the likenesses of the virtues in the people he lives with. Seneca turns in thought to the best people of any country or time; he adds a second place to look and does not say that the first is wrong. His refusal to linger with those whom his position brings him also sits against 6.10, where Marcus waits on the court.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When I give myself to my friends, I do not withdraw from my own company, nor do I linger with those who are associated with me through some special occasion or some case which arises from my official position.
support.follows: Seneca stays in his own company even among friends, and does not linger with people whom an occasion or his office brings to him.
support.context: Letter 62: Seneca denies that business blocks study, since he lends himself to his affairs and does not surrender to them. “My own company” is his own thinking, kept up among others.
gives: When I give myself to my friends I do not leave my own company
I do not linger with those whom my official position brings to me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I spend my time in the company of all the best; no matter in what lands they may have lived, or in what age, I let my thoughts fly to them.
support.follows: Seneca keeps company in thought with the best people, wherever and whenever they lived.
support.context: Letter 62, on good company in the middle of official business. “The best” are the best people of any country or century, with whom Seneca keeps company in his thoughts.
gives: I spend my time with the best people of any land or age: I let my thoughts go to them

items.label: doubt
items.role: If I am not yet fit company
items.t: While it is not yet safe for me to be alone with myself, I set a guard over myself: the authority of a person in whose presence even the worst people would check their bad impulses. And I seek out particular people, because everyone is better off in some company than in his own company alone.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what to do if going back into myself does not help because of what I find there. Seneca asks it, and answers: until I respect myself, I borrow the authority of a good person and keep company with others.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man, whether your choice be the great Cato or Scipio, or Laelius,—or any man in whose presence even abandoned wretches would check their bad impulses
support.follows: I should set over myself as a guard the authority of a man such as Cato, before whom even the worst people would hold back.
support.context: Letter 25 passes on Epicurus’s advice to act as if someone were watching. The guard is for the time before Lucilius has come to respect himself; after that he may dismiss it.
gives: I set a guard over myself: the authority of a person in whose presence even the worst people would check their bad impulses

support.author: seneca
support.quote: while it is not yet safe to withdraw into solitude, seek out certain individuals; for everyone is better off in the company of somebody or other,—no matter who,—than in his own company alone
support.follows: While being alone is not yet safe for me, I should seek out particular people; any company is better than my own alone.
support.context: End of Letter 25, to Lucilius, who is still making himself someone he can respect. Seneca’s reason follows a few lines on: alone, such a man is too close to a rascal.
gives: While it is not yet safe for me to be alone with myself
I seek out particular people, because everyone is better off in some company than in his own company alone

items.t: Seneca passes on Epicurus’s advice to withdraw into myself when I am forced to be in a crowd, and accepts it on one condition: that I am already a good, tranquil and self-restrained person. If I am not, he sends me the other way, into a crowd, to get away from myself. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. He is not uniform about it: in Letter 7 he tells Lucilius to withdraw into himself as far as he can, and adds no such condition (Ep. 7.8).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The time when you should most of all withdraw into yourself is when you are forced to be in a crowd.
support.follows: Epicurus says that being forced into a crowd is the time above all to withdraw into oneself.
support.context: Letter 25. A saying of Epicurus that Seneca promises to allow Lucilius gradually, once Lucilius has made himself someone he holds in some esteem.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Yes, provided that you are a good, tranquil, and self-restrained man; otherwise, you had better withdraw into a crowd in order to get away from your self.
support.follows: Withdrawing into myself is right only if I am good, calm and self-restrained; if not, I do better to go into a crowd.
support.context: End of Letter 25. Seneca repeats Epicurus’s saying about withdrawing into yourself when in a crowd and answers it: “Yes” accepts the saying, and the proviso is Seneca’s own.

items.t: Seneca and Marcus both go to philosophy often; they differ over whether to keep the other business at all, not over how often to go back to philosophy. Marcus waits on the court as one waits on a stepmother, and philosophy is why the things there seem bearable to him. Seneca tells Lucilius to resist the affairs that take up his time and put them out of the way, and calls philosophy the mistress who commands our attendance. He is not consistent with himself: in Letter 62 he lends himself to his affairs without surrendering to them, which is close to what Marcus does.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We must resist the affairs which occupy our time; they must not be untangled, but rather put out of the way.
support.follows: The affairs that take up my time are to be resisted and put aside, not worked through one by one.
support.context: Letter 72, on business as the enemy of philosophy. “The affairs which occupy our time” are the employments that keep springing up and for which people keep postponing study.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: She is not a thing to be followed at odd times, but a subject for daily practice; she is mistress, and she commands our attendance.
support.follows: Philosophy is to be practised daily, not at odd times; she is the mistress, and we attend on her.
support.context: Letter 53: Seneca tells Lucilius to devote himself wholly to philosophy and not to study it in spare time, as a sick man drops his business to get well. “She” is philosophy.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For I do not surrender myself to my affairs, but loan myself to them
support.follows: Seneca lends himself to his affairs and does not give himself up to them.
support.context: Opening of Letter 62: people pretend that many affairs block their studies. Seneca says of himself that his time is free and that wherever he is he is master of himself.
