passages.title: On crowds
passages.text: But both courses are to be avoided; you should not copy the bad simply because they are many, nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.

passages.title: On the dangers of association with our fellow-men [ 1 ]
passages.text: And what may you attain by living such a life? Not necessarily freedom from harm at their hands, but at least freedom from deceit. In so far, however, as you are able, take refuge with philosophy: she will cherish you in her bosom, and in her sanctuary you shall be safe, or, at any rate, safer than before. People collide only when they are travelling the same path.

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: But do not of your own accord make your troubles heavier to bear and burden yourself with complaining. Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it; but if, on the other hand, you begin to encourage yourself and say, “It is nothing,—a trifling matter at most; keep a stout heart and it will soon cease”; then in thinking it slight, you will make it slight. Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, hark back to opinion. It is according to opinion that we suffer.

passages.title: On facing hardships
passages.text: Spite of all do you still chafe and complain, not understanding that, in all the evils to which you refer, there is really only one—the fact that you do chafe and complain? If you ask me, I think that for a man there is no misery unless there be something in the universe which he thinks miserable. I shall not endure myself on that day when I find anything unendurable. I am ill; but that is a part of my lot. My slaves have fallen sick, my income has gone off, my house is rickety, I have been assailed by losses, accidents, toil, and fear; this is a common thing. Nay, that was an understatement; it was an inevitable thing.

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: A man is as wretched as he has convinced himself that he is. I hold that we should do away with complaint about past sufferings and with all language like this: “None has ever been worse off than I. What sufferings, what evils have I endured! No one has thought that I shall recover. How often have my family bewailed me, and the physicians given me over! Men who are placed on the rack are not torn asunder with such agony!” However, even if all this is true, it is over and gone. What benefit is there in reviewing past sufferings, and in being unhappy, just because once you were unhappy? Besides, every one adds much to his own ills, and tells lies to himself. And that which was bitter to bear is pleasant to have borne; it is natural to rejoice at the ending of one’s ills. Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all,—the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.

passages.title: On the vitality of the soul and its attributes
passages.text: Self-Command is the greatest command of all. Let her teach me what a hallowed thing is the Justice which ever regards another’s good and seeks nothing for itself except its own employment. It should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation; it should satisfy itself. Let each man convince himself of this before all else—“I must be just without reward.” And that is not enough; let him convince himself also of this: “May I take pleasure in devoting myself of my own free will to uphold this noblest of virtues.” Let all his thoughts be turned as far as possible from personal interests. You need not look about for the reward of a just deed; a just deed in itself offers a still greater return.

passages.title: On the vitality of the soul and its attributes
passages.text: Fasten deep in your mind that which I remarked a short space above: that it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness. Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown. Are you not willing to be just without being renowned? Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced. And then, if you are wise, let ill repute, well won, be a delight. Farewell.

passages.title: On good company
passages.text: When I give myself to my friends, I do not withdraw from my own company, nor do I linger with those who are associated with me through some special occasion or some case which arises from my official position. But I spend my time in the company of all the best; no matter in what lands they may have lived, or in what age, I let my thoughts fly to them.

passages.title: On reformation
passages.text: And when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant; but until then, set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man, whether your choice be the great Cato or Scipio, or Laelius,—or any man in whose presence even abandoned wretches would check their bad impulses. Meantime, you are engaged in making of yourself the sort of person in whose company you would not dare to sin. When this aim has been accomplished and you begin to hold yourself in some esteem, I shall gradually allow you to do what Epicurus, in another passage, suggests: “The time when you should most of all withdraw into yourself is when you are forced to be in a crowd.”

passages.title: On reformation
passages.text: You ought to make yourself of a different stamp from the multitude. Therefore, while it is not yet safe to withdraw into solitude, seek out certain individuals; for everyone is better off in the company of somebody or other,—no matter who,—than in his own company alone. “The time when you should most of all withdraw into yourself is when you are forced to be in a crowd.” Yes, provided that you are a good, tranquil, and self-restrained man; otherwise, you had better withdraw into a crowd in order to get away from your self. Alone, you are too close to a rascal. Farewell.

passages.title: On business as the enemy of philosophy
passages.text: But the study of philosophy is not to be postponed until you have leisure; everything else is to be neglected in order that we may attend to philosophy, for no amount of time is long enough for it, even though our lives be prolonged from boyhood to the uttermost bounds of time allotted to man. It makes little difference whether you leave philosophy out altogether or study it intermittently; for it does not stay as it was when you dropped it, but, because its continuity has been broken, it goes back to the position in which it was at the beginning, like things which fly apart when they are stretched taut. We must resist the affairs which occupy our time; they must not be untangled, but rather put out of the way. Indeed, there is no time that is unsuitable for helpful studies; and yet many a man fails to study amid the very circumstances which make study necessary.

passages.title: On the faults of the spirit
passages.text: If you were ill, you would stop caring for your personal concerns, and forget your business duties; you would not think highly enough of any client to take active charge of his case during a slight abatement of your sufferings. You would try your hardest to be rid of the illness as soon as possible. What, then? Shall you not do the same thing now? Throw aside all hindrances and give up your time to getting a sound mind; for no man can attain it if he is engrossed in other matters. Philosophy wields her own authority; she appoints her own time and does not allow it to be appointed for her. She is not a thing to be followed at odd times, but a subject for daily practice; she is mistress, and she commands our attendance.

passages.title: On good company
passages.text: We are deceived by those who would have us believe that a multitude of affairs blocks their pursuit of liberal studies; they make a pretence of their engagements, and multiply them, when their engagements are merely with themselves. As for me, Lucilius, my time is free; it is indeed free, and wherever I am, I am master of myself. For I do not surrender myself to my affairs, but loan myself to them, and I do not hunt out excuses for wasting my time. And wherever I am situated, I carry on my own meditations and ponder in my mind some wholesome thought.

claims.t: I gain by going back. By continually going back I get a firmer hold on the harmony, the inner tuning that my rhythm belongs to; I go back often to philosophy and rest in it, and because of philosophy the things at court seem bearable to me, and I seem bearable among them.
claims.shared: Each passage tells me to go back and names what comes with it. 6.9 says “by continually going back”; 6.10 says “Go back here often”. With the going back 6.9 names “a firmer hold on the harmony”, and 6.10 names philosophy, “because of which the things there seem bearable”.
claims.changed: 6.9 goes back to the harmony and 6.10 to philosophy; the claim keeps them apart. The places gone back to are left to the claim on going back. “The inner tuning that my rhythm belongs to” is the editor’s gloss of “the harmony”: in 6.9 the harmony is the tuning of notes, set beside “the rhythm” of the sentence before and gone back to as I go back “into yourself”; the passage does not say that the harmony is the same as myself. “Because of philosophy” is 6.10’s “because of which”, said of philosophy and not given as the reason for going back; “the things at court” are 6.10’s “the things there”, which the sentence before names as the court. “I gain” is the editor’s word.

support.quote: For you will have a firmer hold on the harmony by continually going back to it.
support.follows: Going back to the harmony continually is what gives a firmer hold on it.
gives: I gain by going back
By continually going back I get a firmer hold on the harmony

support.quote: Go back here often and rest in philosophy, because of which the things there seem bearable to you, and you seem bearable among them.
support.follows: Marcus is to go back often to philosophy and rest in it; philosophy is why the court seems bearable to him and he seems bearable there.
gives: I gain by going back
I go back often to philosophy and rest in it, and because of philosophy the things at court seem bearable to me, and I seem bearable among them

claims.t: There is one thing I want and take pleasure in: to act as a member of a community. I move and hold back as civic reason thinks right, and I rest in going from one social act to the next with god in mind.
claims.shared: Both passages say “one thing”, and in both the one thing is acting for a community: “social act” in 6.6, “civic reason” in 9.10. 6.6 makes it the thing to take pleasure in and rest in; 9.10 makes it the thing to want.
claims.changed: 9.10 says “one thing only”; 6.6 has no “only”, and the claim follows 6.6. “To act as a member of a community” is the editor’s summary of “social act” and “civic reason”, which are two different Greek words. 6.10 uses for resting in philosophy the same Greek verb that 6.6 uses for resting in social acts; no passage says how the two rests are related.

support.quote: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.
support.follows: The one thing to take pleasure in and rest in is going from one act for the common life to the next, with god in mind.

claims.t: I go back quickly and continually: into myself when circumstances throw me into confusion, stepping out of my rhythm no more than I am forced to; at a run to my own ruling part, the part of me that judges and decides; and to philosophy as to a mother, while I wait on the court as on a stepmother.
claims.shared: 6.9 and 6.10 both say “go back”: “go back quickly into yourself” and “continually going back to your mother”. 6.9 and 9.20 both ask for speed, “quickly” and “Run”, and both send me to what is my own: “yourself” and “your own ruling part”.
claims.changed: 9.20 says “Run to”, not “go back”; the claim lists the ruling part as one more place gone back to, which is the editor’s reading. Only 6.9 says “quickly” and only 6.10 says “continually”; the claim puts both words at its head. “Quickly” for 9.20 rests on the literal “Run”; the same Greek verb in 11.2 (“run to the parts”) may mean no more than turning straight to something. 6.10 does not say in so many words that the court is the stepmother and philosophy the mother; the claim follows the order of its words. 6.9 says “the rhythm”; the claim says “my rhythm”. “The part of me that judges and decides” is the editor’s gloss of “ruling part”, the Stoic name for the governing part of the soul.

support.quote: When circumstances force you to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, go back quickly into yourself, and do not step out of the rhythm more than you are forced to.
support.follows: When circumstances shake me, I should go back into myself quickly and leave the rhythm no more than I am forced to.

quickly
into myself when circumstances throw me into confusion, stepping out of my rhythm no more than I am forced to

claims.t: Among the things that please, I set virtue apart. To cheer myself I think of the strong points of the people I live with, and I keep them ready to hand, because nothing cheers so much as the likenesses of the virtues in them; everything else that delights I divide into its parts until I look down on it.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of what pleases, “cheers” in 6.43 and “delightful” in 11.2, and both make an exception of virtue. 6.43 says “nothing cheers so much as the likenesses of the virtues”; 11.2 says to divide things and look down on them “except for virtue and what comes from virtue”.
claims.changed: 6.43 speaks of “the likenesses of the virtues” seen in other people, and the claim keeps that. 11.2 does not say that virtue pleases, only that it is not to be divided and looked down on. “I set virtue apart” is the editor’s summary of the two exceptions. 11.2 names singing, dancing and the pankration and then generalises; the claim says “everything else that delights”.

support.quote: When you want to cheer yourself, think of the strong points of the people you live with: the energy of one, for example, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, and something else in someone else.
support.follows: To cheer myself I should think of what is strong in each person I live with: one’s energy, another’s modesty, another’s generosity.

claims.t: I do not complain, to other people or to myself. I toil, but not as someone miserable, and not in order to be pitied or admired; I have found fault with life at court, and from now on no one hears me do it, not even I myself.
claims.shared: Both passages forbid making a grievance of what I have to do, and both name an audience. 9.10 forbids toiling as “someone who wants to be pitied or admired”; 8.8 says “Let no one hear you finding fault”.
claims.changed: “I do not complain” is the editor’s summary: 8.8 says “finding fault”, and 9.10 has no word for complaining. 9.10 is about toil and 8.8 about life at court. “Any more” in 8.8 shows that Marcus had been finding fault; the claim says so in “I have found fault” and “from now on”.

support.quote: Toil, not as someone miserable, and not as someone who wants to be pitied or admired
support.follows: I should toil without being miserable about it and without wanting pity or admiration for it.

single.quote: and to that of the whole, and to this person’s. To your own, so that you make it a just mind. To that of the whole, so that you remember along with it what you are a part of. To this person’s, so that you take note whether there is ignorance there or intent, and at the same time reckon that it is akin.
single.label: Three ruling parts
single.t: I run to three ruling parts: to my own, to make it a just mind; to that of the whole, to remember what I am a part of; and to the other person’s, to see whether that person acts from ignorance or on purpose, and to reckon at the same time that it is akin.
single.why: Only this passage sends me to the ruling part of the whole and to another person’s, and only it gives a purpose for each. Its opening words, on my own ruling part, are quoted in the claim on going back. The Greek does not say what the other person’s ruling part is akin to: mine, that of the whole, or both; so “akin” is left bare. “Acts from ignorance or on purpose” spells out the Greek’s bare “ignorance or intent”.
single.follows: Besides my own ruling part I should go to that of the whole, to remember what I am part of, and to another’s, to see ignorance or intent and count it akin.

members.text:
When thou wilt comfort and cheer thyself, call to mind the
several gifts and virtues of them, whom thou dost daily converse with;
as for example, the industry of the one; the modesty of another; the
liberality of a third; of another some other thing. For nothing can so
much rejoice thee, as the resemblances and parallels of several virtues,
visible and eminent in the dispositions of those who live with thee;
especially when, all at once, as near as may be, they represent
themselves unto thee. And therefore thou must have them always in a
readiness.
members.english: When you want to cheer yourself, think of the strong points of the people you live with: the energy of one, for example, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, and something else in someone else. For nothing cheers so much as the likenesses of the virtues showing in the characters of the people you live with, and coming together, as many at once as possible. And so they must be kept ready to hand.
members.greek: Ὅταν εὐφρᾶναι σεαυτὸν θέλῃς, ἐνθυμοῦ τὰ προτερήματα τῶν συμβιούντων· οἷον τοῦ μὲν τὸ δραστήριον, τοῦ δὲ τὸ αἰδῆμον, τοῦ δὲ τὸ εὐμετάδοτον, ἄλλου δὲ ἄλλο τι. οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως εὐφραίνει ὡς τὰ ὁμοιώματα τῶν ἀρετῶν ἐμφαινόμενα τοῖς ἤθεσι τῶν συζώντων καὶ ἀθρόα ὡς οἷόν τε συμπίπτοντα. διὸ καὶ πρόχειρα αὐτὰ ἑκτέον.

members.text:
Whensoever by some present hard occurrences thou art constrained to
be in some sort troubled and vexed, return unto thyself as soon as may
be, and be not out of tune longer than thou must needs. For so shalt
thou be the better able to keep thy part another time, and to maintain
the harmony, if thou dost use thyself to this continually; once out,
presently to have recourse unto it, and to begin again.
members.english: When circumstances force you to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, go back quickly into yourself, and do not step out of the rhythm more than you are forced to. For you will have a firmer hold on the harmony by continually going back to it.
members.greek: Ὅταν ἀναγκασθῇς ὑπὸ τῶν περιεστηκότων οἱονεὶ διαταραχθῆναι, ταχέως ἐπάνιθι εἰς σεαυτὸν καὶ μὴ ὑπὲρ τὰ ἀναγκαῖα ἐξίστασο τοῦ ῥυθμοῦ· ἔσῃ γὰρ ἐγκρατέστερος τῆς ἁρμονίας τῷ συνεχῶς εἰς αὐτὴν ἐπανέρχεσθαι.

members.text:
As occasion shall require, either to thine own understanding, or to
that of the universe, or to his, whom thou hast now to do with, let thy
refuge be with all speed. To thine own, that it resolve upon nothing
against justice. To that of the universe, that thou mayest remember,
part of whom thou art. Of his, that thou mayest consider whether in the
estate of ignorance, or of knowledge. And then also must thou call to
mind, that he is thy kinsman.
members.english: Run to your own ruling part, and to that of the whole, and to this person’s. To your own, so that you make it a just mind. To that of the whole, so that you remember along with it what you are a part of. To this person’s, so that you take note whether there is ignorance there or intent, and at the same time reckon that it is akin.
members.greek: Τρέχε ἐπὶ τὸ σεαυτοῦ ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ τὸ τοῦ ὅλου καὶ τὸ τούτου. τὸ μὲν σεαυτοῦ, ἵνα νοῦν δικαικὸν αὐτὸ ποιήσῃς· τὸ δὲ τοῦ ὅλου, ἵνα συμμνημονεύσῃς τίνος μέρος εἶ· τὸ δὲ τούτου, ἵνα ἐπιστήσῃς πότερον ἄγνοια ἢ γνώμη, καὶ ἅμα λογίσῃ ὅτι συγγενές.

members.text:
Labour not as one to whom it is appointed to be wretched, nor as one
that either would be pitied, or admired; but let this be thine only care
and desire; so always and in all things to prosecute or to forbear, as
the law of charity, or mutual society doth require.
members.english: Toil, not as someone miserable, and not as someone who wants to be pitied or admired, but want one thing only: to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right.
members.greek: Πόνει μὴ ὡς ἄθλιος μηδὲ ὡς ἐλεεῖσθαι ἢ θαυμάζεσθαι θέλων, ἀλλὰ μόνον ἓν θέλε· κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι, ὡς ὁ πολιτικὸς λόγος ἀξιοῖ.

members.text:
Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable
kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in
thy mind.
members.english: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.
members.greek: Ἑνὶ τέρπου καὶ προσαναπαύου, τῷ ἀπὸ πράξεως κοινωνικῆς μεταβαίνειν ἐπὶ πρᾶξιν κοινωνικὴν σὺν μνήμῃ θεοῦ.

members.text:
If it were that thou hadst at one time both a stepmother, and
a natural mother living, thou wouldst honour and respect her also;
nevertheless to thine own natural mother would thy refuge, and recourse
be continually. So let the court and thy philosophy be unto thee. Have
recourse unto it often, and comfort thyself in her, by whom it is that
those other things are made tolerable unto thee, and thou also in those
things not intolerable unto others.
members.english: If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would wait on the stepmother, and still you would be continually going back to your mother. That is what the court and philosophy are to you now. Go back here often and rest in philosophy, because of which the things there seem bearable to you, and you seem bearable among them.
members.greek: Εἰ μητρυιάν τε ἅμα εἶχες καὶ μητέρα, ἐκείνην τ̓ ἂν ἐθεράπευες καὶ ὅμως ἡ ἐπάνοδός σοι πρὸς τὴν μητέρα συνεχὴς ἐγίνετο. τοῦτό σοι νῦν ἐστιν ἡ αὐλὴ καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὧδε πολλάκις ἐπάνιθι καὶ προσαναπαύου ταύτῃ, δι’ ἣν καὶ τὰ ἐκεῖ σοι ἀνεκτὰ φαίνεται καὶ σὺ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀνεκτός.

members.text:
Forbear henceforth to complain of the trouble of a courtly life,
either in public before others, or in private by thyself.
members.english: Let no one hear you finding fault with life at court any more, and do not hear yourself doing it either.
members.greek: Μηκέτι σου μηδεὶς ἀκούσῃ καταμεμφομένου τὸν ἐν αὐλῇ βίον μηδὲ σὺ σεαυτοῦ.

members.text:
A pleasant song or dance; the Pancratiast's exercise, sports that
thou art wont to be much taken with, thou shalt easily contemn; if
the harmonious voice thou shalt divide into so many particular sounds
whereof it doth consist, and of every one in particular shall ask
thyself; whether this or that sound is it, that doth so conquer thee.
For thou wilt be ashamed of it. And so for shame, if accordingly thou
shalt consider it, every particular motion and posture by itself: and
so for the wrestler's exercise too. Generally then, whatsoever it be,
besides virtue, and those things that proceed from virtue that thou art
subject to be much affected with, remember presently thus to divide
it, and by this kind of division, in each particular to attain unto the
contempt of the whole. This thou must transfer and apply to thy whole
life also.
members.english: You will look down on delightful singing, on dancing and on the pankration, if you divide the tuneful voice into each of its notes and ask yourself at each one whether this gets the better of you, for you will be ashamed; and with dancing, if you do the corresponding thing at each movement or pose; and the same with the pankration too. In general, then, except for virtue and what comes from virtue, remember to run to the parts, and by dividing them to come to look down on them; and carry the same thing over to the whole of life as well.
members.greek: Ὠιδῆς ἐπιτερποῦς καὶ ὀρχήσεως καὶ παγκρατίου καταφρονήσεις, ἐὰν τὴν μὲν ἐμμελῆ φωνὴν καταμερίσῃς εἰς ἕκαστον τῶν φθόγγων καὶ καθ’ ἕνα πύθῃ σεαυτοῦ, εἰ τούτου ἥττων εἶ· διατραπήσῃ γάρ· ἐπὶ δὲ ὀρχήσεως τὸ ἀνάλογον ποιήσας καθ’ ἑκάστην κίνησιν ἢ σχέσιν, τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ παγκρατίου. ὅλως οὖν, χωρὶς ἀρετῆς καὶ τῶν ἀπ’ ἀρετῆς, μέμνησο ἐπὶ τὰ κατὰ μέρος τρέχειν καὶ τῇ διαιρέσει αὐτῶν εἰς καταφρόνησιν ἰέναι, τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν βίον ὅλον μετάφερε.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 6.43 is 6.48, 6.9 is 6.11, 9.20 is 9.22, 9.10 is 9.12, 6.6 is 6.7, 6.10 is 6.12 and 8.8 is 8.9; 11.2 is the same.

In 6.10 reads the court as the stepmother and philosophy as the mother, by the order of the words, and reads “here” as philosophy, because the next clause sets it against “the things there”; the Greek spells out neither. In 9.20 “a just mind” rests on a rare Greek adjective which, by the translators’ note, some editors have doubted and which the note marks as unchecked; and the Greek leaves open what the other person’s ruling part is akin to.

Treats going back “into yourself” (6.9), going back to philosophy (6.10) and running to “your own ruling part” (9.20) as one habit with three places. 9.20 says “Run to” and not “go back”, and no passage says that the three places are one.

Joins 6.43 and 11.2 on one point only: both speak of what pleases, and each makes an exception of virtue. “I set virtue apart” is the editor’s summary. 11.2 is otherwise about another subject, looking down on things by dividing them into parts.

Calls the refusals of 9.10 (“not as someone miserable”, not wanting “to be pitied or admired”) and of 8.8 (“finding fault”) “complaint”, in the last claim and in the statement; 9.10 has no word for complaining. The statement also sets the rest in social acts (6.6) beside the rest in philosophy (6.10), and calls the social acts “acting as a member of a community”, the editor’s summary used in the claim on the one thing wanted; no passage says how the two rests are related.
articles.limit: Much is said elsewhere: Articles 1 and 2 say that what I do aims at the common good and Article 3 that I do not complain of what happens to me; Article 12 (claim 1 and its item from 4.3) has me retreat into myself again and again, with the same limit from Seneca (Ep. 25.7); and Article 11 (claims 2 and 5 and its item from 5.9) has me come back to philosophy and stay in my situation, which Seneca’s Letters 53, 62 and 72 limit there, while here the same letters are marked as a challenge because 6.10 has me wait on the court and Seneca would put such affairs out of the way. What this article adds is the rest found in philosophy, the court as a stepmother I wait on while I keep going back to philosophy as to a mother, and the refusal to complain of my own toil and of the court. The claim on virtue is the weakest, since 6.43 and 11.2 share only the exception they make for virtue and it has no place in the statement; and 6.6 names one thing to take pleasure in while 6.43 says that nothing cheers so much as the virtues seen in other people, which the article keeps without reconciling.

articles.title: The morning, and the question before each action

statement.t: I get up for the work I was made for, I question each thing I do, and when I have done good I look for nothing more.

parts.words: I get up for the work I was made for
I question each thing I do
when I have done good I look for nothing more

statement.form: The statement follows a day: getting up, with claims 1 and 2 as its ground; questioning each action, mine and others’ (claims 3 and 5); and what I look for once the good is done (claim 4). The claims stand side by side; none is derived from another.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, looking for nothing after doing good gains a second author. Under Why he adds the purpose of the whole life, against which each act is weighed; under Practice, death kept in mind at lying down and at waking, so that each morning is a gift, and a review of each day; under When it breaks, owning a fault as the sign that I am awake. He limits and challenges nothing.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a look back: besides questioning what I am about to do, I review each day.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: You need not look about for the reward of a just deed; a just deed in itself offers a still greater return.
piece.follows: I need not look for a reward for a just deed, because the deed itself repays me more.
piece.context: Letter 113, near its end: justice looks to another’s good and seeks nothing for itself, so one must be just without reward. “A just deed” is any act of justice toward others.
gives: I look for nothing more
I want no return

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown.
piece.follows: Whoever wants his virtue made known is after fame, not virtue.
piece.context: The close of Letter 113, on justice practised without reward: it makes no difference how many people know that one is upright. “Their virtue” is that justice.
gives: I do not try to have it seen

items.label: why
items.role: The purpose of my whole life
items.t: Whenever I want to know what to seek or avoid, I consider how it stands to the purpose of my whole life, for whatever I do ought to be in harmony with it. No one can set the details in order without first setting that purpose before himself. If I do not know what harbour I am making for, no wind is the right wind.
items.why: Marcus asks of each action, mine or another’s, to what end it is done, and what it is to me in the face of death. Seneca puts a question before those: the purpose of the whole life, without which no single act can be set in order.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: As often as you wish to know what is to be avoided or what is to be sought, consider its relation to the Supreme Good, to the purpose of your whole life. For whatever we do ought to be in harmony with this; no man can set in order the details unless he has already set before himself the chief purpose of his life.
support.follows: To judge what to seek or avoid, I measure it against the purpose of my whole life, which must be set first.
support.context: Letter 71, on the Supreme Good, opens with this rule for every choice. “The details” are the separate acts and choices of a life; “this” is the purpose of the whole life.
gives: I consider how it stands to the purpose of my whole life
whatever I do ought to be in harmony with it
No one can set the details in order without first setting that purpose before himself

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
support.follows: Without a known aim, nothing that happens can help me toward it.
support.context: Letter 71, on the Supreme Good: our plans miscarry because they have no aim. The “harbour” is the chief purpose of one’s life; the winds are what chance brings.
gives: If I do not know what harbour I am making for, no wind is the right wind

items.label: practice
items.role: Death at both ends of the day
items.t: When I lie down to sleep, I tell myself that I may not wake again, and when I wake, that I may not go to sleep again. I go to sleep gladly and say that I have lived, and that the course Fortune set for me is finished. Then every morning I get up is a gift.
items.why: Marcus’s morning reminder in this section is about the work ahead, and death enters only at each action (8.2, 10.29). Seneca brings death to the two ends of the day, and from it he draws the morning as a gift.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Say to me when I lie down to sleep: “You may not wake again!” And when I have waked: “You may not go to sleep again!”
support.follows: At lying down and at waking I should be reminded that this sleep or this day may be my last.
support.context: Letter 49, on the shortness of life: Seneca asks philosophy for teaching against the fear of death. The words he wants said to him are reminders that any sleep or day may be his last.
gives: When I lie down to sleep, I tell myself that I may not wake again, and when I wake, that I may not go to sleep again

support.author: seneca
support.quote: let us go to our sleep with joy and gladness; let us say: I have lived; the course which Fortune set for me Is finished.
support.follows: Each night I should go to sleep glad, saying that I have lived and my course is finished.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age: each day should be lived as if it completed one’s life. Seneca turns a rich man’s nightly mock funeral into a glad saying at bedtime.
gives: I go to sleep gladly and say that I have lived, and that the course Fortune set for me is finished

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When a man has said: “I have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.
support.follows: Once I have said “I have lived”, each further morning is something extra given to me.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age, ending the thought that each day should be lived as one’s last: whoever can say at night “I have lived” takes each new morning as a bonus.
gives: every morning I get up is a gift

items.label: practice
items.t: I keep watching myself and review each day. What makes us bad is that none of us looks back over his own life: our thoughts go only to what we are about to do.
items.why: Marcus’s questions in this section are asked before or at an action. Seneca adds the look back over the day, and says that thinking only of what comes next is what makes us bad.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day.
support.follows: I should watch myself all the time and go back over each day.
support.context: Letter 83: Lucilius asked for an account of each of Seneca’s days. Seneca agrees and makes a habit of it; “each day” is his own day, reported in order.
gives: I keep watching myself and review each day

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For this is what makes us wicked: that no one of us looks back over his own life. Our thoughts are devoted only to what we are about to do.
support.follows: Never looking back over one’s own life, and thinking only of what comes next, is what makes people bad.
support.context: Letter 83, giving the reason for reviewing each day: our plans for the future depend on the past, yet we think only ahead. “His own life” is one’s past conduct.
gives: What makes us bad is that none of us looks back over his own life
our thoughts go only to what we are about to do

items.label: breaks
items.t: While I will not admit my faults, I am still in their grasp: only someone who is awake can tell his dream. Admitting a fault is a sign that my mind is sound, and I rouse myself so that I can correct my mistakes.
items.why: 6.29 tells me to wake up and see that it was dreams that troubled me. Seneca uses the same image for faults: being able to name them is the sign that I am awake.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Why will no man confess his faults? Because he is still in their grasp; only he who is awake can recount his dream, and similarly a confession of sin is a proof of sound mind.
support.follows: One who cannot confess his faults is still held by them; confessing them shows the mind is sound again.
support.context: Letter 53, on faults of the spirit: the worse a disease of the soul, the less it is felt, as deep sleep leaves no dreams. The “dream” stands for one’s own faults.
gives: While I will not admit my faults, I am still in their grasp
only someone who is awake can tell his dream

passages.title: On the vitality of the soul and its attributes
passages.text: Self-Command is the greatest command of all. Let her teach me what a hallowed thing is the Justice which ever regards another’s good and seeks nothing for itself except its own employment. It should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation; it should satisfy itself. Let each man convince himself of this before all else—“I must be just without reward.” And that is not enough; let him convince himself also of this: “May I take pleasure in devoting myself of my own free will to uphold this noblest of virtues.” Let all his thoughts be turned as far as possible from personal interests. You need not look about for the reward of a just deed; a just deed in itself offers a still greater return.

passages.title: On the vitality of the soul and its attributes
passages.text: Fasten deep in your mind that which I remarked a short space above: that it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness. Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown. Are you not willing to be just without being renowned? Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced. And then, if you are wise, let ill repute, well won, be a delight. Farewell.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: As often as you wish to know what is to be avoided or what is to be sought, consider its relation to the Supreme Good, to the purpose of your whole life. For whatever we do ought to be in harmony with this; no man can set in order the details unless he has already set before himself the chief purpose of his life. The artist may have his colours all prepared, but he cannot produce a likeness unless he has already made up his mind what he wishes to paint. The reason we make mistakes is because we all consider the parts of life, but never life as a whole.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: The archer must know what he is seeking to hit; then he must aim and control the weapon by his skill. Our plans miscarry because they have no aim. When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind. Chance must necessarily have great influence over our lives, because we live by chance.

passages.title: On the shortness of life
passages.text: teach me something with which to face these troubles. Bring it to pass that I shall cease trying to escape from death, and that life may cease to escape from me. Give me courage to meet hardships; make me calm in the face of the unavoidable. Relax the straitened limits of the time which is allotted me. Show me that the good in life does not depend upon life’s length, but upon the use we make of it; also, that it is possible, or rather usual, for a man who has lived long to have lived too little. Say to me when I lie down to sleep: “You may not wake again!” And when I have waked: “You may not go to sleep again!” Say to me when I go forth from my house: “You may not return!” And when I return: “You may never go forth again!”

passages.title: On old age
passages.text: Thus Pacuvius had himself carried out to burial every day. Let us, however, do from a good motive what he used to do from a debased motive; let us go to our sleep with joy and gladness; let us say: I have lived; the course which Fortune set for me Is finished. And if God is pleased to add another day, we should welcome it with glad hearts. That man is happiest, and is secure in his own possession of himself, who can await the morrow without apprehension. When a man has said: “I have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.

passages.title: On drunkenness
passages.text: I shall therefore do as you bid, and shall gladly inform you by letter what I am doing, and in what sequence. I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day. For this is what makes us wicked: that no one of us looks back over his own life. Our thoughts are devoted only to what we are about to do. And yet our plans for the future always depend on the past.

passages.title: On the faults of the spirit
passages.text: Why will no man confess his faults? Because he is still in their grasp; only he who is awake can recount his dream, and similarly a confession of sin is a proof of sound mind. Let us, therefore, rouse ourselves, that we may be able to correct our mistakes. Philosophy, however, is the only power that can stir us, the only power that can shake off our deep slumber. Devote yourself wholly to philosophy. You are worthy of her; she is worthy of you; greet one another with a loving embrace. Say farewell to all other interests with courage and frankness. Do not study philosophy merely during your spare time.

claims.t: When I find it hard to get up, I remind myself that I am getting up to do a human being’s work: social actions, which are according to my nature. I share sleep with the animals that have no reason; this work is more my own, and more agreeable too.
claims.shared: Both passages meet the moment of getting up with one reminder: 8.11, that “to render social actions is according to the way you are made”; 5.1, “I am getting up to do a human being’s work”. Both name social actions and what is according to nature.
claims.changed: 8.11 sets sleep beside the animals, and 5.1 sets lying in bed beside the bees at their work; the claim keeps 8.11’s contrast, and claim 2 takes up 5.1’s bees. That this work is more agreeable is said by 8.11 alone.

support.quote: When you find it hard to wake from sleep, remind yourself that to render social actions is according to the way you are made and according to human nature, whereas sleeping is shared with the animals without reason as well.
support.follows: When waking is hard, I should recall that social action suits the way a human being is made, while sleep is shared with animals.

claims.t: The plants, the birds and the bees take part in the work of the universe, and so do all of us. Each does it in its own way: some knowingly, some without attending to it, even people asleep, even the one who finds fault with what happens. What is left to me is to understand among which of these workers I am placing myself, and to be willing to do what belongs to a human being.
claims.shared: Both passages see other beings at work on the universe and ask me to take my place among them: in 5.1 the plants and bees are “putting the universe together”, in 6.37 all of us, sleepers too, are “fellow workers in the things that happen in the universe”. Both say each does it in its own way.
claims.changed: 5.1 speaks of plants and animals and 6.37 of people; the claim puts them together. “These workers” are the people just named, as in 6.37, where the choice comes right after the one who finds fault: whether I work knowingly or as he does. What 6.37 says of the one who governs the whole, and its line in a play, are kept apart as said once.

support.quote: Do you not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees doing what is their own to do and, for their part, putting the universe together? And then you are not willing to do what belongs to a human being?
support.follows: Plants and small creatures each do their own work and help put the universe together, so I should be willing to do a human being’s.

claims.t: At each thing I do, I stop and ask myself about it with my death in mind: what is this act to me, will I regret it, and is death terrible because it would take this away?
claims.shared: Both passages tell me to question myself at each action (8.2: “At each action ask yourself”; 10.29: “At each of the things you do, one by one, stop and ask yourself”), and in both the question brings in death.
claims.changed: “With my death in mind” is the editor’s summary of two uses of death: 8.2 says “A little while and I am dead”; 10.29 asks whether death is terrible because it takes this away. Each passage’s own question is kept as it asks it. “What is this act to me” is the translators’ plainer reading of 8.2’s “How does this stand with me?”.

claims.t: When I have done good, I look for nothing more: I do not try to have it seen, and I want no return. I do not tire of doing good, but pass on to the next good act, as a vine bears its grapes again in season.
claims.shared: Three passages say that once the work is done nothing more is looked for: 7.43 “why do you look for a third thing”, 5.6 “looks for nothing more”, 8.2 “What more do I look for”. 7.43 and 5.6 both speak of one who has done good, and both turn away from having it seen: “to be seen to have done good”, “do not shout about it”.
claims.changed: 8.2 speaks of the work in hand, not of a good turn. 5.6’s “another thing” is read as the next good act, because the vine bears its grapes again. 7.43’s “do not tire of being benefited, in that you give benefit” becomes “I do not tire of doing good”, which drops its point that giving benefits the giver.

support.quote: When you have done good and another has had good done to them, why do you look for a third thing beside these, as fools do: to be seen to have done good as well, or to get a return?
support.follows: Once I have done good and someone has received it, it is foolish to want also to be seen doing it or to be repaid.

single.quote: Is my mind enough for this or not? If it is enough, I use it for the work as a tool given by the nature of the whole. If it is not enough, either I step back from the work in favour of someone who can carry it out better, unless for some other reason it is my duty, or I do it as best I can, taking on to help me someone who, by making use of my ruling part as well, can do what is timely and useful for the community now.
single.label: Whether I am enough
single.t: Before a task I ask whether my mind is enough for it. If it is, I use it as a tool that the nature of the whole has given me. If it is not, I step back for someone who can do the work better, unless it is my duty for some other reason, or I do it as best I can and take on someone to help me.
single.why: Only this passage asks whether I am able for a task and what to do if I am not. Its aim, what is useful to the community, is already Article 1’s.
single.follows: If my mind is equal to a task I use it; if not, I give the task to someone better or do it with help.

single.quote: Ask yourself as soon as you come out of sleep: will it make any difference to you if what is just and right is blamed by someone else? It will not.
single.label: A morning question
single.t: As soon as I wake, I ask myself whether it will make any difference to me if someone else blames what is just and right. It will not.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of other people’s blame. It also asks its question on waking, as 5.1 and 8.11 do, but its question is about blame, not about the day’s work.
single.follows: If someone else blames what is just and right, that makes no difference to me.

single.quote: Nature, though, has given measures for this as well; it has given them for eating and drinking as well; and yet you go beyond the measures, beyond what is enough. But in your actions it is not so: there you stop short of what you can do. For you do not love yourself, since otherwise you would love your nature too, and what it wills.
single.label: Too much rest
single.t: Nature has set a measure for rest, as it has for eating and drinking. I fail when I go beyond that measure and stop short of what I can do in action. Then I do not love myself, or I would love my nature too, and what it wills.
single.why: Only this passage says what failing looks like here: too much rest and too little action. 8.11 knows that waking is hard but does not describe the failure.
single.follows: Going past nature’s measure in rest while falling short in action shows that I do not love my nature, and so do not love myself.

single.quote: Sober up and call yourself back. And when you have woken up again and understood that it was dreams that were troubling you, then, awake again, look at these things as you looked at those.
single.label: Waking again
single.t: I sober up and call myself back. Once I am awake again and understand that it was dreams that were troubling me, I look at what troubles me now as I looked at what troubled me in those dreams.
single.why: Only this passage gives a way back. Its waking is an image for coming to my senses, not the morning of 5.1 and 8.11, so it is not fused with them.
single.follows: Having seen that what troubled me were dreams, I should look at my waking troubles as I looked at the dreams.

single.quote: For the one who governs the whole will in any case use you well, and will take you in as some part of the fellow workers and of those who help the work along. But you, do not become the kind of part that the cheap and ridiculous line is in the play, the one Chrysippus mentions.
single.label: Not a worthless part
single.t: Whatever I do, the one who governs the whole will make good use of me and take me in among those who help the work along. Even so, I must not become the part that Chrysippus likened to a cheap and ridiculous line in a play: poor in itself, though it still adds to the play as a whole.
single.why: Only this passage says what kind of part I can fail to be. 5.1 asks me to work, but does not say I will be used whatever I do. What the cheap line is, poor in itself though it adds to the whole play, is from the translators’ note on Chrysippus (from memory), not from the passage.
single.follows: The one who governs the whole will use me well in any case, but I should not be the worthless line of the play.

members.text:
In the morning as soon as thou art awaked, when thy judgment, before
either thy affections, or external objects have wrought upon it, is yet
most free and impartial: put this question to thyself, whether if that
which is right and just be done, the doing of it by thyself, or by
others when thou art not able thyself; be a thing material or no. For
sure it is not. And as for these that keep such a life, and stand so
much upon the praises, or dispraises of other men, hast thou forgotten
what manner of men they be? that such and such upon their beds, and such
at their board: what their ordinary actions are: what they pursue after,
and what they fly from: what thefts and rapines they commit, if not with
their hands and feet, yet with that more precious part of theirs, their
minds: which (would it but admit of them) might enjoy faith, modesty,
truth, justice, a good spirit.
members.english: Ask yourself as soon as you come out of sleep: will it make any difference to you if what is just and right is blamed by someone else? It will not. Have you forgotten that these people who snort and prance in their praise and blame of others are like this in bed and like this at table, and what things they do, what they run from, what they chase, what they steal, what they seize, not with hands and feet but with the most precious part of themselves, the part that becomes, when it wants to, good faith, a sense of shame, truth, law, a good spirit?
members.greek: Πυνθάνεσθαι ἑαυτοῦ εὐθὺς ἐξ ὕπνου γενόμενον· μήτι διοίσει σοι, ἐὰν ὑπὸ ἄλλου ψέγηται τὰ δίκαια καὶ καλῶς ἔχοντα; οὐ διοίσει. μήτι ἐπιλέλησαι ὅτι οὗτοι οἱ ἐν τοῖς περὶ ἄλλων ἐπαίνοις καὶ ψόγοις φρυαττόμενοι τοιοῦτοι μὲν ἐπὶ τῆς κλίνης εἰσί, τοιοῦτοι δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης, οἷα δὲ ποιοῦσιν, οἷα δὲ φεύγουσιν, οἷα δὲ διώκουσιν, οἷα δὲ κλέπτουσιν, οἷα δὲ ἁρπάζουσιν, οὐ χερσὶ καὶ ποσίν, ἀλλὰ τῷ τιμιωτάτῳ ἑαυτῶν μέρει, ὃ γίνεται ὅταν θέλῃ, πίστις, αἰδώς, ἀλήθεια, νόμος, ἀγαθὸς δαίμων;

members.text:
Upon every action that thou art about, put this question to thyself;
How will this when it is done agree with me? Shall I have no occasion
to repent of it? Yet a very little while and I am dead and gone; and
all things are at end. What then do I care for more than this, that my
present action whatsoever it be, may be the proper action of one that
is reasonable; whose end is, the common good; who in all things is ruled
and governed by the same law of right and reason, by which God Himself
is.
members.english: At each action ask yourself: “How does this stand with me? Will I come to regret it? A little while and I am dead, and everything is cleared away. What more do I look for, if the work in hand is the work of a living being that has mind, is social, and is under the same law as god?”
members.greek: Καθ’ ἑκάστην πρᾶξιν ἐρώτα σεαυτόν· πῶς μοι αὕτη ἔχει; μὴ μετανοήσω ἐπ’ αὐτῇ; μικρὸν καὶ τέθνηκα καὶ πάντ’ ἐκ μέσου· τί πλέον ἐπιζητῶ, εἰ τὸ παρὸν ἔργον ζῴου νοεροῦ καὶ κοινωνικοῦ καὶ ἰσονόμου θεῷ;

members.text:
When thou art hard to be stirred up and awaked out of thy sleep,
admonish thyself and call to mind, that, to perform actions tending to
the common good is that which thine own proper constitution, and
that which the nature of man do require. But to sleep, is common to
unreasonable creatures also. And what more proper and natural, yea what
more kind and pleasing, than that which is according to nature?
members.english: When you find it hard to wake from sleep, remind yourself that to render social actions is according to the way you are made and according to human nature, whereas sleeping is shared with the animals without reason as well. And what is according to each one’s nature is more its own, more closely grown to it, and indeed more agreeable too.
members.greek: Ὅταν ἐξ ὕπνου δυσχερῶς ἐγείρῃ, ἀναμιμνῄσκου ὅτι κατὰ τὴν κατασκευήν σου ἐστὶ καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπικὴν φύσιν τὸ πράξεις κοινωνικὰς ἀποδιδόναι, τὸ δὲ καθεύδειν κοινὸν καὶ τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων· ὃ δὲ κατὰ φύσιν ἑκάστῳ, τοῦτο οἰκειότερον καὶ προσφυέστερον καὶ δὴ καὶ προσηνέστερον.

members.text:
In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider
with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred
up. Am I then yet unwilling to go about that, for which I myself was
born and brought forth into this world? Or was I made for this, to
lay me down, and make much of myself in a warm bed? 'O but this is
pleasing.' And was it then for this that thou wert born, that thou
mightest enjoy pleasure? Was it not in very truth for this, that thou
mightest always be busy and in action? Seest thou not how all things
in the world besides, how every tree md plant, how sparrows and ants,
spiders and bees: how all in their kind are intent as it were orderly to
perform whatsoever (towards the preservation of this orderly universe)
naturally doth become and belong unto thin? And wilt not thou do that,
which belongs unto a man to do? Wilt not thou run to do that, which thy
nature doth require? 'But thou must have some rest.' Yes, thou must.
Nature hath of that also, as well as of eating and drinking, allowed
thee a certain stint. But thou guest beyond thy stint, and beyond that
which would suffice, and in matter of action, there thou comest short of
that which thou mayest. It must needs be therefore, that thou dost not
love thyself, for if thou didst, thou wouldst also love thy nature, and
that which thy nature doth propose unto herself as her end. Others,
as many as take pleasure in their trade and profession, can even pine
themselves at their works, and neglect their bodies and their food for
it; and doest thou less honour thy nature, than an ordinary mechanic
his trade; or a good dancer his art? than a covetous man his silver, and
vainglorious man applause? These to whatsoever they take an affection,
can be content to want their meat and sleep, to further that every one
which he affects: and shall actions tending to the common good of
human society, seem more vile unto thee, or worthy of less respect and
intention?
members.english: At dawn, when you are reluctant to get up, have this ready to hand: “I am getting up to do a human being’s work. Why then am I discontented, if I am on my way to do the things I was born for, the things for whose sake I was brought into the universe? Or was I made for this, to lie under the blankets and keep myself warm?” “But this is more pleasant.” So were you born to feel pleasure? And in general, were you born to be acted on or to act? Do you not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees doing what is their own to do and, for their part, putting the universe together? And then you are not willing to do what belongs to a human being? You do not run to what is according to your nature? “But one must rest too.” I say so too. Nature, though, has given measures for this as well; it has given them for eating and drinking as well; and yet you go beyond the measures, beyond what is enough. But in your actions it is not so: there you stop short of what you can do. For you do not love yourself, since otherwise you would love your nature too, and what it wills. But those who love their own crafts wear themselves away at the works of those crafts, unwashed and unfed. Do you honour your own nature less than the engraver honours engraving, or the dancer dancing, or the money-lover money, or the lover of empty fame their scrap of fame? These people too, when the passion takes them, would sooner advance the things they care about than eat or sleep. But to you do social actions seem cheaper and worth less effort?
members.greek: Ὄρθρου, ὅταν δυσόκνως ἐξεγείρῃ, πρόχειρον ἔστω ὅτι ἐπὶ ἀνθρώπου ἔργον ἐγείρομαι· τί οὖν δυσκολαίνω, εἰ πορεύομαι ἐπὶ τὸ ποιεῖν ὧν ἕνεκεν γέγονα καὶ ὧν χάριν προῆγμαι εἰς τὸν κόσμον; ἢ ἐπὶ τοῦτο κατεσκεύασμαι, ἵνα κατακείμενος ἐν στρωματίοις ἐμαυτὸν θάλπω; ἀλλὰ τοῦτο ἥδιον. πρὸς τὸ ἥδεσθαι οὖν γέγονας, ὅλως δὲ σὺ πρὸς πεῖσιν ἢ πρὸς ἐνέργειαν; οὐ βλέπεις τὰ φυτάρια, τὰ στρουθάρια, τοὺς μύρμηκας, τοὺς ἀράχνας, τὰς μελίσσας τὸ ἴδιον ποιούσας, τὸ καθ’ αὑτὰς συγκροτούσας κόσμον; ἔπειτα σὺ οὐ θέλεις τὰ ἀνθρωπικὰ ποιεῖν; οὐ τρέχεις ἐπὶ τὸ κατὰ τὴν σὴν φύσιν; ἀλλὰ δεῖ καὶ ἀναπαύεσθαι. φημὶ κἀγώ· ἔδωκε μέντοι καὶ τούτου μέτρα ἡ φύσις ἔδωκε μέντοι καὶ τοῦ ἐσθίειν καὶ πίνειν καὶ ὅμως σὺ ὑπὲρ τὰ μέτρα, ὑπὲρ τὰ ἀρκοῦντα προχωρεῖς, ἐν δὲ ταῖς πράξεσιν οὐκέτι, ἀλλ’ ἐντὸς τοῦ δυνατοῦ. οὐ γὰρ φιλεῖς σεαυτόν, ἐπεί τοι καὶ τὴν φύσιν ἄν σου καὶ τὸ βούλημα ταύτης ἐφίλεις. ἀλλ’ οἵ γε τὰς τέχνας ἑαυτῶν φιλοῦντες συγκατατήκονται τοῖς κατ’ αὐτὰς ἔργοις ἄλουτοι καὶ ἄσιτοι· σὺ τὴν φύσιν τὴν σαυτοῦ ἔλασσον τιμᾷς ἢ ὁ τορευτὴς τὴν τορευτικὴν ἢ ὁ ὀρχηστὴς τὴν ὀρχηστικὴν ἢ ὁ φιλάργυρος τὸ ἀργύριον ἢ ὁ κενόδοξος τὸ δοξάριον; καὶ οὗτοι, ὅταν προσπαθῶσιν, οὔτε φαγεῖν οὔτε κοιμηθῆναι θέλουσι μᾶλλον ἢ ταῦτα συναύξειν, πρὸς ἃ διαφέρονται· σοὶ δὲ αἱ κοινωνικαὶ πράξεις εὐτελέστεραι φαίνονται καὶ ἥσσονος σπουδῆς ἄξιαι;

members.text:
Use thyself; as often, as thou seest any man do anything,
presently (if it be possible) to say unto thyself, What is this man's
end in this his action? But begin this course with thyself first of all,
and diligently examine thyself concerning whatsoever thou doest.
members.english: Train yourself, as far as you can, with everything that anyone does, to ask in your own mind: “To what end is this person doing this?” But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.
members.greek: Ἔθισον ἐπὶ παντός, ὡς οἷόν τε, τοῦ πρασσομένου ὑπό τινος ἐπιζητεῖν κατὰ σαυτόν· οὗτος τοῦτο ἐπὶ τί ἀναφέρει; ἄρχου δὲ ἀπὸ σαυτοῦ καὶ σαυτὸν πρῶτον ἐξέταζε.

members.text:
Is my reason, and understanding sufficient for this, or no? If it be
sufficient, without any private applause, or public ostentation as of an
instrument, which by nature I am provided of, I will make use of it for
the work in hand, as of an instrument, which by nature I am provided of.
if it be not, and that otherwise it belong not unto me particularly as
a private duty, I will either give it over, and leave it to some other
that can better effect it: or I will endeavour it; but with the help
of some other, who with the joint help of my reason, is able to bring
somewhat to pass, that will now be seasonable and useful for the common
good. For whatsoever I do either by myself, or with some other, the
only thing that I must intend, is, that it be good and expedient for
the public. For as for praise, consider how many who once were much
commended, are now already quite forgotten, yea they that commended
them, how even they themselves are long since dead and gone. Be not
therefore ashamed, whensoever thou must use the help of others. For
whatsoever it be that lieth upon thee to effect, thou must propose it
unto thyself, as the scaling of walls is unto a soldier. And what if
thou through either lameness or some other impediment art not able to
reach unto the top of the battlements alone, which with the help of
another thou mayst; wilt thou therefore give it over, or go about it
with less courage and alacrity, because thou canst not effect it all
alone?
members.english:
Is my mind enough for this or not? If it is enough, I use it for the work as a tool given by the nature of the whole. If it is not enough, either I step back from the work in favour of someone who can carry it out better, unless for some other reason it is my duty, or I do it as best I can, taking on to help me someone who, by making use of my ruling part as well, can do what is timely and useful for the community now. For whatever I do, by myself or with another, must be directed to this alone: what is useful to the community and fits well with it.

How many who were much sung of have already been handed over to forgetting, and how many who sang of them are long since out of the way.

Do not be ashamed of being helped. For what is set before you is to do what falls to you, like a soldier at the storming of a wall. What then, if you are lame and cannot climb up onto the battlement alone, but with another it is possible?

members.text:
At thy first encounter with any one, say presently to thyself:
This man, what are his opinions concerning that which is good or evil?
as concerning pain, pleasure, and the causes of both; concerning honour,
and dishonour, concerning life and death? thus and thus. Now if it be
no wonder that a man should have such and such opinions, how can it be
a wonder that he should do such and such things? I will remember then,
that he cannot but do as he doth, holding those opinions that he doth.
Remember, that as it is a shame for any man to wonder that a fig tree
should bear figs, so also to wonder that the world should bear anything,
whatsoever it is which in the ordinary course of nature it may bear.
To a physician also and to a pilot it is a shame either for the one to
wonder, that such and such a one should have an ague; or for the other,
that the winds should prove Contrary.
members.english:
Whoever you meet, say to yourself at once, beforehand: “What principles does this person hold about what is good and what is bad? For if they hold principles of such-and-such a kind about pleasure and pain and the things that produce each, and about fame, disrepute, death, life, it will seem to me nothing surprising or strange if they do such-and-such things, and I will remember that they are compelled to do so.”

Remember that, just as it is shameful to find it strange if the fig tree bears figs, so it is if the universe bears such-and-such things that it is a bearer of. And for a doctor and a helmsman too it is shameful to find it strange if so-and-so has come down with a fever or if a contrary wind has got up.
members.greek:
Ὧι ἂν ἐντυγχάνῃς, εὐθὺς σαυτῷ πρόλεγε· οὖτος τίνα δόγματα ἔχει περὶ ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν; εἰ γὰρ περὶ ἡδονῆς καὶ πόνου καὶ τῶν ποιητικῶν ἑκατέρου καὶ περὶ δόξης, ἀδοξίας, θανάτου, ζωῆς, τοιάδε τινὰ δόγματα ἔχει, οὐδὲν θαυμαστὸν· ἢ ξένον μοι δόξει, ἐὰν τάδε τινὰ ποιῇ, καὶ μεμνήσομαι ὅτι ἀναγκάζεται οὕτως ποιεῖν.

Μέμνησο ὅτι, ὥσπερ αἰσχρόν ἐστι ξενίζεσθαι, εἰ ἡ συκῆ σῦκα φέρει, οὕτως, εἰ ὁ κόσμος τάδε τινὰ φέρει ὧν ἐστι φορός· καὶ ἰατρῷ δὲ καὶ κυβερνήτῃ αἰσχρὸν ξενίζεσθαι, εἰ πεπύρεχεν οὗτος ἢ εἰ ἀντίπνοια γέγονεν.

members.text:
When thou hast done well, and another is benefited by thy action,
must thou like a very fool look for a third thing besides, as that
it may appear unto others also that thou hast done well, or that thou
mayest in time, receive one good turn for another? No man useth to be
weary of that which is beneficial unto him. But every action according
to nature, is beneficial. Be not weary then of doing that which is
beneficial unto thee, whilst it is so unto others.
members.english:
When you have done good and another has had good done to them, why do you look for a third thing beside these, as fools do: to be seen to have done good as well, or to get a return?

No one tires of being benefited, and benefit is action according to nature. So do not tire of being benefited, in that you give benefit.
members.greek:
Ὅταν σὺ εὖ πεποιηκὼς ᾖς καὶ ἄλλος εὖ πεπονθώς, τί ἐπιζητεῖς τρίτον παρὰ ταῦτα, ὥσπερ οἱ μωροί, τὸ καὶ δόξαι εὖ πεποιηκέναι ἢ τὸ ἀμοιβῆς τυχεῖν;

Οὐδεὶς κάμνει ὠφελούμενος, ὠφέλεια δὲ πρᾶξις κατὰ φύσιν·μὴ οὖν κάμνε ὠφελούμενος, ἐν ᾧ ὠφελεῖς.

members.text:
Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready
to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation. Others
there be, who though they stand not upon retaliation, to require any,
yet they think with themselves nevertheless, that such a one is their
debtor, and they know as their word is what they have done. Others again
there be, who when they have done any such thing, do not so much as
know what they have done; but are like unto the vine, which beareth her
grapes, and when once she hath borne her own proper fruit, is contented
and seeks for no further recompense. As a horse after a race, and a
hunting dog when he hath hunted, and a bee when she hath made her honey,
look not for applause and commendation; so neither doth that man that
rightly doth understand his own nature when he hath done a good turn:
but from one doth proceed to do another, even as the vine after she hath
once borne fruit in her own proper season, is ready for another time.
Thou therefore must be one of them, who what they do, barely do it
without any further thought, and are in a manner insensible of what they
do. 'Nay but,' will some reply perchance, 'this very thing a rational
man is bound unto, to understand what it is, that he doeth.' For it
is the property, say they, of one that is naturally sociable, to be
sensible, that he doth operate sociably: nay, and to desire, that the
party him self that is sociably dealt with, should be sensible of it
too. I answer, That which thou sayest is true indeed, but the true
meaning of that which is said, thou dost not understand. And therefore
art thou one of those first, whom I mentioned. For they also are led by
a probable appearance of reason. But if thou dost desire to understand
truly what it is that is said, fear not that thou shalt therefore give
over any sociable action.
members.english: One kind of person, when they have done someone a good turn, is ready also to charge the favour to that person’s account. Another is not ready to do that, but all the same thinks of the other, privately, as a debtor, and knows what they have done. A third, in a way, does not even know what they have done, but is like a vine that has borne its grapes and looks for nothing more after it has once borne its own fruit. A horse that has run, a dog that has tracked, a bee that has made honey, and a human being who has done good, do not shout about it, but pass on to another thing, as a vine passes on to bearing its grapes again in season. So one must be among these, the ones who in a way do it without being aware of it. “Yes, but this is the very thing one must be aware of. For it is characteristic of the social being,” someone says, “to perceive that it is acting socially and, by Zeus, to want its fellow to perceive it too.” What you say is true, but you take what is being said now in the wrong way. Because of this you will be one of those I mentioned before, for they too are led astray by a certain plausible reasoning. But if you want to understand what it is that is being said, do not be afraid that because of it you will leave undone any social act.
members.greek: Ὁ μέν τίς ἐστιν, ὅταν τι δεξιὸν περί τινα πράξῃ, πρόχειρος καὶ λογίσασθαι αὐτῷ τὴν χάριν. ὁ δὲ πρὸς μὲν τοῦτο οὐ πρόχειρος, ἄλλως μέντοι παρ’ ἑαυτῷ ὡς περὶ χρεώστου διανοεῖται καὶ οἶδεν ὃ πεποίηκεν. ὁ δέ τις τρόπον τινὰ οὐδὲ οἶδεν ὃ πεποίηκεν, ἀλλὰ ὅμοιός ἐστιν ἀμπέλῳ βότρυν ἐνεγκούσῃ καὶ μηδὲν ἄλλο προσεπιζητούσῃ μετὰ τὸ ἅπαξ τὸν ἴδιον καρπὸν ἐνηνοχέναι. ἵππος δραμών, κύων ἰχνεύσας, μέλισσα μέλι ποιήσασα, ἄνθρωπος δ’ εὖ ποιήσας οὐκ ἐπιβοᾶται, ἀλλὰ μεταβαίνει ἐφ’ ἕτερον, ὡς ἄμπελος ἐπὶ τὸ πάλιν ἐν τῇ ὥρᾳ τὸν βότρυν ἐνεγκεῖν. ἐν τούτοις οὗν δεῖ εἶναι τοῖς τρόπον τινὰ ἀπαρακολουθήτως αὐτὸ ποιοῦσι.— ναί ἀλλ’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο δεῖ παρακολουθεῖν· ἴδιον γάρ, φησί, τοῦ κοινωνικοῦ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι, ὅτι κοινωνικῶς ἐνεργεῖ, καὶ νὴ Δία βούλεσθαι καὶ τὸν κοινωνὸν αἰσθέσθαι.—ἀληθὲς μέν ἐστιν ὃ λέγεις, τὸ δὲ νῦν λεγόμενον παρεκδέχῃ· διὰ τοῦτο ἔσῃ εἶς ἐκείνων ὦν πρότερον ἐπεμνήσθην· καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖνοι λογικῇ τινι πιθανότητι παράγονται. ἐὰν δὲ θελήσῃς συνεῖναι τί ποτέ ἐστι τὸ λεγόμενον, μὴ φοβοῦ, μὴ παρὰ τοῦτο παραλίπῃς τι ἔργον κοινωνικόν.

members.text:
Whatsoever it is that thou goest about, consider of it by thyself,
and ask thyself, What? because I shall do this no more when I am dead,
should therefore death seem grievous unto me?
members.english: At each of the things you do, one by one, stop and ask yourself whether death is something terrible because of being deprived of this.
members.greek: Κατὰ μέρος ἐφ’ ἑκάστου ὧν ποιεῖς ἐφιστάνων ἐπερώτα σεαυτὸν εἰ ὁ θάνατος δεινὸν διὰ τὸ τούτου στέρεσθαι.

members.text:
We all work to one effect, some willingly, and with a rational
apprehension of what we do: others without any such knowledge. As I
think Heraclitus in a place speaketh of them that sleep, that even they
do work in their kind, and do confer to the general operations of the
world. One man therefore doth co-operate after one sort, and another
after another sort; but even he that doth murmur, and to his power doth
resist and hinder; even he as much as any doth co-operate. For of such
also did the world stand in need. Now do thou consider among which of
these thou wilt rank thyself. For as for him who is the Administrator
of all, he will make good use of thee whether thou wilt or no, and make
thee (as a part and member of the whole) so to co-operate with him,
that whatsoever thou doest, shall turn to the furtherance of his own
counsels, and resolutions. But be not thou for shame such a part of the
whole, as that vile and ridiculous verse (which Chrysippus in a place
doth mention) is a part of the comedy.
members.english: We are all working together towards one finished result, some of us knowingly and with awareness, others without attending to it, just as Heraclitus, I think, says that even those who are asleep are workers and fellow workers in the things that happen in the universe. One works together in one way, another in another, and, into the bargain, so does even the one who finds fault and the one who tries to stand against the things that happen and do away with them, for the universe had need of such a person too. What remains, then, is for you to understand among which of them you are placing yourself. For the one who governs the whole will in any case use you well, and will take you in as some part of the fellow workers and of those who help the work along. But you, do not become the kind of part that the cheap and ridiculous line is in the play, the one Chrysippus mentions.
members.greek: Πάντες εἰς ἓν ἀποτέλεσμα συνεργοῦμεν, οἱ μὲν εἰδότως καὶ παρακολουθητικῶς, οἱ δὲ ἀνεπιστάτως, ὥσπερ καὶ τοὺς καθεύδοντας, οἶμαι, ὁ Ἡράκλειτος ἐργάτας εἶναι λέγει καὶ συνεργοὺς τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ γινομένων. ἄλλος δὲ κατ’ ἄλλο συνεργεῖ, ἐκ περιουσίας δὲ καὶ ὁ μεμφόμενος καὶ ὁ ἀντιβαίνειν πειρώμενος καὶ ἀναιρεῖν τὰ γινόμενα· καὶ γὰρ τοῦ τοιούτου ἔχρῃζεν ὁ κόσμος. λοιπὸν οὖν σύνες εἰς τίνας σεαυτὸν κατατάσσεις· ἐκεῖνος μὲν γὰρ πάντως σοι καλῶς χρήσεται ὁ τὰ ὅλα διοικῶν καὶ παραδέξεταί σε ὡς μέρος τι τῶν συνεργῶν καὶ συνεργητικῶν, ἀλλὰ σὺ μὴ τοιοῦτο μέρος γένῃ, οἷος ὁ εὐτελὴς καὶ γελοῖος στίχος ἐν τῷ δράματι, οὗ Χρύσιππος μέμνηται.

members.text:
Stir up thy mind, and recall thy wits again from thy natural
dreams, and visions, and when thou art perfectly awoken, and canst
perceive that they were but dreams that troubled thee, as one newly
awakened out of another kind of sleep look upon these worldly things
with the same mind as thou didst upon those, that thou sawest in thy
sleep.
members.english: Sober up and call yourself back. And when you have woken up again and understood that it was dreams that were troubling you, then, awake again, look at these things as you looked at those.
members.greek: Ἀνάνηφε καὶ ἀνακαλοῦ σεαυτὸν καὶ ἐξυπνισθεὶς πάλιν καὶ ἐννοήσας ὅτι ὄνειροί σοι ἠνώχλουν, πάλιν ἐγρηγορὼς βλέπε ταῦτα, ὡς ἐκεῖνα ἔβλεπες.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 10.15 is 10.13, 8.11 is 8.12, 8.13 is 8.14–15, 7.5 is 7.5–7, 7.43 is 7.73–74, 6.37 is 6.42 and 6.29 is 6.31; 8.2, 5.1, 10.37, 5.6 and 10.29 have the same number.
Joins the questions of 8.2 and 10.29 by their form and by death, which both bring in. The words “with my death in mind” are the editor’s summary; each passage’s own question is kept as it stands.

Brings 8.2’s “What more do I look for” into the claim on doing good, though 8.2 speaks of the work in hand, not a good turn; and reads 7.43’s “do not tire of being benefited, in that you give benefit” as not tiring of doing good.

Keeps 10.15 said once and quotes it as printed, “is blamed”. The translators note from memory that the manuscripts may read “is done”; with that reading the question is whether it matters that someone else does what is right.
articles.limit: Claims 1 and 2 come near Article 5 (made for reason and fellowship) and Article 1 (each act aims at the common good); claim 3 near Articles 9 and 10 (each thing done as if leaving life now); claim 4 repeats Articles 9 and 11 (no show, no witness) and Article 19’s said-once 9.43d (looking for something back); and claim 5 is close to Article 19’s claims 1 and 6 (what they took to be good or bad, they can do nothing else, then I turn to myself). What this section adds is when and how: getting up in the morning; a question at each action; after a good act, passing on to the next as a vine bears again; and the question about others asked of everyone I meet, not only of someone who wrongs me. The middle of the statement joins questions that differ in content (regret, death, another’s aim) by their form alone.
